Follow-up: If CNNs are efficient, why use Vision Transformers? Self-attention directly connects distant patches through content-dependent weights. ViTs benefit from large-scale pretraining and flexible global interactions, but standard global attention is costly at high resolution.

Follow-up: Does a CNN provide translation invariance or equivariance? Convolution principally provides equivariance; a classification head may encourage invariance through global pooling. They are not interchangeable.

Follow-up: Why not use a huge MLP with unlimited compute and data? An expressive MLP can approximate complex visual functions. CNNs still offer an efficient parameterization and useful spatial priors; unlimited resources do not establish that either architecture universally wins.

63. What is the difference between convolution and self-attention?

Convolution applies shared, learned local kernels; their weights do not depend on the current input content. Self-attention computes content-dependent interactions:

Attention⁡(Q,K,V)=softmax⁡(QK⊤/dk)V.\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V.Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QK⊤/dk​​)V.

Global attention connects every token pair in one layer, whereas local convolutions expand their receptive field across layers. Its core attention cost is O(N2d)O(N^2d)O(N2d); convolution cost is approximately O(HWk2CinCout)O(HWk^2C_{in}C_{out})O(HWk2Cin​Cout​). Projection/MLP costs and hardware also matter. CNNs impose stronger local spatial priors; attention offers more flexible interactions.

64. Explain ResNet. Why do residual connections help?

A residual block learns a correction to an identity path:

y=x+F(x),∂L∂x=(I+JF(x))⊤∂L∂y.y=x+F(x),\qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial x} =\left(I+J_F(x)\right)^\top\frac{\partial L}{\partial y}.y=x+F(x),∂x∂L​=(I+JF​(x))⊤∂y∂L​.

The identity term supplies a direct gradient path, making deep networks easier to optimize and allowing a block to approximate identity by learning F(x)≈0F(x)\approx0F(x)≈0. It does not guarantee gradients never vanish or explode. If dimensions change, use a projection shortcut y=P(x)+F(x)y=P(x)+F(x)y=P(x)+F(x).

65. BatchNorm vs LayerNorm — what's the difference?

Both use x^=(x−μ)/σ2+ϵ\hat x=(x-\mu)/\sqrt{\sigma^2+\epsilon}x^=(x−μ)/σ2+ϵ​ followed by learned scale and shift. For CNN activations [B,C,H,W][B,C,H,W][B,C,H,W], BatchNorm usually computes each channel's training statistics over (B,H,W)(B,H,W)(B,H,W) and uses running statistics at evaluation. LayerNorm normalizes each example over specified feature dimensions; for Transformer tensors [B,N,d][B,N,d][B,N,d], typically over ddd independently at each token. BN can be sensitive to small or nonrepresentative batches; LN does not depend on other examples, which suits variable-length token processing.

66. Why does Vision Transformer divide images into patches?

Patches convert an image into a manageable token sequence:

[B,C,H,W]→[B,N,P2C]→[B,N,d],N=(H/P)(W/P).[B,C,H,W]\rightarrow[B,N,P^2C]\rightarrow[B,N,d], \qquad N=(H/P)(W/P).[B,C,H,W]→[B,N,P2C]→[B,N,d],N=(H/P)(W/P).

For 224×224224\times224224×224 inputs, P=16P=16P=16 gives N=196N=196N=196; P=8P=8P=8 gives N=784N=784N=784. Ignoring a possible CLS token, halving patch size yields four times as many tokens and 16 times the quadratic attention term, not necessarily 16 times total runtime. Smaller patches preserve finer detail. High-resolution options include window attention, hierarchical features, token pruning/merging, and efficient attention variants.

67. How does positional encoding work in ViT?

Self-attention alone is permutation equivariant and does not identify spatial order. Add positional information to patch embeddings:

Z0=XpatchWE+Epos,Epos∈RN×d.Z_0=X_{patch}W_E+E_{pos},\qquad E_{pos}\in\mathbb R^{N\times d}.Z0​=Xpatch​WE​+Epos​,Epos​∈RN×d.

Learned or sinusoidal absolute embeddings can encode grid locations; relative position biases encode relationships between locations. A flattened patch grid can still represent two-dimensional position. Absolute embeddings often need grid interpolation when resolution changes.

68. What are the advantages and limitations of ViT compared with CNN?

ViTs flexibly model global dependencies and often benefit greatly from large-scale pretraining. Standard global attention becomes expensive as resolution increases, and weaker local priors can increase data/training requirements. CNNs efficiently exploit local structure and naturally produce multiscale features. Performance depends on dataset, training recipe, architecture, and deployment constraints; neither universally dominates.

69. How would you handle variable image resolutions?

Choose resize/crop for fixed-size inputs, or aspect-ratio-preserving resize plus padding when distortion or cropping is harmful. Use masks where padding would otherwise affect computation. Multiscale training/features and high-resolution crops preserve small-object detail. For ViTs, adapt absolute position embeddings by interpolating the patch grid. Explain the accuracy, memory, aspect-ratio, and batching trade-offs.

70. What is transfer learning? When should the backbone be frozen?

Reuse pretrained representations for a new task. A frozen backbone plus a trained head is a linear probe when the head is linear; partial or full fine-tuning adapts more features. Start frozen when labels/compute are limited or representations already transfer well. Consider unfreezing with sufficient data or substantial domain mismatch, often using a smaller backbone learning rate. Select the strategy on validation performance and monitor overfitting or forgetting.

71. What is the difference between classification, detection, and segmentation?

Classification predicts image-level labels, e.g. [B,K][B,K][B,K] logits. Detection predicts a variable-size set of class labels and bounding boxes. Semantic segmentation predicts a class for each pixel, often [B,K,H,W][B,K,H,W][B,K,H,W] logits; instance segmentation also separates individual objects with instance masks. Choose image classification if presence/absence is sufficient, detection for object locations, and segmentation when precise boundaries are required.

Training, Optimization, and Loss Functions

72. Why use cross-entropy instead of MSE for image classification?

Cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli or categorical model, so it directly rewards probability assigned to the correct class. For binary labels, use a sigmoid probability ppp; for mutually exclusive classes, use softmax probabilities pkp_kpk​:

LBCE=−[ylog⁡p+(1−y)log⁡(1−p)],LCE=−∑k=1Kyklog⁡pk.\mathcal L_{\mathrm{BCE}}=-[y\log p+(1-y)\log(1-p)], \qquad \mathcal L_{\mathrm{CE}}=-\sum_{k=1}^{K}y_k\log p_k.LBCE​=−[ylogp+(1−y)log(1−p)],LCE​=−k=1∑K​yk​logpk​.

MSE on probabilities is possible, but cross-entropy with sigmoid/softmax has useful likelihood and gradient properties; for a softmax logit, its gradient is pk−ykp_k-y_kpk​−yk​. Independent multi-label classes normally use one sigmoid and a BCE term per class, rather than one softmax.

73. When would you use focal loss?

Focal loss is useful when numerous easy examples dominate training, such as background candidates in dense detection. It reduces their contribution while preserving more weight for difficult examples:

Lfocal=−αt(1−pt)γlog⁡pt,pt={p,y=11−p,y=0.\mathcal L_{\mathrm{focal}}=-\alpha_t(1-p_t)^\gamma\log p_t, \quad p_t=\begin{cases}p,&y=1\\1-p,&y=0.\end{cases}Lfocal​=−αt​(1−pt​)γlogpt​,pt​={p,1−p,​y=1y=0.​

Here γ>0\gamma>0γ>0 controls the focusing effect, and αt\alpha_tαt​ can balance classes; it does not remove the need to inspect noisy labels and evaluate minority-class performance.

74. What is label smoothing, and why does it work?

Replace a one-hot target with a slightly softened distribution:

qk=(1−ε)1[k=y]+εK,L=−∑kqklog⁡pk.q_k=(1-\varepsilon)\mathbf 1[k=y]+\frac{\varepsilon}{K}, \qquad \mathcal L=-\sum_k q_k\log p_k.qk​=(1−ε)1[k=y]+Kε​,L=−k∑​qk​logpk​.

This discourages driving the true-class logit arbitrarily far above all others and can regularize training. Its effects on accuracy and calibration depend on the setting; smoothing is not a guarantee of well-calibrated probabilities.

75. Adam vs SGD with momentum — which would you choose?

Adam uses running gradient moments to adapt updates per parameter; AdamW additionally decouples weight decay. SGD with momentum uses a shared learning rate and an accumulated update direction, and can work very well for CNN training with an appropriate schedule. I would compare validation quality, tuning cost, convergence, and optimizer-state memory rather than claim that one always generalizes better.

76. Why is weight decay useful? Is it the same as L2 regularization?

Weight decay shrinks parameters and can help control overfitting. For ordinary SGD, an L2 penalty λ2∥w∥2\frac{\lambda}{2}\|w\|^22λ​∥w∥2 gives

w←(1−ηλ)w−η∇wLdata,w\leftarrow (1-\eta\lambda)w-\eta\nabla_w\mathcal L_{\mathrm{data}},w←(1−ηλ)w−η∇w​Ldata​,

which is the corresponding multiplicative decay update. With adaptive optimization, adding λw\lambda wλw to the gradient changes the adaptive statistics too; AdamW instead applies decay separately, so the two procedures are not generally equivalent.

77. How would you address overfitting in a vision model?

First check a genuine training–validation gap, label quality, duplicate leakage, and whether the split reflects deployment. Then consider task-preserving augmentation, weight decay, early stopping, pretrained features, a smaller model, or additional representative data. Change a controlled set of factors and evaluate both aggregate and important slice metrics.

78. How does contrastive learning work, and what is InfoNCE?

Contrastive learning brings compatible representations closer and separates alternatives. For paired image/text embeddings (vi,ti)(v_i,t_i)(vi​,ti​), image-to-text InfoNCE treats the paired text as the positive and other batch texts as negatives:

LiI→T=−log⁡exp⁡(sim⁡(vi,ti)/τ)∑j=1Bexp⁡(sim⁡(vi,tj)/τ).\mathcal L_i^{I\to T} =-\log\frac{\exp(\operatorname{sim}(v_i,t_i)/\tau)} {\sum_{j=1}^{B}\exp(\operatorname{sim}(v_i,t_j)/\tau)}.LiI→T​=−log∑j=1B​exp(sim(vi​,tj​)/τ)exp(sim(vi​,ti​)/τ)​.

Here BBB is batch size and τ\tauτ is temperature; CLIP-style training also includes the reverse text-to-image loss. Larger candidate sets provide more negatives, but their semantic quality matters as much as their count.

  • What happens when temperature becomes very small? The softmax concentrates on the most similar candidates, emphasizing hard mistakes; overly small values can amplify noisy negatives and make optimization unstable.
  • Why is L2 normalization applied to embeddings? With unit vectors, dot product equals cosine similarity, so increasing vector norms cannot improve scores; temperature separately controls score sharpness.
  • What happens if two different samples have the same semantic meaning? They may be false negatives, and forcing them apart damages the representation; deduplication, multi-positive objectives, or masking known matches can help.
  • How would you build hard negatives for visual search? Retrieve visually similar but genuinely nonmatching items, then verify relevance using labels or review; exclude duplicates and alternative valid matches before training.

79. How does negative sampling affect training?

Random negatives provide broad coverage but may become too easy; hard negatives teach finer distinctions but can include false negatives. In-batch negatives are efficient because embeddings are reused, while mined negatives can target current retrieval errors. Mix negative types and check whether improvements persist on a representative evaluation set rather than only a curated hard set.

80. What data augmentation strategies are useful for CV?

Common choices include random crops, flips, color jitter, MixUp, and CutMix. Transformations must preserve the task: a crop can remove a safety-relevant object, and a flip can alter text or direction labels. Detection boxes and segmentation masks must undergo the same geometry, while MixUp/CutMix require appropriate target mixing.

81. How do you handle severe class imbalance?

Use class weighting, resampling, or focal loss when justified, and inspect precision–recall behavior and per-class recall rather than relying on accuracy. Select a threshold using validation data to reflect false-positive/false-negative costs and review capacity. Reweighting or resampling changes the effective training distribution, so separately check calibration and the class prevalence expected in deployment.

Classical CV Tasks and Model Design

82. How would you design an image classification system from scratch?

Define whether labels are mutually exclusive or multi-label, annotation rules, evaluation slices, and deployment constraints. Split by the relevant user, asset, or time boundary, then start with a pretrained backbone and a small head: I→fθ(I)∈Rd→Wfθ(I)+b∈RKI\to f_\theta(I)\in\mathbb R^d\to Wf_\theta(I)+b\in\mathbb R^KI→fθ​(I)∈Rd→Wfθ​(I)+b∈RK. Train with CE or per-class BCE as appropriate, evaluate per-class metrics and calibration, and measure serving latency.

Detection design follow-up: How would you detect inappropriate objects in Roblox screenshots? First ask whether an image-level decision is sufficient or whether boxes/masks are required; do not choose YOLO before defining the output. For localization, compare detectors or segmenters while explicitly handling small objects, occlusion, low resolution, and different rendering styles. Set thresholds against missed violations, false accusations, and human-review cost, then evaluate those failure slices.

83. What is the difference between one-stage and two-stage object detectors?

One-stage detectors such as YOLO predict classes and locations directly from image features. Two-stage detectors such as Faster R-CNN first propose candidate regions, then classify and refine them. Compare measured accuracy, latency, object sizes, and deployment hardware; two-stage is not universally more accurate, nor is one-stage universally the right choice.

84. What are IoU and Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS)?

Intersection over Union measures overlap between predicted and reference regions:

IoU⁡(A,B)=∣A∩B∣∣A∪B∣.\operatorname{IoU}(A,B)=\frac{|A\cap B|}{|A\cup B|}.IoU(A,B)=∣A∪B∣∣A∩B∣​.

NMS sorts candidate boxes by confidence, keeps a high-scoring box, and suppresses sufficiently overlapping alternatives, usually within a class. Its threshold trades duplicate removal against suppressing distinct nearby objects, especially in crowded scenes.

85. How do you evaluate object detection?

Evaluate confidence-ranked predictions using class labels and one-to-one matching to ground-truth boxes at a specified IoU threshold. A duplicate prediction or a poorly localized box can count as a false positive, so detection AP is not merely classification AP on image labels. Report mAP across classes and, where specified, IoU thresholds, together with size-specific recall and latency; explicitly distinguish AP50 from COCO-style AP averaged over IoU 0.50–0.95.

86. What is the difference between semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation?

Semantic segmentation assigns each pixel a class but does not distinguish two objects of the same class. Instance segmentation produces a separate mask for each countable object. Panoptic segmentation combines both: every pixel receives a semantic label, and countable “thing” objects also receive instance identities, while “stuff” such as sky is not split into object instances.

87. How would you handle small objects in high-resolution images?

Avoid shrinking the entire image until relevant objects disappear: consider higher resolution, overlapping tiles/crops, and multi-scale features. Match the detection head's feature stride and training data to expected object sizes. Measure the added compute and merge detections across overlapping tiles without double-counting objects.

88. What is Feature Pyramid Network (FPN)?

FPN combines semantically rich, low-resolution backbone features with finer-resolution features through top-down upsampling and lateral connections. A typical pyramid has P3:[B,d,H/8,W/8]P_3:[B,d,H/8,W/8]P3​:[B,d,H/8,W/8], P4:[B,d,H/16,W/16]P_4:[B,d,H/16,W/16]P4​:[B,d,H/16,W/16], and P5:[B,d,H/32,W/32]P_5:[B,d,H/32,W/32]P5​:[B,d,H/32,W/32]. Heads use these scales to detect differently sized objects, giving small objects finer spatial support without discarding high-level semantics.

89. How would you build an image similarity search engine?

Encode images into normalized embeddings, store them with asset metadata in an approximate-nearest-neighbor index, and retrieve candidates using cosine similarity or equivalent unit-vector distance. Optionally apply filters and a more expensive reranker to the shortlist. Evaluate Recall@K against relevance judgments, serving latency, index freshness, and representation drift; separate visual similarity from the product's actual relevance definition.

90. How would you detect out-of-distribution images?

Consider embedding distance from training examples, calibrated uncertainty, or energy-based scores, and choose thresholds using representative in-domain and OOD validation data. Include unfamiliar rendering styles, corrupted inputs, and new content categories, then evaluate OOD recall versus false alarms on normal traffic. High maximum softmax probability does not guarantee an input is familiar; uncertain cases may require abstention or review.

91. What is the difference between zero-shot and fine-tuned classification?

In CLIP-style zero-shot classification, encode class descriptions and compare an image embedding with those text embeddings without training on labeled examples from the target task. Fine-tuning updates some or all model parameters using target-domain data; a frozen encoder with a trained linear head is another useful baseline. Compare domain accuracy, annotation cost, compute, and robustness, and keep evaluation data separate from prompt and hyperparameter selection.

VLM and multimodal learning

92. How is CLIP trained from scratch?

Train an image encoder and a text encoder on paired images and captions, projecting both outputs into a shared embedding space. Normalize embeddings and use symmetric image-to-text and text-to-image contrastive losses so matching pairs receive higher similarity than mismatches; semantically related in-batch examples can be false negatives.

vi=fI(Ii)∥fI(Ii)∥2,tj=fT(Tj)∥fT(Tj)∥2,sij=vi⊤tjτ,LCLIP=12(LI→T+LT→I).v_i=\frac{f_I(I_i)}{\|f_I(I_i)\|_2},\qquad t_j=\frac{f_T(T_j)}{\|f_T(T_j)\|_2},\qquad s_{ij}=\frac{v_i^\top t_j}{\tau},\qquad \mathcal L_{\mathrm{CLIP}}=\tfrac12(\mathcal L_{I\to T}+\mathcal L_{T\to I}).vi​=∥fI​(Ii​)∥2​fI​(Ii​)​,tj​=∥fT​(Tj​)∥2​fT​(Tj​)​,sij​=τvi⊤​tj​​,LCLIP​=21​(LI→T​+LT→I​).

93. What is the difference between CLIP and a generative VLM?

CLIP is a dual-encoder representation model: similarity supports retrieval and text-prompt-based classification, but CLIP itself does not generate answers. A generative VLM conditions a language model on visual information and produces text autoregressively; generation adds flexibility but also decoding cost and hallucination risk.

94. How does a vision-language model connect the visual encoder to an LLM?

A common architecture projects visual patch features into the LLM hidden dimension, then combines visual and text embeddings for conditional generation. A resampler or Q-Former can instead extract a smaller set of visual tokens, while other architectures introduce cross-attention.

I→vision encoderZv∈RB×Nv×dv,Hv=ZvWp∈RB×Nv×dLLM,Wp∈Rdv×dLLM.I\xrightarrow{\text{vision encoder}}Z_v\in\mathbb R^{B\times N_v\times d_v},\qquad H_v=Z_vW_p\in\mathbb R^{B\times N_v\times d_{\mathrm{LLM}}},\quad W_p\in\mathbb R^{d_v\times d_{\mathrm{LLM}}}.Ivision encoder​Zv​∈RB×Nv​×dv​,Hv​=Zv​Wp​∈RB×Nv​×dLLM​,Wp​∈Rdv​×dLLM​.
(Hv,text embeddings)→LLMp(answer∣I,prompt).(H_v,\text{text embeddings})\xrightarrow{\text{LLM}}p(\text{answer}\mid I,\text{prompt}).(Hv​,text embeddings)LLM​p(answer∣I,prompt).

95. Why is a visual projector needed?

It adapts visual feature dimensions and distributions to the language model's input representation. A linear layer or MLP supplies a trainable interface, but compatible dimensions alone do not guarantee semantic alignment: the interface must learn from suitable image-text supervision.

96. When would you freeze the vision encoder versus fine-tune it?

Freeze it initially when target data is limited, existing features transfer well, or compute is constrained. If evaluation reveals domain-specific failures, compare tuning later layers, adapters or LoRA, and full fine-tuning; control overfitting and forgetting with held-out domains and a suitable learning rate.

97. What is the purpose of instruction tuning in a VLM?

Instruction tuning teaches the model to answer a user's request using the image, rather than merely align image and text embeddings. In answer-only supervised fine-tuning, teacher forcing supplies the preceding correct tokens and a mask excludes prompt and visual positions from the loss.

LSFT=−∑i,tmitlog⁡pθ(ait∣Ii,qi,ai,<t)∑i,tmit,mit=1 only for supervised answer tokens.\mathcal L_{\mathrm{SFT}}= -\frac{\sum_{i,t}m_{it}\log p_\theta(a_{it}\mid I_i,q_i,a_{i,<t})} {\sum_{i,t}m_{it}},\qquad m_{it}=1\text{ only for supervised answer tokens}.LSFT​=−∑i,t​mit​∑i,t​mit​logpθ​(ait​∣Ii​,qi​,ai,<t​)​,mit​=1 only for supervised answer tokens.

98. How do you reduce visual token count?

Use larger patches, spatial pooling, learned resampling, token merging, or task-aware pruning. These reduce LLM prefill and attention costs, but may remove small objects or text, so evaluate detailed visual tasks rather than only average accuracy.

99. How would you evaluate hallucination in VLMs?

Construct grounded tests for object presence, attributes, spatial relationships, and questions that the image cannot answer. Measure unsupported-claim rates and grounded answer quality using annotated evidence and human review, including negation and out-of-domain cases. Evaluate abstention too, so a model cannot appear reliable merely by refusing every question.

100. Early fusion vs late fusion for multimodal learning?

Early fusion permits interactions between modalities before final prediction, for example through joint token attention; it can capture detailed relationships but increases coupled computation. Late fusion combines independently produced embeddings, predictions, or scores and is easier to cache and modularize, but may miss fine-grained cross-modal interactions. Intermediate fusion is also possible, so define exactly where information is exchanged.

101. How would you adapt a pretrained VLM to a specialized visual domain?

Define the target tasks and curate representative, grounded examples with creator-, source-, or time-separated evaluation sets. Choose contrastive adaptation for retrieval or supervised instruction tuning for answer generation, beginning with a frozen backbone and lightweight trainable components. Compare broader fine-tuning only when justified, and evaluate domain transfer, hallucination, forgetting, and deployment cost.

VLM architecture follow-ups

Why not train the vision encoder and LLM jointly from scratch? Reusing pretrained components saves substantial data and compute and preserves useful representations. Joint training from scratch may be justified with sufficient resources and a strong reason existing representations are unsuitable, but it is not the default for a modest domain dataset.

How do you select image-text pretraining data? Check image-text alignment, diversity, domain coverage, provenance, permissions, and harmful or sensitive content. Deduplicate across training and evaluation sets, remove misleading captions, and inspect minority domains rather than maximizing raw pair count.

Why might a linear projector be sufficient? Strong pretrained visual features may already encode the information the LLM needs, leaving a relatively simple mapping to learn. Test that hypothesis against an MLP or resampler using grounded accuracy and cost; linear capacity is not sufficient for every task.

What if the domain is video rather than images? Encode sampled frames and add temporal positions or temporal fusion so the model can distinguish motion and event order. Compress tokens across space and time, and evaluate short events that coarse sampling might miss.

How would you reduce end-to-end latency on a mobile device? Profile preprocessing, visual encoding, LLM prefill, token decoding, and memory transfers separately. Reduce resolution or visual tokens, use supported quantization and smaller models, and benchmark actual-device latency, memory, thermals, and grounded quality.

Video understanding and video quality

102. How would you build a video classification model?

Begin with sampled frames, a pretrained frame encoder, temporal pooling, and a classification head. Pooling gives a cheap baseline, while temporal models can capture motion and order; split by source video to avoid related clips leaking across sets.

I∈RB×T×C×H×W→frame encoderF∈RB×T×d→temporal meanh=1T∑t=1TFt∈RB×d→headz∈RB×K.I\in\mathbb R^{B\times T\times C\times H\times W} \xrightarrow{\text{frame encoder}}F\in\mathbb R^{B\times T\times d} \xrightarrow{\text{temporal mean}}h=\tfrac1T\sum_{t=1}^TF_t \in\mathbb R^{B\times d} \xrightarrow{\text{head}}z\in\mathbb R^{B\times K}.I∈RB×T×C×H×Wframe encoder​F∈RB×T×dtemporal mean​h=T1​t=1∑T​Ft​∈RB×dhead​z∈RB×K.

103. What is the difference between a 2D CNN and a 3D CNN?

A 2D CNN uses spatial kernels independently on images or frames, whereas a 3D CNN uses kernels spanning time and space. A kernel of size kt×kh×kwk_t\times k_h\times k_wkt​×kh​×kw​ learns local spatiotemporal patterns, but increases computation and depends on the clip's temporal sampling.

104. How do you efficiently sample frames from long videos?

Uniform sampling gives temporal coverage; keyframe, motion-aware, or adaptive sampling can spend more compute on informative intervals. Sparse sampling can entirely miss a brief harmful event, and motion alone does not establish semantic importance. Consider overlapping clips or a cheap dense first pass followed by targeted high-resolution analysis, measuring event recall against compute.

105. How would you model temporal dependencies in video?

Temporal pooling ignores order, RNNs maintain sequential state, 3D convolutions model local motion, and temporal attention connects more distant observations. Choose clip length, sampling rate, and model capacity according to event duration and required ordering information. Include temporal positions for attention and test order-sensitive cases explicitly.

106. How would you build a perceptual video quality prediction model?

First determine whether the task has a pristine reference: full-reference and no-reference prediction have different available inputs. Combine spatial artifacts with temporal degradation, motion, viewing conditions, and source characteristics, then train against subjective scores or pairwise judgments. MOS commonly increases with perceived quality, whereas DMOS often increases with impairment, but verify each dataset's scale and sign; report rank correlation and calibrated prediction error on source-separated splits.

Production CV and model optimization

107. How would you deploy a large vision model under a strict latency budget?

Profile the complete request path, including preprocessing, queueing, inference, and transfers, using realistic hardware and p95/p99 latency. Compare smaller backbones, supported quantization, distillation, caching, and input reduction; batching can improve throughput while increasing waiting time. Asynchronous execution changes scheduling, not necessarily a user's time to result, so measure the actual service objective.

108. Knowledge distillation vs quantization vs pruning?

Distillation trains a smaller student to reproduce teacher predictions or representations. Quantization reduces numerical precision, while pruning removes weights, channels, tokens, or other structures. Their training needs and quality effects differ, and unstructured sparsity or lower precision only accelerates inference when the runtime and hardware exploit it.

109. What is the trade-off between model accuracy and inference latency?

Compare quality, tail latency, throughput, memory, and cost to identify a Pareto frontier rather than choosing the highest offline accuracy. A design is dominated if another meets or improves every relevant objective. Select among remaining designs using latency constraints and the actual costs of false positives and false negatives.

110. How would you monitor a deployed CV model?

Monitor input and embedding drift, missing or corrupted inputs, score distributions, failure rates, and p95/p99 latency. Collect delayed labels and audited samples to measure per-class and subgroup quality, because drift and confidence alone do not prove an accuracy change. Version models and data transformations so regressions can be investigated and rolled back.

111. How would you design a cost-efficient moderation system at large scale?

Use a cascade in which a cheap model resolves validated low-risk cases and routes uncertain or high-risk cases to stronger models or human reviewers. Tune class-specific decisions against recall, false-positive costs, review capacity, and latency; high confidence alone does not establish safety, particularly under shift. Audit auto-approved content and measure the whole cascade, since an early false negative cannot be repaired by a later model that never sees it.

Five modeling design cases

112. How would you design a computer vision system to detect unsafe images uploaded to Roblox?

Start by defining the unsafe categories, the costs of each error, and whether the output is image-level labels or object locations. Multiple categories can coexist, so a multi-label classifier is often a more appropriate starting point than a mutually exclusive softmax classifier.

  1. Problem formulation. “First, I would clarify which unsafe categories matter, whether several can occur in one image, and whether reviewers need an image-level decision or localized evidence.” Define latency, upload volume, review capacity, and the consequences of false negatives and false positives before selecting a model.
  2. Data and labels. “I would use reviewed UGC images, consistent annotation guidelines, and splits that account for creators, near-duplicates, and time.” Include benign lookalikes, rare classes, low-quality inputs, adversarial examples, and different rendering styles. Resolve ambiguous labels and evaluate reviewer agreement.
  3. Baseline model. “I would start with a pretrained ViT or CLIP image encoder and a lightweight multi-label head.” For an embedding h∈Rdh\in\mathbb R^dh∈Rd and KKK safety categories, use z=Wh+b∈RKz=Wh+b\in\mathbb R^Kz=Wh+b∈RK and independent probabilities pk=σ(zk)p_k=\sigma(z_k)pk​=σ(zk​). Add a larger VLM only if complex semantic reasoning measurably improves grounded decisions.
  4. Loss and optimization. “I would train with binary cross-entropy, test class weighting for rare categories, and mine visually similar benign hard negatives.” With yik∈{0,1}y_{ik}\in\{0,1\}yik​∈{0,1}, the basic objective is below; implement it with a numerically stable logits-based loss. Focal loss is an option, not a mandatory extra.
L=−1NK∑i=1N∑k=1K[yiklog⁡pik+(1−yik)log⁡(1−pik)].\mathcal L=-\frac{1}{NK}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K} \left[y_{ik}\log p_{ik}+(1-y_{ik})\log(1-p_{ik})\right].L=−NK1​i=1∑N​k=1∑K​[yik​logpik​+(1−yik​)log(1−pik​)].
  1. Evaluation. “I would report per-category precision and recall, average precision, and recall at a constrained false-positive rate.” Select thresholds on validation data, then evaluate once on a held-out test set. Inspect new game styles and other distribution shifts; aggregate accuracy alone can hide rare-category failures.
  2. Deployment. “I would use a cascade: a small model handles validated low-risk cases, while uncertain or high-risk examples go to a stronger model or a reviewer.” Monitor end-to-end safety quality, review volume, cost, and p95 latency. Audit auto-approved examples too: downstream review cannot repair an item that the first stage incorrectly filters out.

Follow-up: If false negatives are extremely costly, how would you choose the decision threshold? Choose per-class thresholds on validation data to satisfy a recall requirement or minimize an explicit error-cost objective, subject to review capacity. Lowering a threshold generally raises recall and false positives; if no threshold meets both safety and capacity constraints, improve the model or review process rather than claiming the conflict is solved.

113. How would you retrieve Roblox assets using a text query or reference image?

Use a CLIP-style dual encoder: embed a text query or reference image and each candidate asset in a shared space. For a 3D asset, begin with multiple rendered views and useful metadata; an image encoder does not directly consume a mesh.

  1. Training data. Collect relevant query–asset pairs, captions, and human relevance judgments. Fine-tune with a contrastive objective such as InfoNCE, mixing random and hard negatives while checking for false negatives. Split related assets and creators carefully.
  2. Retrieval. Normalize embeddings and rank by s(q,a)=eq⊤eas(q,a)=e_q^\top e_as(q,a)=eq⊤​ea​. Precompute asset embeddings, store them in an approximate-nearest-neighbor index, retrieve a candidate set, and optionally rerank it with a more expensive cross-modal model. An image query uses the image encoder; a text query uses the text encoder.
  3. Evaluation and serving. Report Recall@K for candidate retrieval, and a relevance-aware ranking metric such as NDCG when graded judgments exist. Measure query latency, index freshness, and quality on new styles. Version the encoder and index together because embeddings from incompatible model versions should not be mixed blindly.

Follow-up: How would you handle new assets or text queries not represented in training data? Encode new assets from their content and update the index without requiring interaction history. A pretrained text encoder can represent unseen queries, but representation does not guarantee relevance: evaluate held-out concepts, new rendering styles, and difficult vocabulary, then collect domain-specific pairs for adaptation.

Follow-up: Why choose CLIP instead of a ViT classifier, and when would it fail? CLIP supports open-vocabulary text queries and retrieval without a fixed classification head. A supervised ViT classifier may be better for a stable, well-labeled category set; CLIP can fail on unusual rendering styles, fine-grained distinctions, or misleading captions. Compare both on held-out domain data, improve positives and hard negatives, and profile the actual serving path before choosing.

114. How would you detect harmful events in short gameplay videos?

Clarify whether the product needs a single clip label or the start and end of each harmful event. Begin with frame sampling, a pretrained spatial encoder, temporal pooling, and a classification head; add a temporal model when motion, ordering, or localization matters.

I∈RB×T×C×H×W⟶F∈RB×T×d⟶temporal model⟶Z∈RB×T×K.I\in\mathbb R^{B\times T\times C\times H\times W} \longrightarrow F\in\mathbb R^{B\times T\times d} \longrightarrow \text{temporal model} \longrightarrow Z\in\mathbb R^{B\times T\times K}.I∈RB×T×C×H×W⟶F∈RB×T×d⟶temporal model⟶Z∈RB×T×K.

Per-frame scores can be pooled for a clip-level decision or decoded into event intervals. Collect event boundaries when localization is required; clip-level labels alone give weaker temporal supervision. Use source-video-separated splits, account for rare events with suitable sampling or loss weighting, and evaluate event recall, false alarms, temporal localization, and inference cost rather than frame accuracy alone.

Follow-up: What if the harmful event appears in only 0.5 seconds of a 60-second video? Sparse uniform frames can miss it entirely. Use denser sampling or overlapping short windows, possibly with a cheap high-coverage first pass and a stronger second pass. Motion-guided sampling is useful but not sufficient—a brief harmful image can be static. Measure recall specifically for short events and ensure a missed first-stage event is included in the end-to-end error analysis.

115. How would you adapt a pretrained VLM using 100K labeled image-text examples from Roblox?

First establish whether the target is retrieval, captioning, visual question answering, or another task: the same image-text pairs do not imply the same training objective. Inspect label quality and deduplicate before constructing creator-, style-, and time-aware evaluation sets.

For question answering, format each example as an image, instruction, and grounded answer. Start with the vision encoder frozen and train the projector and/or LoRA adapters; compare broader fine-tuning only when validation failures justify it. Use teacher forcing and answer-only cross-entropy, masking prompt, visual, and padding positions. For retrieval, use a contrastive objective instead of assuming answer-generation SFT is appropriate.

Evaluate task quality, hallucination, refusal or abstention behavior, general-capability forgetting, and unfamiliar game styles. Select checkpoints and hyperparameters on validation data, then measure latency, memory, and token count on the intended deployment hardware.

Follow-up: The model performs well on training data but poorly on new Roblox game styles. What would you do? Separate ordinary overfitting from a genuine domain shift using style-held-out evaluation. Add representative styles and hard cases, rebalance coverage, apply semantics-preserving augmentation, and compare lower learning rates, stronger regularization, or selective unfreezing. Keep a truly unseen-style test set so improvements are not just repeated tuning to the same examples.

116. How would you build a low-latency VLM that answers questions about gameplay screenshots on mobile?

Define whether the latency budget means time to first token or time to a complete answer, and specify image size, answer length, target device, privacy constraints, and expected load. Profile the complete path: capture and preprocessing, visual encoder, projector, LLM prefill, autoregressive decoding, memory transfers, and network time if inference is remote.

Use an efficient visual backbone, reduce visual tokens with pooling or a resampler, and compare a distilled or quantized language model on supported hardware. Cache unchanged visual features only when their freshness is valid. Compare on-device inference with cloud or hybrid execution using measured latency, battery use, thermal behavior, memory, connectivity, and grounded answer quality.

Follow-up: What if the VLM takes 500 ms but the product requires 100 ms? Break down the 500 ms first and optimize the dominant stage: fewer visual tokens, a smaller encoder or decoder, supported quantization, shorter outputs, or carefully valid caching. Verify each change on the target device. Streaming can improve time to first visible output but does not make a 500 ms complete answer finish in 100 ms; if no configuration meets both quality and latency constraints, explicitly renegotiate the scope or budget.

Additional prompts from the conversation

These are alternative wordings and combined follow-ups from the same conversation; the linked answers above cover their underlying concepts.

  • Why does ViT need positional embeddings? Without spatial positions, patch self-attention treats patches as an unordered set. See the positional-encoding answer.
  • CNN vs ViT: which would you choose for a small image dataset? Consider pretrained features and domain fit; a CNN's local priors can help with limited training data, while a pretrained ViT can still be strong. See the comparison.
  • How would you improve detection of small objects? Preserve resolution, use appropriate multiscale features, and consider tiled inference. See small-object detection.
  • Why use focal loss instead of cross-entropy? It downweights easy examples when they dominate training; validate the trade-off rather than using it automatically. See focal loss.
  • How does InfoNCE work and what is the role of temperature? Contrast a positive against negatives; temperature controls the sharpness of similarity logits and the training gradients. See InfoNCE and its follow-ups.
  • How would you address overfitting and severe class imbalance? Diagnose leakage and label quality, regularize, and compare sampling or weighting using class-specific held-out metrics. See overfitting and imbalance.
  • How would you fine-tune CLIP for a domain-specific retrieval task? Use representative paired data, a contrastive objective, and carefully chosen negatives; evaluate held-out retrieval quality. See CLIP training and the retrieval case.
  • How would you reduce visual tokens without losing key information? Compare pooling, resampling, or pruning while explicitly testing small objects and text. See visual token reduction.
  • How would you build a video understanding model for rare events? Match temporal coverage to event duration and evaluate event-level recall. See the video case.
  • Design an unsafe-image detection system for Roblox. See the worked moderation case, including its data, loss, evaluation, and deployment decisions.
  • Design an image-text retrieval system for 3D assets. See the retrieval case, including how rendered views connect 3D assets to image encoders.
  • Design a low-latency VLM for gameplay understanding. See the mobile case, including the 500 ms to 100 ms follow-up.

Chapter link ↗

One sentence, followed through every equation of the original encoder–decoder Transformer (Attention Is All You Need). Each step states its input, the operation, and its output, with the concrete shapes of the example next to the general ones. The code is kept out of the book: transformer_encoder_decoder.py transcribes these equations line by line, and transformer_encoder_decoder.ipynb runs it block by block on this example, printing the shape written here at every step.

The example. Source sentence we watch a short video, target sentence nous regardons video, one tiny vocabulary per language with PAD = 0, BOS = 1, EOS = 2:

source idss=(3⏟we, 4⏟watch, 5⏟a, 6⏟short, 7⏟video)n=5decoder inputt=(1⏟BOS, 3⏟nous, 4⏟regardons, 5⏟video)m=4labelsy=(3⏟nous, 4⏟regardons, 5⏟video, 2⏟EOS)yj=tj+1\begin{aligned} \text{source ids}\quad \mathbf{s} &= (\underbrace{3}_{\text{we}},\ \underbrace{4}_{\text{watch}},\ \underbrace{5}_{\text{a}},\ \underbrace{6}_{\text{short}},\ \underbrace{7}_{\text{video}}) && n = 5 \\[6pt] \text{decoder input}\quad \mathbf{t} &= (\underbrace{1}_{\text{BOS}},\ \underbrace{3}_{\text{nous}},\ \underbrace{4}_{\text{regardons}},\ \underbrace{5}_{\text{video}}) && m = 4 \\[6pt] \text{labels}\quad \mathbf{y} &= (\underbrace{3}_{\text{nous}},\ \underbrace{4}_{\text{regardons}},\ \underbrace{5}_{\text{video}},\ \underbrace{2}_{\text{EOS}}) && y_j = t_{j+1} \end{aligned}source idssdecoder inputtlabelsy​=(we3​​, watch4​​, a5​​, short6​​, video7​​)=(BOS1​​, nous3​​, regardons4​​, video5​​)=(nous3​​, regardons4​​, video5​​, EOS2​​)​​n=5m=4yj​=tj+1​​

An id is nothing but a row number. The source vocabulary is the list <pad>, <bos>, <eos>, we, watch, a, short, video, so we is 333 only because it is entry 333 of that list; the target vocabulary is a separate list (<pad>, <bos>, <eos>, nous, regardons, video, ...) with its own embedding table, so target id 333 (nous) has nothing to do with source id 333. The number carries no meaning and no order; its only use is to pick a row of the embedding table in step 1.

The decoder input is the target shifted right by one token, and every position predicts the token after it:

position jjjdecoder input tjt_jtj​may read (mask of step 6)label yjy_jyj​
0BOSBOSnous
1nousBOS, nousregardons
2regardonsBOS, nous, regardonsvideo
3videoBOS, nous, regardons, videoEOS

The answer of position jjj is always one step to its right, and the mask hides everything to the right, so no position is shown its own answer. Feeding the whole known target at once is teacher forcing: all mmm predictions are trained in one forward pass instead of mmm sequential ones, and each position sees exactly the information it would have during generation. Feeding the true prefix rather than the model's own guesses keeps the supervision clean early in training; at inference (step 11) the prefix comes from the model's previous outputs instead. Sizes used throughout: model width d=8d = 8d=8, heads h=2h = 2h=2, width per head dk=d/h=4d_k = d/h = 4dk​=d/h=4, feed-forward width dff=32d_{ff} = 32dff​=32, vocabularies Vsrc=8V_{\text{src}} = 8Vsrc​=8 and Vtgt=10V_{\text{tgt}} = 10Vtgt​=10. Every matrix below has one row per token. PyTorch puts a batch axis BBB in front of every shape; for this single sentence B=1B = 1B=1.

The d\sqrt{d}d​ is the paper's convention. Its embedding rows are initialized at scale 1/d1/\sqrt{d}1/d​ because the same matrix is reused as the output projection, and the factor lifts them to the O(1)O(1)O(1) scale of PPP, whose rows have norm d/2\sqrt{d/2}d/2​: token and position signals must be comparable when they are added. With PyTorch's default N(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0, 1)N(0,1) initialization the factor is not needed, and the first LayerNorm rescales everything anyway. GPT-2 omits it because its token and position tables are both learned and start at a comparable small scale, LLaMA because it adds no position vector at all; Gemma keeps it. Most current LLMs drop the addition of PPP altogether and rotate queries and keys inside attention instead: see Rotary positions (RoPE) after the code.

The addition is the residual path: the sublayer only has to learn a correction to XXX. LayerNorm treats each row x∈Rdx \in \mathbb{R}^{d}x∈Rd (one token) on its own, so the 555 tokens get 555 separate means and variances; γ,β∈Rd\gamma, \beta \in \mathbb{R}^{d}γ,β∈Rd are learned and shared by all tokens. Nothing is averaged across tokens or across the batch (with a batch there are B×nB \times nB×n separate statistics), which is why variable lengths and batch size 111 are no problem, unlike BatchNorm. RMSNorm, used by most current LLMs, normalizes the same axis without subtracting the mean.

Shapes: [5,8]→[5,32]→[5,8][5, 8] \to [5, 32] \to [5, 8][5,8]→[5,32]→[5,8]: widen, apply the nonlinearity, come back to ddd so the residual addition works. Attention decides which tokens to read; the FFN transforms what was read, and with 2 d dff2\,d\,d_{ff}2ddff​ weights it holds about two thirds of a layer's parameters. HHH is the encoder output, one contextual vector per source token; the code calls it memory. With NNN stacked encoder layers, steps 2–4 repeat NNN times with separate weights and HHH is the output of the last one.

Queries come from the target, keys and values from the source: this is the only place where the decoder reads the sentence it is translating. Code. The implementation is read in VS Code, not here. transformer_encoder_decoder.py implements the eleven steps with plain nn.Embedding, nn.Linear and nn.LayerNorm: boolean masks with True = this key may be read, the paper's post-norm order, no dropout. transformer_encoder_decoder.ipynb runs it block by block on this example with a check after every step, and test_transformer_encoder_decoder.py compares the attention with a per-head loop and with F.scaled_dot_product_attention.

Rotary positions (RoPE)#

Step 1 tells the model where a token stands by adding a position vector to its embedding, once, at the input. Most current LLMs do it differently (RoFormer): nothing is added in step 1, and inside every attention layer the query and key vectors are turned by an angle that depends on the position of their token. This section says where that happens and what every symbol means, then gives the rule and the reason it works, and then the three cases in use: 1D for text, 2D for images, 3D for video.

Where it happens. Two places of the walkthrough change; everything else stays.

The turn is repeated in every layer and every head, in the self-attention of steps 2 and 6. Cross-attention (step 7) usually has none, because its queries and keys stand in two different sequences.

(R(p θj) aj)⊤(R(p′θj) bj)=aj⊤ R((p′−p) θj) bj=∥aj∥ ∥bj∥cos⁡(ϕaj−ϕbj+(p−p′) θj)\big(R(p\,\theta_j)\, a_j\big)^{\top} \big(R(p'\theta_j)\, b_j\big) = a_j^{\top}\, R\big((p' - p)\,\theta_j\big)\, b_j = \lVert a_j \rVert\, \lVert b_j \rVert \cos\big(\phi_{a_j} - \phi_{b_j} + (p - p')\,\theta_j\big)(R(pθj​)aj​)⊤(R(p′θj​)bj​)=aj⊤​R((p′−p)θj​)bj​=∥aj​∥∥bj​∥cos(ϕaj​​−ϕbj​​+(p−p′)θj​)

The score is the sum over the pairs:

The score. Call aj,bja_j, b_jaj​,bj​ the row pair jjj of qqq and of kkk, and aˉj,bˉj\bar a_j, \bar b_jaˉj​,bˉj​ their column pair jjj. The argument of the 1D case applies to every pair on its own, with h−h′h - h'h−h′ for the row pairs and w−w′w - w'w−w′ for the column pairs:

q~(h,w)⊤ k~(h′,w′)=q(h,w)⊤ R(h′−h, w′−w) k(h′,w′)=∑j=0m−1∥aj∥ ∥bj∥cos⁡(ϕaj−ϕbj+(h−h′) θj)+∑j=0m−1∥aˉj∥ ∥bˉj∥cos⁡(ϕaˉj−ϕbˉj+(w−w′) θj)\begin{aligned} \tilde q_{(h,w)}^{\top}\, \tilde k_{(h',w')} &= q_{(h,w)}^{\top}\, R_{(h'-h,\ w'-w)}\, k_{(h',w')} \\[4pt] &= \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} \lVert a_j \rVert\, \lVert b_j \rVert \cos\big(\phi_{a_j} - \phi_{b_j} + (h - h')\,\theta_j\big) \\[4pt] &\quad + \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} \lVert \bar a_j \rVert\, \lVert \bar b_j \rVert \cos\big(\phi_{\bar a_j} - \phi_{\bar b_j} + (w - w')\,\theta_j\big) \end{aligned}q~​(h,w)⊤​k~(h′,w′)​​=q(h,w)⊤​R(h′−h, w′−w)​k(h′,w′)​=j=0∑m−1​∥aj​∥∥bj​∥cos(ϕaj​​−ϕbj​​+(h−h′)θj​)+j=0∑m−1​∥aˉj​∥∥bˉj​∥cos(ϕaˉj​​−ϕbˉj​​+(w−w′)θj​)​

The first sum sees only the row offset, the second only the column offset. Both are visible and they are kept apart: moving the key one row up changes the first sum, moving it one column to the left changes the second, and the model can weight the two directions differently by putting different content into row pairs and column pairs. Each half has its own speeds from fast to slow, so each direction can tell neighbours apart as well as far patches.

With the same content in both halves the score cannot tell "above" from "to the left"; a model separates the two by giving its row pairs and column pairs different content. One index is not enough for an image. Written row after row, the grid has the 1D indices 0,1,2,30, 1, 2, 30,1,2,3:

The 1D difference gives the same number to a neighbour and to a diagonal, and its number for "one row below" is the width of the grid, which changes with the resolution. The pair of offsets says what the image says, at any resolution. This is what replaces the learned position table inside the vision encoder from Qwen2-VL on: an image of any size or aspect ratio only changes the range of hhh and www, so no interpolation of positions is needed.

3D: video, and words and images in one sequence. The position has three numbers: the frame ttt, the row hhh and the column www. Every pair belongs to one of the three coordinates and is turned by that coordinate times its speed, so the score depends on (t−t′, h−h′, w−w′)(t - t',\ h - h',\ w - w')(t−t′, h−h′, w−w′). This is M-RoPE, used inside the LLM of a vision-language model, where words, image patches and video patches stand in one sequence:

For a word the three coordinates are equal, every pair is turned by p θjp\,\theta_jpθj​, and the rule is exactly the 1D rule: a text-only input behaves like an ordinary LLM. Which pair belongs to which coordinate matters, because the speeds run from fast to slow. With six pairs, θj=10000−j/6\theta_j = 10000^{-j/6}θj​=10000−j/6:

In blocks, the frame index owns only fast pairs. It is a watch with a second hand and no hour hand: good at telling neighbouring frames apart, unable to tell frames that are far apart, which hurts on long video. Interleaving gives every coordinate both fast and slow pairs.

Nothing here is learned: the angles are fixed by the position and by θj\theta_jθj​. What the model learns is where to put the energy of qqq and kkk, on fast pairs to be sensitive to near offsets and on slow pairs for far ones. RoPE also fits the KV cache of §7: a key is turned once by its own position and stored, a new query is turned by its position, and their product contains the offset.

In code. transformer_encoder_decoder.py has one function per case that returns the angle of every pair of every token, angles_1d, angles_2d and angles_3d, and one rotate shared by all three; the RoPE part of the notebook runs them. The tests check rotate against the explicit matrices RpR_pRp​, the scores of the tables above, and that shifting both tokens by the same amount along any coordinate leaves the score unchanged.

Decoder-only LLMs: GPT-2, step by step#

A decoder-only language model keeps one half of the walkthrough. Drop the encoder (steps 1–4) and the cross-attention of step 7, and what is left is the decoder: embeddings, masked self-attention, feed-forward, logits, loss and generation. The prompt and its continuation form one sequence in one causal stream, and every position predicts the token after it. GPT-2 (2019) is the reference design that modern LLMs refine: LLaMA, Qwen and Mistral keep its skeleton (the comparison below). Compared with the walkthrough, GPT-2 also moves every LayerNorm to the input of its sub-block. In this section, "step kkk" alone refers to the walkthrough and "GPT-2 step kkk" to the steps below.

The example. The source sentence of the walkthrough, we watch a short video, is now a prompt for GPT-2 small. GPT-2's byte-level BPE starts from the 256 byte values, so no string is out of vocabulary. Its 50,000 learned merges and one end-of-text token bring the vocabulary to V=50257V = 50257V=50257. Each word is one token, the last four with their leading space, so n=5n = 5n=5. The ids are just the tokenizer's row numbers for these five strings. There is no separate decoder input: the labels are the same tokens shifted left by one.

t=(t1, t2, t3, t4, t5)input, n=5y=(t2, t3, t4, t5)yj=tj+1\begin{aligned} \mathbf{t} &= (t_1,\ t_2,\ t_3,\ t_4,\ t_5) && \text{input, } n = 5 \\[4pt] \mathbf{y} &= (t_2,\ t_3,\ t_4,\ t_5) && y_j = t_{j+1} \end{aligned}ty​=(t1​, t2​, t3​, t4​, t5​)=(t2​, t3​, t4​, t5​)​​input, n=5yj​=tj+1​​

Matrices have one row per token and the batch axis is left out. Where the heads are separate, the head axis comes first, as in [12,5,64][12, 5, 64][12,5,64].

There is no row for position 102510251025, so the model cannot take a longer input. Both tables start as small random values of comparable scale, so the d\sqrt{d}d​ factor is gone. Shapes: [5]→[5,768][5] \to [5, 768][5]→[5,768]. X0X_0X0​ starts the residual stream, which every later sub-block reads and adds to.

Each third is reshaped into 121212 heads of 646464 columns, [12,5,64][12, 5, 64][12,5,64]. Per head the scores SiS_iSi​ are [5,64]×[64,5]=[5,5][5, 64] \times [64, 5] = [5, 5][5,64]×[64,5]=[5,5], scaled by 64=8\sqrt{64} = 864​=8; all heads together hold [12,5,5][12, 5, 5][12,5,5]. The causal mask is that of step 6, now 5×55 \times 55×5: we reads only itself and video reads all five tokens. The weighted values are [12,5,64][12, 5, 64][12,5,64], the heads concatenate back to [5,768][5, 768][5,768], and WO∈Rd×dW^{O} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}WO∈Rd×d mixes them. This is the feed-forward of step 4 with GELU in place of ReLU, applied to each row on its own: W1∈Rd×4dW_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times 4d}W1​∈Rd×4d and W2∈R4d×dW_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{4d \times d}W2​∈R4d×d take [5,768]→[5,3072]→[5,768][5, 768] \to [5, 3072] \to [5, 768][5,768]→[5,3072]→[5,768]. Φ\PhiΦ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function, so GELU is a smooth ReLU that lets small negative inputs through a little. GPT-2 evaluates it with the tanh⁡\tanhtanh approximation of the last line.

GPT-2 step 4 · Twelve blocks, then a final LayerNorm. X0∈Rn×d  ⟶  Xf∈Rn×dX_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d} \;\longrightarrow\; X_f \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}X0​∈Rn×d⟶Xf​∈Rn×d

A block is GPT-2 steps 2 and 3 with its own weights, and each of the 121212 maps [5,768][5, 768][5,768] to [5,768][5, 768][5,768]. The extra LN⁡f\operatorname{LN}_fLNf​ is required by pre-norm. After the last block the stream is the embedding plus 242424 sub-block outputs. It has never been normalized as a whole, so its scale grows with depth. LN⁡f\operatorname{LN}_fLNf​ normalizes each row once more, with its own γ\gammaγ and β\betaβ, before the vocabulary projection. A post-norm model needs no final norm, because its last sub-block already ends with a LayerNorm.

Z=LN⁡f(XL) E⊤=Xf E⊤p(tj+1=v∣t1:j)=softmax⁡(Zj)v\begin{aligned} Z &= \operatorname{LN}_f(X_L)\, E^{\top} = X_f\, E^{\top} \\[4pt] p(t_{j+1} = v \mid t_{1:j}) &= \operatorname{softmax}(Z_j)_v \end{aligned}Zp(tj+1​=v∣t1:j​)​=LNf​(XL​)E⊤=Xf​E⊤=softmax(Zj​)v​​

The LM head is the token table of GPT-2 step 1, transposed: no new matrix and no bias. Zj,vZ_{j,v}Zj,v​ scores token vvv by how well its embedding matches the final vector of position jjj. Shapes: [5,768]×[768,50257]=[5,50257][5, 768] \times [768, 50257] = [5, 50257][5,768]×[768,50257]=[5,50257], the largest single product in the model. Tying saves Vd=38.6Vd = 38.6Vd=38.6M parameters; untied, GPT-2 small would have 163.0M.

Row 111, which has read only we, is scored on watch; row 444, which has read we watch a short, is scored on video. Row 555 has no label inside these five tokens. The usual pretraining recipe cuts a window of nmax⁡+1n_{\max} + 1nmax​+1 tokens from one long stream of documents joined by the end-of-text token. All 102410241024 positions then have a label, and one forward pass trains 102410241024 predictions; the causal mask makes this legal, as with teacher forcing in step 6. The prompt tokens are targets too; instruction tuning usually drops them from the average. Shapes: Z1:4Z_{1:4}Z1:4​ is [4,50257][4, 50257][4,50257], y\mathbf{y}y is [4][4][4], and L\mathcal{L}L is a scalar.

GPT-2 step 7 · Generation with the KV cache. t  ⟶  t6,t7,…\mathbf{t} \;\longrightarrow\; t_6, t_7, \dotst⟶t6​,t7​,…

tn+1=arg max⁡v Zn,vgreedytn+1∼softmax⁡(Zn/τ)sampling\begin{aligned} t_{n+1} &= \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{v}\ Z_{n,v} && \text{greedy} \\[4pt] t_{n+1} &\sim \operatorname{softmax}(Z_n / \tau) && \text{sampling} \end{aligned}tn+1​tn+1​​=vargmax​ Zn,v​∼softmax(Zn​/τ)​​greedysampling​

Only the last row of ZZZ is used: the chosen token is appended and the model runs again. Greedy decoding takes the arg max; sampling draws from the softmax at temperature τ\tauτ. The KV cache stores every layer's Ki,ViK_i, V_iKi​,Vi​ for the positions already seen. After the prompt has been processed once (prefill), each new token goes through the 121212 blocks alone. Its query, [12,1,64][12, 1, 64][12,1,64] per layer, reads the cached keys plus its own, [12,6,64][12, 6, 64][12,6,64] for the first new token. The cache grows by 2Ld=18,4322 L d = 18{,}4322Ld=18,432 numbers per token, 36 KiB in 16-bit floats. Generation stops at end-of-text or at 102410241024 positions, where the position table ends.

Post-norm vs pre-norm. The 2017 Transformer and GPT-1 put the LayerNorm after the residual addition. GPT-2 moved it to the input of each sub-block and added the final LN⁡f\operatorname{LN}_fLNf​. Count sub-blocks rather than blocks, ℓ=0,…,N−1\ell = 0, \dots, N - 1ℓ=0,…,N−1 with N=2L=24N = 2L = 24N=2L=24. Let xℓx_\ellxℓ​ be the stream that enters sub-block ℓ\ellℓ and FℓF_\ellFℓ​ its attention or MLP:

xℓ+1=LN⁡(xℓ+Fℓ(xℓ))post-normxℓ+1=xℓ+Fℓ(LN⁡(xℓ))pre-norm\begin{aligned} x_{\ell+1} &= \operatorname{LN}(x_\ell + F_\ell(x_\ell)) && \text{post-norm} \\[4pt] x_{\ell+1} &= x_\ell + F_\ell(\operatorname{LN}(x_\ell)) && \text{pre-norm} \end{aligned}xℓ+1​xℓ+1​​=LN(xℓ​+Fℓ​(xℓ​))=xℓ​+Fℓ​(LN(xℓ​))​​post-normpre-norm​

Write Gk=Fk(LN⁡(xk))G_k = F_k(\operatorname{LN}(x_k))Gk​=Fk​(LN(xk​)) for what pre-norm sub-block kkk adds. Pre-norm unrolls into a sum, so the Jacobian from any sub-block to the top contains the identity:

xN=xℓ+∑k=ℓN−1Gk∂xN∂xℓ=I+∑k=ℓN−1∂Gk∂xℓ\begin{aligned} x_N &= x_\ell + \sum_{k=\ell}^{N-1} G_k \\[4pt] \frac{\partial x_N}{\partial x_\ell} &= I + \sum_{k=\ell}^{N-1} \frac{\partial G_k}{\partial x_\ell} \end{aligned}xN​∂xℓ​∂xN​​​=xℓ​+k=ℓ∑N−1​Gk​=I+k=ℓ∑N−1​∂xℓ​∂Gk​​​

With ℓ=0\ell = 0ℓ=0 the top is xN=x0+∑k=0N−1Gkx_N = x_0 + \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} G_kxN​=x0​+∑k=0N−1​Gk​: the embeddings plus one correction per sub-block. The gradient ∂L/∂xN\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial x_N∂L/∂xN​, which has crossed only the head and LN⁡f\operatorname{LN}_fLNf​, reaches every sub-block and the embeddings unchanged through III. The sub-blocks above only add their own terms to it. Post-norm has no such path: the gradient crosses every LayerNorm Jacobian on the way down.

∂xN∂xℓ=JN−1(I+FN−1′)⋯Jℓ(I+Fℓ′)Jk=1σkdiag⁡(γ) ΠkΠk=I−1d(11⊤+z^kz^k⊤)\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial x_N}{\partial x_\ell} &= J_{N-1}(I + F'_{N-1}) \cdots J_\ell (I + F'_\ell) \\[4pt] J_k &= \tfrac{1}{\sigma_k} \operatorname{diag}(\gamma)\, \Pi_k \\[4pt] \Pi_k &= I - \tfrac{1}{d}\big(\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top + \hat z_k \hat z_k^\top\big) \end{aligned}∂xℓ​∂xN​​Jk​Πk​​=JN−1​(I+FN−1′​)⋯Jℓ​(I+Fℓ′​)=σk​1​diag(γ)Πk​=I−d1​(11⊤+z^k​z^k⊤​)​

Here Fk′=∂Fk/∂xkF'_k = \partial F_k / \partial x_kFk′​=∂Fk​/∂xk​, and JkJ_kJk​ is the Jacobian of the LayerNorm of sub-block kkk, whose input is uk=xk+Fk(xk)u_k = x_k + F_k(x_k)uk​=xk​+Fk​(xk​). It acts on each token's row separately, and the formula is that of one row: σk\sigma_kσk​ is the standard deviation of that row of uku_kuk​ and z^k\hat z_kz^k​ its normalized version. Since z^k\hat z_kz^k​ has zero mean and squared norm close to ddd, Πk\Pi_kΠk​ projects out two directions, 1\mathbf{1}1 and z^k\hat z_kz^k​. JkJ_kJk​ then rescales by γ/σk\gamma / \sigma_kγ/σk​. No part of the gradient passes through unchanged, so its size at sub-block ℓ\ellℓ depends on every layer above it.

Xiong et al. (2020) show that at initialization the post-norm gradients of the parameters near the output are large. A large learning rate at the start then makes training unstable, so post-norm needs a warmup. Later work on deeper models (Liu et al. 2020, Wang et al. 2022) found that deep post-norm stacks can diverge even with one. With pre-norm these gradients shrink like 1/L1/\sqrt{L}1/L​, and warmup can be shortened or dropped. Pre-norm has a price. Every sub-block adds to a stream that is never renormalized, so the norm of xℓx_\ellxℓ​ grows with depth and a late sub-block changes it relatively less. The final norm becomes necessary, and a post-norm model that does train is often slightly better (the interview answer lists the compromises).

The same growth sets GPT-2's initialization. If x0x_0x0​ and the NNN sub-block outputs are uncorrelated, each output with variance s2s^2s2, the top of the stream has variance Var⁡(x0)+Ns2\operatorname{Var}(x_0) + N s^2Var(x0​)+Ns2, which grows with depth. The paper scales the weights of residual layers by 1/N1/\sqrt{N}1/N​, with NNN the number of residual layers. Common implementations apply it to the two projections that write into the stream, WOW^{O}WO and W2W_2W2​:

WO, W2∼N(0, σ02/N)σ0=0.02,N=2L\begin{aligned} W^{O},\ W_2 &\sim \mathcal{N}\big(0,\ \sigma_0^2 / N\big) \\[4pt] \sigma_0 &= 0.02, \quad N = 2L \end{aligned}WO, W2​σ0​​∼N(0, σ02​/N)=0.02,N=2L​

Then s2s^2s2 falls like 1/N1/N1/N and Ns2N s^2Ns2 stays the same at any depth. For GPT-2 small the standard deviation is 0.02/24≈0.00410.02 / \sqrt{24} \approx 0.00410.02/24​≈0.0041 instead of 0.020.020.02.

Vision Transformers, from ViT to today#

The encoder of this chapter does not care what its tokens are. Give it image patches instead of words and it is a Vision Transformer (ViT): the same step for an image above and steps 1–3 of Chapter 4 follow one tiny image through it. This section is the family that grew out of that model. Each member changes some of five choices, and the model line at the end compares them on these choices.

  1. Tokens. How pixels become tokens: square patches, a pyramid of grids, tubes of video, or patches of any aspect ratio.
  2. Attention range. Which keys a query reads: every token, a local window, a pooled set of keys, or one axis of space-time at a time.
  3. Shape. One grid from the first layer to the last, like ViT, or a pyramid that halves the grid and widens the channels at each stage, like a CNN.
  4. Positions. A learned table added to the tokens, a relative bias inside the softmax, or the 2D RoPE above.
  5. Training signal. Labels, a teacher's labels, masked reconstruction, self-distillation, or captions (CLIP and SigLIP in Chapter 4).

The example. One RGB image, to be classified into the K=1000K = 1000K=1000 ImageNet classes. A plain ViT cuts it into 16×1616 \times 1616×16 patches; the hierarchical models start four times finer:

I∈R224×224×C,C=3 channelsP=16:N=14×14=196 patches of 16⋅16⋅3=768 numbersP=4:N=56×56=3136 patches of 4⋅4⋅3=48 numbers\begin{aligned} I &\in \mathbb{R}^{224 \times 224 \times C}, \quad C = 3 \text{ channels} \\[4pt] P = 16: \quad N &= 14 \times 14 = 196 \ \text{patches of}\ 16 \cdot 16 \cdot 3 = 768 \ \text{numbers} \\[4pt] P = 4: \quad N &= 56 \times 56 = 3136 \ \text{patches of}\ 4 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 = 48 \ \text{numbers} \end{aligned}IP=16:NP=4:N​∈R224×224×C,C=3 channels=14×14=196 patches of 16⋅16⋅3=768 numbers=56×56=3136 patches of 4⋅4⋅3=48 numbers​

Where a width is needed, the sizes are those of ViT-B/16: D=768D = 768D=768, L=12L = 12L=12 layers, 121212 heads, 86M parameters. The code of this section, vision_transformers.py (note at the end), implements the core of ViT, DeiT, Swin, PVT, MAE, DINO, TimeSformer, ViViT, NaViT and DiT at these sizes; ViTDet, SAM, BEiT and the later DINO versions are described but not coded.

ViT · patches, a class token, a learned position table. I∈R224×224×3  ⟶  y^∈R1000I \in \mathbb{R}^{224 \times 224 \times 3} \;\longrightarrow\; \hat y \in \mathbb{R}^{1000}I∈R224×224×3⟶y^​∈R1000

z0=[ xcls; xp1E; … ; xpNE ]+Epos,E∈RP2C×D,  Epos∈R(N+1)×Dzℓ=Block⁡(zℓ−1),ℓ=1,…,Ly^=LN⁡(zL0) Whead,Whead∈RD×K\begin{aligned} z_0 &= \big[\, x_{\text{cls}};\ x_p^1 E;\ \dots;\ x_p^N E \,\big] + E_{\text{pos}}, && E \in \mathbb{R}^{P^2 C \times D},\ \ E_{\text{pos}} \in \mathbb{R}^{(N+1) \times D} \\[4pt] z_\ell &= \operatorname{Block}(z_{\ell-1}), && \ell = 1, \dots, L \\[4pt] \hat y &= \operatorname{LN}\big(z_L^0\big)\, W_{\text{head}}, && W_{\text{head}} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times K} \end{aligned}z0​zℓ​y^​​=[xcls​; xp1​E; …; xpN​E]+Epos​,=Block(zℓ−1​),=LN(zL0​)Whead​,​​E∈RP2C×D,  Epos​∈R(N+1)×Dℓ=1,…,LWhead​∈RD×K​

xpix_p^ixpi​ is patch iii flattened, and Block is the pre-norm block of Chapter 4, step 3, with no mask. The class token xclsx_{\text{cls}}xcls​ is a learned row in front of the patches. It has no pixels of its own, so its output zL0z_L^0zL0​ holds only what attention gathered from the patches, and the classifier reads that one row; the paper finds that averaging the patch outputs works as well once the learning rate is tuned. Shapes: [224,224,3]→[196,768]→[197,768]→[1000][224, 224, 3] \to [196, 768] \to [197, 768] \to [1000][224,224,3]→[196,768]→[197,768]→[1000]. Two facts that interviews probe:

  • Data. Trained on ImageNet-1k alone, ViT-B/16 reaches 77.9%, a few points below ResNets of its size. Pretrained on JFT-300M, it matches or beats the best CNNs (BiT-L 87.5%, Noisy Student 88.5%) for less pretraining compute, up to 88.55% for ViT-H/14; pretrained on ImageNet-21k it comes close, 85.3% for ViT-L/16. The paper's explanation: ViT has much less image-specific inductive bias than a CNN, so locality and translation equivariance must be learned from data (CNN vs Transformer).
  • Resolution. Pretraining is at 224 px and fine-tuning at 384 px with the same P=16P = 16P=16, so NNN grows to 24×24=57624 \times 24 = 57624×24=576 and the learned table no longer fits. It is resized as a 14×1414 \times 1414×14 image of vectors, and the class-token row is kept:
Epos 24×24=interp⁡(Epos 14×14)linear in the ViT code, bicubic in DeiTE_{\text{pos}}^{\,24 \times 24} = \operatorname{interp}\big(E_{\text{pos}}^{\,14 \times 14}\big) \qquad \text{linear in the ViT code, bicubic in DeiT}Epos24×24​=interp(Epos14×14​)linear in the ViT code, bicubic in DeiT

The patching and this resize are the only places where ViT is told that the image is two-dimensional.

The cost of one attention sublayer. (N,D)  ⟶  Ω(N, D) \;\longrightarrow\; \Omega(N,D)⟶Ω, in multiply–adds

Ωglobal=4ND2+2N2D,Ωwindow=4ND2+2M2ND\Omega_{\text{global}} = 4ND^2 + 2N^2 D, \qquad \Omega_{\text{window}} = 4ND^2 + 2M^2 N DΩglobal​=4ND2+2N2D,Ωwindow​=4ND2+2M2ND

The first term is the four projections WQ,WK,WV,WOW_Q, W_K, W_V, W_OWQ​,WK​,WV​,WO​ and is linear in NNN. The second is QK⊤QK^\topQK⊤ plus the weighted sum of VVV. It is quadratic in NNN for global attention and becomes linear when every query reads only the M×MM \times MM×M tokens of its window. These are equations 1 and 2 of the Swin paper, which leave out the softmax.

At 224 px the attention matrix of ViT is cheap. It dominates when the tokens are many: high resolution, small patches, video. Every variant below that limits the attention range does so to shrink the second term: windows (Swin, ViTDet) make it linear in NNN, reduced keys (PVT) divide it by R2R^2R2, and divided space-time attention (TimeSformer) divides it by TN/(T+N)TN/(T + N)TN/(T+N).

DeiT · ImageNet only, plus a distillation token. I  ⟶  (Zcls, Zdist)I \;\longrightarrow\; (Z_{\text{cls}},\ Z_{\text{dist}})I⟶(Zcls​, Zdist​), two vectors in R1000\mathbb{R}^{1000}R1000

ψ\psiψ is the softmax, yyy the true label, ZtZ_tZt​ the logits of the teacher, a CNN (RegNetY-16GF, 82.9%), and Zcls,ZdistZ_{\text{cls}}, Z_{\text{dist}}Zcls​,Zdist​ are linear heads on the outputs of the two tokens. The distillation token is a second learned row trained to reproduce the teacher's hard decision instead of the label; at test time the softmax outputs of the two heads are added. Otherwise the network is ViT-B. What changed is the recipe: ImageNet-1k alone (1.28M images), 300 epochs, strong augmentation (RandAugment, Mixup, CutMix, random erasing), stochastic depth instead of dropout, AdamW. DeiT-B reaches 81.8% at 224 px after 53 hours on one 8-GPU node, and 83.4% with the distillation token, above its own teacher. A CNN teacher works better than a transformer teacher, plausibly because the student inherits some of its inductive bias.

Swin · windows, shifted windows, patch merging. I  ⟶  562×96,  282×192,  142×384,  72×768I \;\longrightarrow\; 56^2 \times 96,\ \ 28^2 \times 192,\ \ 14^2 \times 384,\ \ 7^2 \times 768I⟶562×96,  282×192,  142×384,  72×768

Tokens are 4×44 \times 44×4 patches, 484848 numbers each, embedded to a width C=96C = 96C=96; from here to PVT, CCC is the token width, not the 3 image channels. Attention runs inside non-overlapping M×MM \times MM×M windows, M=7M = 7M=7, and adds a learned bias for the relative position of the two tokens:

Attn⁡(Q,K,V)=softmax⁡(QK⊤/dk+B) Vper head, over the M2 tokens of one windowBij=B^[ yi−yj+M−1,  xi−xj+M−1 ],B^∈R(2M−1)×(2M−1)\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Attn}(Q, K, V) &= \operatorname{softmax}\big(QK^\top / \sqrt{d_k} + B\big)\, V && \text{per head, over the } M^2 \text{ tokens of one window} \\[4pt] B_{ij} &= \hat B\big[\, y_i - y_j + M - 1,\ \ x_i - x_j + M - 1 \,\big], && \hat B \in \mathbb{R}^{(2M-1) \times (2M-1)} \end{aligned}Attn(Q,K,V)Bij​​=softmax(QK⊤/dk​​+B)V=B^[yi​−yj​+M−1,  xi​−xj​+M−1],​​per head, over the M2 tokens of one windowB^∈R(2M−1)×(2M−1)​

dk=C/hd_k = C/hdk​=C/h is the head width, 323232 in Swin-T. On the 56×5656 \times 5656×56 grid that is 646464 windows of 494949 tokens; per head, BBB is a 49×4949 \times 4949×49 matrix read from a 13×1313 \times 1313×13 table. Swin has no position table at all. Windows alone would never exchange information, so consecutive blocks alternate between the regular partition (W-MSA) and one displaced by ⌊M/2⌋=3\lfloor M/2 \rfloor = 3⌊M/2⌋=3 tokens in both directions (SW-MSA):

Displacing the partition would cut extra, smaller windows at the border. Instead the map is rolled by −3-3−3 along both axes and the same 646464 windows are used. A window can then hold pieces of up to four regions rrr that were not neighbours in the image, so their pairs are masked before the softmax, and the map is rolled back by +3+3+3:

mask⁡ij={0r(i)=r(j)−100otherwise: a weight below 10−43 after the softmax\operatorname{mask}_{ij} = \begin{cases} 0 & r(i) = r(j) \\ -100 & \text{otherwise: a weight below } 10^{-43} \text{ after the softmax} \end{cases}maskij​={0−100​r(i)=r(j)otherwise: a weight below 10−43 after the softmax​

−100-100−100 is the official code's value; the code below masks with −∞-\infty−∞, which gives exact zeros. The cost is linear because MMM is fixed; the shift adds connections across windows, not cost. Between stages, patch merging halves the grid and doubles the width:

xu,v′=LN⁡([ x2u,2v; x2u+1,2v; x2u,2v+1; x2u+1,2v+1 ]) Wmerge,Wmerge∈R4C×2Cx'_{u,v} = \operatorname{LN}\big(\big[\, x_{2u,2v};\ x_{2u+1,2v};\ x_{2u,2v+1};\ x_{2u+1,2v+1} \,\big]\big)\, W_{\text{merge}}, \qquad W_{\text{merge}} \in \mathbb{R}^{4C \times 2C}xu,v′​=LN([x2u,2v​; x2u+1,2v​; x2u,2v+1​; x2u+1,2v+1​])Wmerge​,Wmerge​∈R4C×2C

Swin-T: C=96C = 96C=96, blocks (2,2,6,2)(2, 2, 6, 2)(2,2,6,2) per stage, heads (3,6,12,24)(3, 6, 12, 24)(3,6,12,24), 29M parameters, 4.5 GFLOPs, 81.3%. The four maps have strides 4, 8, 16 and 32, those of a ResNet, so Swin drops into FPN, Mask R-CNN or UPerNet unchanged. That, more than ImageNet accuracy, made it the default backbone for detection and segmentation in 2021. At stage 4 the 7×77 \times 77×7 map is a single window, so the shift is switched off and attention is global.

SRA⁡(Q,K,V)=Attn⁡(QWQ, SR⁡(K) WK, SR⁡(V) WV)SR⁡(x)=LN⁡(Reshape⁡(x,R) WS),WS∈RR2C×C\begin{aligned} \operatorname{SRA}(Q, K, V) &= \operatorname{Attn}\big(Q W^Q,\ \operatorname{SR}(K)\, W^K,\ \operatorname{SR}(V)\, W^V\big) \\[4pt] \operatorname{SR}(x) &= \operatorname{LN}\big(\operatorname{Reshape}(x, R)\, W^S\big), \qquad W^S \in \mathbb{R}^{R^2 C \times C} \end{aligned}SRA(Q,K,V)SR(x)​=Attn(QWQ, SR(K)WK, SR(V)WV)=LN(Reshape(x,R)WS),WS∈RR2C×C​

Reshape⁡(x,R)\operatorname{Reshape}(x, R)Reshape(x,R) turns each R×RR \times RR×R block of tokens into one row of R2CR^2 CR2C numbers and WSW^SWS maps it back to CCC, a learned stride-RRR projection rather than a pooling, so the NNN queries read N/R2N / R^2N/R2 keys and values. Stage 1 of the example has 313631363136 queries and R=8R = 8R=8, so 494949 keys; with R=8,4,2,1R = 8, 4, 2, 1R=8,4,2,1 over the four stages, every stage reads a 7×77 \times 77×7 grid of keys at 224 px. PVT is a pyramid like Swin, with widths 64,128,320,51264, 128, 320, 51264,128,320,512, but makes the opposite trade: every query still sees the whole image, coarsely, where a Swin query sees a small region exactly. The cost falls by R2R^2R2 yet stays quadratic in NNN; the linear variant of PVTv2 pools the keys to a fixed 7×77 \times 77×7 grid instead.

The encoder, a full ViT, sees only the 494949 visible patches; there are no mask tokens in it. A light decoder (8 blocks of width 512, 9% of ViT-L's compute per token and about 30% of ViT-B's) receives the encoded patches, projected to its width, plus one shared learned vector mmm for every hidden patch, put back in image order; its last linear layer predicts P2C=768P^2 C = 768P2C=768 pixel values per token. The loss counts only the hidden patches, and the target is each patch normalized by its own mean μj\mu_jμj​ and standard deviation σj\sigma_jσj​. After pretraining the decoder is thrown away and the encoder is fine-tuned on all patches. Three reasons it works. Images are redundant, so with 75% hidden the task cannot be solved by copying neighbours and needs a model of objects. The encoder runs on a quarter of the tokens, so pretraining is 3× or more faster, which makes huge models affordable. And cropping and flipping are all the augmentation it needs. ImageNet-1k fine-tuned: ViT-B 83.6%, ViT-L 85.9%, ViT-H 86.9%, 87.8% at 448 px, from ImageNet-1k alone. Its predecessor BEiT kept all 196 tokens in the encoder, replaced about 40% of them by a mask embedding, and classified each into one of 8,192 visual tokens produced by DALL-E's discrete VAE, a relative of the VQ-VAE; VideoMAE hides 90% of a video's space-time tubes.

DINO · self-distillation without labels. crops of III   ⟶  \;\longrightarrow\;⟶ a loss, no label
