One image gives a set VVV of crops: two global crops x1g,x2gx^g_1, x^g_2x1g​,x2g​ at 224 px and several local crops at 96 px. The student gθsg_{\theta_s}gθs​​, a ViT plus a projection head with K=65,536K = 65{,}536K=65,536 outputs, sees all crops; the teacher gθtg_{\theta_t}gθt​​ sees only the global ones. The student is trained to give, from a small local crop, the same distribution the teacher gives from a large view of the same image: local-to-global correspondence. The teacher is not trained; it is an exponential moving average of the student, with λ\lambdaλ from 0.9960.9960.996 to 111. Two operations on the teacher's output prevent collapse to a constant: centering by ccc, a running mean of the teacher's outputs over batches of BBB images with momentum m=0.9m = 0.9m=0.9 (not MAE's mask token), stops one dimension from dominating, and sharpening with a low temperature (τt=0.04\tau_t = 0.04τt​=0.04 to 0.070.070.07 against τs=0.1\tau_s = 0.1τs​=0.1) stops the output from becoming uniform. Each pushes the opposite way, and either one alone collapses. No labels and no negative pairs. The code below, like the official one, divides the sum by the number of crop pairs. The self-attention of the class token in the last layer turns out to segment the main object without any supervision. DINOv2 scales this to a curated set of 142M images and a 1.1B-parameter ViT-g/14, adds a masked-patch loss (iBOT), and gives frozen features good enough for classification, segmentation and depth without fine-tuning. Large ViTs trained long, with or without labels (DINOv2, DeiT-III, OpenCLIP), grow a few high-norm tokens in empty background patches; they hold global information and spoil the attention maps. Four learned register tokens, appended to the input and dropped at the output, give that information a place to go. DINOv3 grows to a 6.7B-parameter ViT/16 with RoPE. Its dense features degrade during very long training, so a late refinement phase adds Gram anchoring: a loss ∥XSXS⊤−XGXG⊤∥F2\lVert X_S X_S^\top - X_G X_G^\top \rVert_F^2∥XS​XS⊤​−XG​XG⊤​∥F2​, where XSX_SXS​ and XGX_GXG​ hold the L2-normalized patch features of the student and of an early teacher checkpoint, which pulls the student's patch-to-patch cosine-similarity matrix back to the early one and repairs the dense features.

ViTDet and SAM · a plain backbone for detection and segmentation. I∈R1024×1024×3  ⟶  F∈R64×64×D  ⟶  P2,…,P5I \in \mathbb{R}^{1024 \times 1024 \times 3} \;\longrightarrow\; F \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 64 \times D} \;\longrightarrow\; P_2, \dots, P_5I∈R1024×1024×3⟶F∈R64×64×D⟶P2​,…,P5​

The opposite answer to Swin: keep the pretrained ViT plain, one grid at stride 16, and build the pyramid only at the end, from the last map FFF:

P5=MaxPool⁡2×2(F),P4=F,P3=Deconv⁡2×2(F),P2=Deconv⁡2×2(Deconv⁡2×2(F))P_5 = \operatorname{MaxPool}_{2 \times 2}(F), \qquad P_4 = F, \qquad P_3 = \operatorname{Deconv}_{2 \times 2}(F), \qquad P_2 = \operatorname{Deconv}_{2 \times 2}\big(\operatorname{Deconv}_{2 \times 2}(F)\big)P5​=MaxPool2×2​(F),P4​=F,P3​=Deconv2×2​(F),P2​=Deconv2×2​(Deconv2×2​(F))

Each level then passes a 1×11 \times 11×1 and a 3×33 \times 33×3 convolution to 256 channels, and a LayerNorm and GELU sit between the two deconvolutions of P2P_2P2​. At 1024 px the backbone carries 409640964096 tokens, the row of the cost table where global attention is most of the work. ViTDet therefore uses 14×1414 \times 1414×14 windows, the grid size of pretraining and not shifted, in most blocks and global attention in four blocks spread evenly through the depth (blocks 3, 6, 9 and 12 of ViT-B). Windows, the four global blocks and the pyramid are added only for fine-tuning; the backbone is pretrained as a plain ViT with MAE, which adds 3.1 box AP for ViT-B and 4.6 for ViT-L over random initialization, while supervised ImageNet-1k pretraining is slightly worse than random initialization (−0.5 and −0.4). Mask R-CNN on COCO reaches 51.6, 55.6 and 56.7 box AP with ViT-B, L and H. SAM's image encoder is this design: an MAE-pretrained ViT-H/16 at 1024 px with 14×1414 \times 1414×14 windows in 28 blocks and global attention in 4, and a neck to a 256×64×64256 \times 64 \times 64256×64×64 embedding. It runs once per image; only the light prompt encoder and mask decoder run for each click.

TimeSformer and ViViT · attention over space and time. X∈RT×H×W×3  ⟶  z∈RT×N×DX \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times H \times W \times 3} \;\longrightarrow\; z \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times N \times D}X∈RT×H×W×3⟶z∈RT×N×D

With T=8T = 8T=8 frames of the example, each cut into N=196N = 196N=196 patches, joint attention over all TN=1568TN = 1568TN=1568 tokens costs (TN)2≈2.46(TN)^2 \approx 2.46(TN)2≈2.46M pairs per head. TimeSformer's divided attention splits every block into a temporal and a spatial step, each with its own weights:

z′=z+MSA⁡time(LN⁡(z))token (t,p) reads (t′,p) for all frames t′z′′=z′+MSA⁡space(LN⁡(z′))token (t,p) reads (t,p′) for all patches p′z′′′=z′′+MLP⁡(LN⁡(z′′))\begin{aligned} z' &= z + \operatorname{MSA}_{\text{time}}\big(\operatorname{LN}(z)\big) && \text{token } (t, p) \text{ reads } (t', p) \text{ for all frames } t' \\[4pt] z'' &= z' + \operatorname{MSA}_{\text{space}}\big(\operatorname{LN}(z')\big) && \text{token } (t, p) \text{ reads } (t, p') \text{ for all patches } p' \\[4pt] z''' &= z'' + \operatorname{MLP}\big(\operatorname{LN}(z'')\big) \end{aligned}z′z′′z′′′​=z+MSAtime​(LN(z))=z′+MSAspace​(LN(z′))=z′′+MLP(LN(z′′))​​token (t,p) reads (t′,p) for all frames t′token (t,p) reads (t,p′) for all patches p′​

Each query now reads T+N=204T + N = 204T+N=204 keys instead of TN=1568TN = 1568TN=1568, TN(T+N)≈0.32TN(T + N) \approx 0.32TN(T+N)≈0.32M pairs per head, about 7.77.77.7 times fewer, and two steps still connect every pair of tokens. The cost is parameters: separate temporal weights take ViT-B from 86M to 121M. Order matters a little: time first, then space, is 0.5% better on Kinetics than the reverse. ViViT changes the tokens: a tubelet of t×P×Pt \times P \times Pt×P×P pixels, a 3D convolution with kernel and stride (2,16,16)(2, 16, 16)(2,16,16), makes one token from two frames, which halves TTT before attention starts; initializing it with the 2D patch filter on frame ⌊t/2⌋\lfloor t/2 \rfloor⌊t/2⌋ and zeros elsewhere, which the paper calls central-frame initialization, works best in its ablation (79.2% against 77.6% for copying the filter to every frame, with t=4t = 4t=4). ViViT compares four models: joint attention and three factorizations, from a separate spatial and temporal encoder to splitting the heads between space and time. The same factorization appears in step 5 of the Cosmos tokenizer.

NaViT · images of any shape in one packed sequence. images Ik∈RHk×Wk×3I_k \in \mathbb{R}^{H_k \times W_k \times 3}Ik​∈RHk​×Wk​×3   ⟶  \;\longrightarrow\;⟶ one sequence of ∑kNk\sum_k N_k∑k​Nk​ tokens

Nk=HkP⋅WkP,Epos(y,x)=ϕy(y)+ϕx(x)mask⁡ij={0tokens i and j come from the same image−∞otherwise\begin{aligned} N_k &= \frac{H_k}{P} \cdot \frac{W_k}{P}, \qquad E_{\text{pos}}(y, x) = \phi_y(y) + \phi_x(x) \\[4pt] \operatorname{mask}_{ij} &= \begin{cases} 0 & \text{tokens } i \text{ and } j \text{ come from the same image} \\ -\infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \end{aligned}Nk​maskij​​=PHk​​⋅PWk​​,Epos​(y,x)=ϕy​(y)+ϕx​(x)={0−∞​tokens i and j come from the same imageotherwise​​

ViT resizes every image to one square. NaViT keeps each image's aspect ratio, patches it, and concatenates the patches of several images into one sequence of fixed length, as LLM training packs documents. The block-diagonal mask keeps each image to itself, pooling is per image, and positions come from one table per axis, so any grid has positions. Example: a 224×160224 \times 160224×160 and a 96×22496 \times 22496×224 image give 14⋅10=14014 \cdot 10 = 14014⋅10=140 and 6⋅14=846 \cdot 14 = 846⋅14=84 tokens, one sequence of 224224224. During training the resolution is sampled per image and a random fraction of tokens is dropped, so the model sees about five times more images for the same compute, and NaViT matches the best ViT with four times less compute. Qwen2-VL's encoder in Chapter 4 takes the whole idea: it cites NaViT and packs images of different sizes into one sequence, with 2D RoPE in place of a position table. SigLIP 2's NaFlex variant takes only the native aspect ratio: one padded image per sequence, with its learned position table resized to the patch grid.

DiT · a transformer as the diffusion denoiser. xt∈R32×32×4, t, y  ⟶  (ϵ^,Σ^)x_t \in \mathbb{R}^{32 \times 32 \times 4},\ t,\ y \;\longrightarrow\; (\hat\epsilon, \hat\Sigma)xt​∈R32×32×4, t, y⟶(ϵ^,Σ^), both 32×32×432 \times 32 \times 432×32×4

The noisy latent of a 256 px image, from the Stable Diffusion VAE, is cut into p×p=2×2p \times p = 2 \times 2p×p=2×2 patches, T=(32/2)2=256T = (32/2)^2 = 256T=(32/2)2=256 tokens. The timestep ttt and the class yyy steer every block through adaLN-Zero:

(β1,γ1,α1,β2,γ2,α2)=WSiLU⁡(et+ey),W∈R6D×D, W=0 at firstx←x+α1⊙MSA⁡((1+γ1)⊙LN⁡(x)+β1)x←x+α2⊙MLP⁡((1+γ2)⊙LN⁡(x)+β2)\begin{aligned} (\beta_1, \gamma_1, \alpha_1, \beta_2, \gamma_2, \alpha_2) &= W \operatorname{SiLU}(e_t + e_y), && W \in \mathbb{R}^{6D \times D},\ W = 0 \text{ at first} \\[4pt] x &\leftarrow x + \alpha_1 \odot \operatorname{MSA}\big((1 + \gamma_1) \odot \operatorname{LN}(x) + \beta_1\big) \\[4pt] x &\leftarrow x + \alpha_2 \odot \operatorname{MLP}\big((1 + \gamma_2) \odot \operatorname{LN}(x) + \beta_2\big) \end{aligned}(β1​,γ1​,α1​,β2​,γ2​,α2​)xx​=WSiLU(et​+ey​),←x+α1​⊙MSA((1+γ1​)⊙LN(x)+β1​)←x+α2​⊙MLP((1+γ2​)⊙LN(x)+β2​)​W∈R6D×D, W=0 at first

ete_tet​ is a sinusoidal embedding of ttt passed through an MLP and eye_yey​ a learned class embedding, both in RD\mathbb{R}^DRD. The LayerNorms have no learned scale and shift of their own; γ\gammaγ and β\betaβ come from the condition, one value per channel. With W=0W = 0W=0 every α\alphaα is 000, so each block starts as the identity. On ImageNet 256 after 400K steps, adaLN-Zero reaches FID 19.5 against 25.2 for adaLN, 26.1 for cross-attention and 35.2 for appending the condition as tokens. The last layer maps each token to p×p×2⋅4p \times p \times 2 \cdot 4p×p×2⋅4 numbers, the noise and a diagonal covariance. DiT-XL/2 (28 layers, D=1152D = 1152D=1152, 119 GFLOPs) reaches FID 2.27 with classifier-free guidance, and FID falls steadily as GFLOPs grow, whether by a larger configuration (S to XL, deeper and wider together) or by smaller patches. It is the denoiser of diffusion written as a transformer, the design that later video and image generators build on.

The model line. Ordered by the first arXiv version.

ModelTokens and shapeAttentionTrained withWhat it changed
ViT, 202016×1616 \times 1616×16 patches, one gridgloballabels on JFT-300M or ImageNet-21kA plain Transformer on patches matches the best CNNs, given enough data.
DeiT, 2020as ViT, plus a distillation tokenglobalImageNet-1k and a CNN teacherViT without extra data, in about two days on one 8-GPU node: augmentation, regularization, distillation.
TimeSformer, 20218 frames of 16×1616 \times 1616×16 patchestime, then spaceImageNet weights, then video labelsVideo at a fraction of joint attention's cost.
PVT, 2021pyramid, strides 4 to 32keys and values reduced by RRRlabelsThe first pyramid ViT, a backbone for dense prediction.
Swin, 2021pyramid by patch mergingshifted 7×77 \times 77×7 windows, relative biaslabelsLinear cost and ResNet strides: the 2021 detection and segmentation backbone.
ViViT, 20212×16×162 \times 16 \times 162×16×16 tubeletsjoint and three factorizations comparedImageNet or JFT weights, then video labelsTokens that span time, and a map of how to factorize space-time.
DINO, 2021one gridglobalself-distillation, no labelsLabel-free features; attention maps segment objects.
BEiT, 2021one grid, about 40% maskedglobalmasked patches to dVAE token idsBERT's masked prediction for images.
MAE, 2021the encoder sees 25% of the patchesglobalmasked pixel reconstructionSimple, fast self-supervised pretraining that scales to ViT-H.
ViTDet, 2022one grid, pyramid built at the end14×1414 \times 1414×14 windows plus 4 global blocksMAE, then detectionA plain ViT is enough for detection.
DiT, 20222×22 \times 22×2 patches of a VAE latentglobal, conditioned by adaLN-Zerodiffusion denoisingThe transformer replaces the U-Net in diffusion; quality follows GFLOPs.
SAM, 2023ViT-H/16 at 1024 pxwindows plus 4 global blocksMAE, then 1.1B masksPromptable segmentation on the ViTDet design.
DINOv2, 202314×1414 \times 1414×14 patchesglobalDINO and iBOT on 142M curated imagesFrozen general-purpose features for classification, segmentation and depth.
NaViT, 2023any aspect ratio, packedglobal within each imagelabels or image–text pairsNative resolution, the ancestor of dynamic-resolution VLM encoders.
Registers, 2023plus 4 register tokensglobalas the base modelRemoves the high-norm artifact tokens of large ViTs.
DINOv3, 2025ViT-7B/16 with RoPE and registersglobalDINO and iBOT, then Gram anchoringRepairs dense features that degrade during very long training.

What the line shows.

  • Tokens: square patches on one grid (ViT), then pyramids like a CNN's (PVT, Swin) and tubes of video (TimeSformer, ViViT), then one grid again with the pyramid built at the end (ViTDet), and finally any aspect ratio (NaViT).
  • Attention range: global attention is restricted only where the tokens are many: windows for high-resolution detection and segmentation (Swin, ViTDet, SAM), spatially reduced keys (PVT), one axis at a time for video (TimeSformer). At 224 px plain global attention stayed, and FlashAttention made it cheaper still.
  • Training signal: labels on 300M images (ViT), then ImageNet with a teacher (DeiT), then no labels at all (DINO, BEiT, MAE), and image–text pairs (CLIP, SigLIP). Image–text pretraining is still the usual route for VLM encoders, and SigLIP 2 adds masked prediction and self-distillation to it as extra losses; label-free self-distillation (DINOv2, DINOv3) gives the strongest frozen dense features.
  • What won: the plain ViT. It is the encoder of CLIP, SigLIP and every VLM in Chapter 4, the denoiser of DiT and the backbone of SAM; hierarchical designs survive mostly as detection and segmentation backbones.

Code. Read it in VS Code: vision_transformers.py writes the mechanisms of ViT, DeiT, registers, Swin, PVT, MAE, DINO, TimeSformer, ViViT, NaViT and DiT as small modules, in the order above, and test_vision_transformers.py checks the fast implementations against direct ones, such as shifted windows against masked global attention in image coordinates, and pins each formula of this section.

04VLM: From Image and Question to Answer2 sections
Chapter link ↗

One image and one question, followed through every equation of the classic projector-based vision-language model: a ViT vision encoder, a small MLP projector, and a decoder-only LLM (LLaVA, LLaVA-1.5). The format is that of Chapter 3: each step states its input, the operation, and its output, with the toy shapes next to the general ones and the real LLaVA-1.5 sizes in the final table. Attention (MHA⁡\operatorname{MHA}MHA), FFN⁡\operatorname{FFN}FFN, LN⁡\operatorname{LN}LN, the causal mask, and cross-entropy are those of Chapter 3 and are not derived again. The PyTorch implementation at the end transcribes these equations and trains the toy model.

This is your TikTok and AquaVLM territory — expect the deepest questioning here.

The example. A tiny RGB image III of a cat, the question what is this ?, and the answer a cat. The text is one token sequence with a placeholder <image> where the picture goes:

Cut the image into a grid of non-overlapping P×PP \times PP×P squares and flatten each one into a row. A patch plays the role of a word, and reading the grid left to right, top to bottom gives the "sentence". Shapes: [8,8,3]→[4,48][8, 8, 3] \to [4, 48][8,8,3]→[4,48].

The block of Chapter 3 in pre-norm order: LN⁡\operatorname{LN}LN is applied to the input of each sublayer and the residual path is left untouched. There is no mask, so every patch reads every patch in both directions; an image has no future to hide. Scores are [4,4][4, 4][4,4] per head, and the FFN uses GELU instead of ReLU. A two-layer MLP applied to each patch vector on its own, like an FFN. The vision encoder and the LLM are downloaded already trained, each on its own task: CLIP learned to match images with their captions, the LLM learned to predict the next word. Only the projector between them starts from noise. Training the VLM then takes two stages that minimize the same loss L\mathcal{L}L of step 9 over different sets of weights:

Every update is ordinary gradient descent on the trainable set. In stage 1:

θproj←θproj−η ∇θprojL,∇θprojL=∂L∂U⋅∂U∂θproj\theta_{\text{proj}} \leftarrow \theta_{\text{proj}} - \eta\, \nabla_{\theta_{\text{proj}}} \mathcal{L}, \qquad \nabla_{\theta_{\text{proj}}} \mathcal{L} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial U} \cdot \frac{\partial U}{\partial \theta_{\text{proj}}}θproj​←θproj​−η∇θproj​​L,∇θproj​​L=∂U∂L​⋅∂θproj​∂U​

Frozen means not updated, not skipped. The forward pass still runs through the frozen LLM, and ∂L/∂U\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial U∂L/∂U is obtained by backpropagating from the loss through every frozen LLM layer down to the image positions of X0X_0X0​; the optimizer simply holds no weights of the LLM.

The order of the stages matters. At the start the projector emits noise, and letting that noise update a pretrained LLM would damage its language ability. So the small new module is trained first, with a large learning rate, until what it writes looks like input the LLM already understands; only then is the LLM allowed to move, with a learning rate fifty times smaller. The vision encoder stays frozen because its features are already good and updating it is expensive; later models unfreeze it with a small learning rate to gain fine detail and OCR.

U=Proj⁡(ViT⁡(I)) once;t^j+1=arg max⁡v Zjout([ BOS; U; question; t^≤j ])v,stop at EOSU = \operatorname{Proj}\big(\operatorname{ViT}(I)\big) \ \text{once}; \qquad \hat t_{j+1} = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{v}\ Z^{\text{out}}_j\big([\,\text{BOS};\ U;\ \text{question};\ \hat t_{\le j}\,]\big)_v, \qquad \text{stop at EOS}U=Proj(ViT(I)) once;t^j+1​=vargmax​ Zjout​([BOS; U; question; t^≤j​])v​,stop at EOS

The image is encoded once and its tokens sit in the prefix, so with a KV cache (Chapter 7, step 2) they are paid for in prefill only. The prefix has 1+N1 + N1+N positions plus the question, and NNN dominates: 576576576 image tokens against a question of perhaps 202020. That makes the image resolution the main cost lever of a VLM.

Attention in the LLM costs O(L2d)O(L^2 d)O(L2d) with L≈N+mL \approx N + mL≈N+m. Doubling the side of the image gives 4N4N4N patches, so about 16×16\times16× the attention work in prefill and 4×4\times4× the KV cache, before a single word of the answer is produced.

Classic models, from CLIP to today#

Every model in the line answers the same four questions, and they are the steps of the walkthrough: which vision encoder (steps 1–3), how the image reaches the language model (steps 4 and 6), how many image tokens that costs (the NNN of step 1), and what is trained (step 10). The history below is the history of those four choices.

Three ways for the image to reach the language model. With Z∈RN×dvZ \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d_v}Z∈RN×dv​ the patch features of step 3:

  1. Contrastive dual encoder. No language model at all: an image encoder fff and a text encoder ggg are trained so that matching pairs score high, s(I,T)=cos⁡(f(I), g(T))/τs(I, T) = \cos\big(f(I),\ g(T)\big) / \taus(I,T)=cos(f(I), g(T))/τ. It can rank and retrieve but cannot write text. CLIP, SigLIP.
  2. Projection into the input (this chapter). U=MLP⁡(Z)∈RN×dU = \operatorname{MLP}(Z) \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}U=MLP(Z)∈RN×d is spliced into the token sequence and read by ordinary self-attention. Every patch is kept, so the token count follows the resolution. Simple, cheap, dominant: LLaVA, InternVL, Qwen2-VL and its successors, Gemma 3, MobileVLM.
  3. Resampler. U=MHA⁡(Q,Z,Z)∈RK×dU = \operatorname{MHA}(Q, Z, Z) \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times d}U=MHA(Q,Z,Z)∈RK×d: KKK learned query vectors QQQ cross-attend to the patches, so the output has KKK tokens whatever NNN is. It compresses hard and loses fine detail. BLIP-2's Q-Former with K=32K = 32K=32, Qwen-VL with K=256K = 256K=256.

The model line. The column "way in" uses the numbers of the list above.

ModelVision encoderWay inImage tokensWhat it changed

What the line shows.

  • Vision encoder: CLIP, then SigLIP and SigLIP 2, then encoders built for variable resolution (2D-RoPE, window attention, native aspect ratio).
  • Way in: the resampler was the early answer because it keeps the sequence short. Plain projection won, because keeping every patch preserves the detail that OCR and grounding need; compression moved to a cheap 2×2 merge in front of the MLP.
  • Image tokens: one fixed low resolution, then tiles, then native dynamic resolution. The token count has become a budget that the user sets.
  • Training: two frozen models and a small bridge (BLIP-2), then the two stages of step 10 (LLaVA), then joint training of all parts at scale (Qwen2-VL and later), and finally multimodal data in pretraining itself (InternVL3).

PyTorch implementation: ViT + projector + LLM#

vlm_vit_projector_llm.py implements the eleven steps and reuses the attention module of Chapter 3. It is a toy with random initial weights, so the demo also plays the part of pretraining. The tests check that patching equals a strided convolution, that the vision encoder is bidirectional while the LLM is causal, that only answer positions carry loss, and that each stage updates only its own parameters.

bash
.venv-transformer/bin/python vlm_vit_projector_llm.py                   # runs the example below
.venv-transformer/bin/python -m unittest -v test_vlm_vit_projector_llm  # 10 tests
python
import torch
from torch import Tensor, nn
from torch.nn import functional as F

from transformer_encoder_decoder import MultiHeadAttention  # Chapter 2, step 2

IGNORE = -100  # label of a position that is not trained on (F.cross_entropy's ignore_index)

Steps 1 and 2 — patches and patch embeddings. patchify is the vec⁡\operatorname{vec}vec of step 1 written as reshape and permute; the linear layer is WEW^{E}WE and the parameter positions is PvisP^{\text{vis}}Pvis.

python
def patchify(images: Tensor, patch: int) -> Tensor:
    """Step 1: [B, C, H, W] -> [B, N, P*P*C], patches in row-major order."""
    B, C, H, W = images.shape                                     # PyTorch stores images channel-first
    x = images.reshape(B, C, H // patch, patch, W // patch, patch)
    x = x.permute(0, 2, 4, 3, 5, 1)                               # [B, H/P, W/P, P, P, C]
    return x.reshape(B, (H // patch) * (W // patch), patch * patch * C)


class PatchEmbedding(nn.Module):
    """Step 2:  Z0 = X_p W_E + b_E + P_vis.  Equal to Conv2d(C, d_v, kernel=P, stride=P)."""

    def __init__(self, image_size: int, patch: int, channels: int, d_vision: int):
        super().__init__()
        self.patch = patch
        self.linear = nn.Linear(patch * patch * channels, d_vision)                        # W_E, b_E
        self.positions = nn.Parameter(0.02 * torch.randn((image_size // patch) ** 2, d_vision))  # P_vis

    def forward(self, images: Tensor) -> Tensor:
        return self.linear(patchify(images, self.patch)) + self.positions                  # [B, N, d_v]

Steps 3 and 7 — one pre-norm block, two uses. Without a mask it is a ViT layer; with the causal mask it is an LLM layer.

python
class Block(nn.Module):
    """Steps 3 and 7, pre-norm:  x' = x + MHA(LN(x));  x = x' + FFN(LN(x'))."""

    def __init__(self, d_model: int, num_heads: int, d_ff: int):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.attention = MultiHeadAttention(d_model, num_heads)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.ffn = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model))

    def forward(self, x: Tensor, mask: Tensor = None) -> Tensor:
        h = self.norm1(x)
        x = x + self.attention(h, h, h, mask)   # mask=None: every token reads every token
        return x + self.ffn(self.norm2(x))

Steps 3 and 4 — vision encoder and projector.

python
class VisionEncoder(nn.Module):
    """Steps 1-3: image -> one contextual vector per patch. No mask, so it is bidirectional."""

    def __init__(self, image_size: int = 8, patch: int = 4, channels: int = 3,
                 d_vision: int = 8, num_heads: int = 2, num_layers: int = 2):
        super().__init__()
        self.d_vision = d_vision
        self.embed = PatchEmbedding(image_size, patch, channels, d_vision)
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList(Block(d_vision, num_heads, 4 * d_vision) for _ in range(num_layers))

    def forward(self, images: Tensor) -> Tensor:
        z = self.embed(images)        # steps 1-2: [B, C, H, W] -> [B, N, d_v]
        for layer in self.layers:
            z = layer(z)              # step 3
        return z                      # Z: [B, N, d_v]


class Projector(nn.Module):
    """Step 4:  U = GELU(Z W_1 + b_1) W_2 + b_2, from the vision width d_v to the LLM width d."""

    def __init__(self, d_vision: int, d_model: int):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear1 = nn.Linear(d_vision, d_model)
        self.linear2 = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)

    def forward(self, z: Tensor) -> Tensor:
        return self.linear2(F.gelu(self.linear1(z)))   # [B, N, d_v] -> [B, N, d]

Steps 5 to 11 — the whole model, the answer loss, the stages, and generation. splice finds the placeholder and puts the image tokens in its place; splice_labels gives the image positions the label IGNORE; set_stage switches requires_grad; generate encodes the image once.

python
class VLM(nn.Module):
    """Steps 1-8: image + text ids -> next-token logits over the vocabulary."""

    def __init__(self, vocab_size: int, image_token_id: int, d_model: int = 16, num_heads: int = 2,
                 num_layers: int = 2, max_len: int = 64, vision: VisionEncoder = None):
        super().__init__()
        self.image_token_id = image_token_id
        self.vision = vision if vision is not None else VisionEncoder()
        self.projector = Projector(self.vision.d_vision, d_model)
        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)                      # E
        self.positions = nn.Parameter(0.02 * torch.randn(max_len, d_model))     # P_txt (real LLMs: RoPE)
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList(Block(d_model, num_heads, 4 * d_model) for _ in range(num_layers))
        self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.vocab_projection = nn.Linear(d_model, vocab_size, bias=False)      # W_vocab

    def encode_image(self, images: Tensor) -> Tensor:
        return self.projector(self.vision(images))                 # steps 1-4: [B, C, H, W] -> [B, N, d]

    def splice(self, text_ids: Tensor, image_tokens: Tensor) -> Tensor:
        """Steps 5-6: embed the text, then put the N image tokens where <image> stands."""
        text = self.embedding(text_ids)                                         # T: [B, m, d]
        rows = []
        for b in range(text_ids.shape[0]):
            k = (text_ids[b] == self.image_token_id).nonzero()[0, 0]            # position of <image>
            rows.append(torch.cat([text[b, :k], image_tokens[b], text[b, k + 1:]]))
        x = torch.stack(rows)                                                   # [B, L, d], L = m - 1 + N
        return x + self.positions[:x.shape[1]]

    def splice_labels(self, text_ids: Tensor, text_labels: Tensor, num_image_tokens: int) -> Tensor:
        """Labels for the spliced sequence: image positions are never trained on."""
        ignore = torch.full((num_image_tokens,), IGNORE, dtype=text_labels.dtype, device=text_labels.device)
        rows = []
        for b in range(text_ids.shape[0]):
            k = (text_ids[b] == self.image_token_id).nonzero()[0, 0]
            rows.append(torch.cat([text_labels[b, :k], ignore, text_labels[b, k + 1:]]))
        return torch.stack(rows)                                                # [B, L]

    def forward(self, images: Tensor, text_ids: Tensor, image_tokens: Tensor = None) -> Tensor:
        if image_tokens is None:
            image_tokens = self.encode_image(images)
        x = self.splice(text_ids, image_tokens)                                 # X0: [B, L, d]
        L = x.shape[1]
        causal = torch.ones(L, L, dtype=torch.bool, device=x.device).tril()[None, None]  # [1, 1, L, L]
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x, causal)                                                # step 7
        return self.vocab_projection(self.norm(x))                              # step 8: [B, L, V]


def answer_loss(logits: Tensor, labels: Tensor) -> Tensor:
    """Step 9: cross-entropy averaged over the answer positions only."""
    return F.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, logits.shape[-1]), labels.reshape(-1), ignore_index=IGNORE)


def set_stage(model: VLM, stage: int) -> None:
    """Step 10: which parameters are updated. The vision encoder stays frozen throughout.

    0 = the LLM alone (stands in for language pretraining), 1 = the projector alone (alignment),
    2 = projector and LLM (instruction tuning).
    """
    for parameter in model.parameters():
        parameter.requires_grad = stage in (0, 2)
    for parameter in model.vision.parameters():
        parameter.requires_grad = False
    for parameter in model.projector.parameters():
        parameter.requires_grad = stage in (1, 2)


@torch.no_grad()
def generate(model: VLM, images: Tensor, prompt_ids: Tensor, eos_id: int = 2, pad_id: int = 0,
             max_new_tokens: int = 8) -> Tensor:
    """Step 11: encode the image once, then append argmax tokens until every row produced EOS."""
    image_tokens = model.encode_image(images)
    ids = prompt_ids
    finished = torch.zeros(ids.shape[0], dtype=torch.bool, device=ids.device)
    for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
        next_id = model(images, ids, image_tokens)[:, -1].argmax(dim=-1)        # last row of Z only
        next_id = torch.where(finished, pad_id, next_id)
        ids = torch.cat([ids, next_id[:, None]], dim=1)
        finished |= next_id == eos_id
        if finished.all():
            break
    return ids

The example, step by step, then trained. main() prints the shape of every step for the cat example. It then trains on two examples with the same question, a cat image answered a cat and a dog image answered a dog, so the answer can only come from the image. Stage 0 stands in for a pretrained LLM: the image slot holds the four words of a caption (photo of a cat), and the LLM learns to answer from them. Stage 1 puts the real image tokens in the slot and trains the projector alone; stage 2 trains projector and LLM together. The toy vision encoder is never trained: its random features are already enough to tell the two images apart, which is the part CLIP pretraining plays in a real model.

python
VOCAB = ["<pad>", "<bos>", "<eos>", "<image>", "what", "is", "this", "?", "a", "cat", "dog", "photo", "of"]


def toy_batch():
    """Two 8x8 images that differ in which patch is bright, the same question, different answers."""
    cat, dog = torch.zeros(3, 8, 8), torch.zeros(3, 8, 8)
    cat[:, :4, :4] = 1.0                                   # top-left patch bright     -> "a cat"
    dog[:, 4:, 4:] = 1.0                                   # bottom-right patch bright -> "a dog"
    full = torch.tensor([[1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 2],      # BOS <image> what is this ? a cat EOS
                         [1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 2]])    # BOS <image> what is this ? a dog EOS
    text_ids, next_ids = full[:, :-1], full[:, 1:].clone() # input and next token at every position
    next_ids[:, :-3] = IGNORE                              # only the answer (a, cat/dog, EOS) is a label
    captions = torch.tensor([[11, 12, 8, 9],               # photo of a cat
                             [11, 12, 8, 10]])             # photo of a dog
    return torch.stack([cat, dog]), text_ids, next_ids, captions


def words(ids) -> str:
    return " ".join(VOCAB[i] for i in ids)


def train(model: VLM, stage: int, forward, labels: Tensor, steps: int, lr: float = 1e-2):
    """Minimize the answer loss over the parameters that the stage leaves trainable."""
    set_stage(model, stage)
    trainable = [parameter for parameter in model.parameters() if parameter.requires_grad]
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(trainable, lr=lr)
    before = answer_loss(forward(), labels).item()
    for _ in range(steps):
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = answer_loss(forward(), labels)
        loss.backward()                                    # gradients pass through the frozen parts
        optimizer.step()
    return sum(parameter.numel() for parameter in trainable), before, loss.item()


def main() -> None:
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    images, text_ids, text_labels, captions = toy_batch()
    model = VLM(vocab_size=len(VOCAB), image_token_id=3)
    I, t = images[:1], text_ids[:1]                        # the cat example, B = 1
    print("t =", t[0].tolist(), "=", words(t[0]), "\n")

    def show(step: str, name: str, tensor: Tensor) -> Tensor:
        print(f"step {step:<3} {name:<34} {list(tensor.shape)}")
        return tensor

    show("0", "I (channel-first)", I)
    show("1", "X_p = patchify(I)", patchify(I, 4))
    show("2", "Z0 = X_p W_E + b_E + P_vis", model.vision.embed(I))
    Z = show("3", "Z = ViT(Z0)", model.vision(I))
    show("3", "    attention weights, per head", model.vision.layers[-1].attention.attention_weights)
    U = show("4", "U = projector(Z)", model.projector(Z))
    show("5", "T = E[t]", model.embedding(t))
    show("6", "X0 = splice(T, U) + P_txt", model.splice(t, U))
    logits = model(I, t)
    show("7", "    causal weights, per head", model.layers[-1].attention.attention_weights)
    show("8", "Z_out = LN(X) W_vocab", logits)

    labels = model.splice_labels(text_ids, text_labels, U.shape[1])             # both examples: [2, 11]
    print("\nlabels y =", labels[0].tolist())
    print(f"step 9   loss over positions 8, 9, 10 = {answer_loss(logits, labels[:1]).item():.4f}  (untrained)\n")

    total = sum(parameter.numel() for parameter in model.parameters())
    with_words = lambda: model(None, text_ids, model.embedding(captions))       # a caption fills the image slot
    with_images = lambda: model(images, text_ids)                               # projected patches fill it
    for stage, forward, steps, note in ((0, with_words, 300, "LLM, caption words in the image slot"),
                                        (1, with_images, 300, "projector only, real image tokens"),
                                        (2, with_images, 100, "projector + LLM")):
        count, before, after = train(model, stage, forward, labels, steps)
        print(f"step 10  stage {stage} ({note}): {count} of {total} parameters, loss {before:.3f} -> {after:.3f}")

    model.eval()
    prompt = text_ids[:, :6]                               # BOS <image> what is this ?
    for name, ids in zip(("cat image", "dog image"), generate(model, images, prompt)):
        print(f"step 11  {name}: {words(ids.tolist())}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

With an untrained projector the frozen LLM finds noise in the image slot and the loss jumps from 0.0010.0010.001 to 1.3711.3711.371. Training 416416416 projector parameters brings it back to 0.0010.0010.001: the projector has learned to write the image in a form the LLM already reads. The projected tokens need not coincide with the embedding of any word; they only need to have the same effect on the LLM.

05Post-Training: LoRA1 section
Chapter link ↗

Post-training is everything done to a pretrained model to shape its behaviour: supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, then preference optimization such as DPO or GRPO. Each stage minimizes a loss over the weights exactly as in steps 9–10 of Chapter 3; what differs between stages is the data and the loss. The question they all share is which weights are allowed to move and what that costs, and the standard answer is LoRA (Hu et al., 2021): keep every pretrained matrix frozen and learn a small low-rank correction next to it. This chapter follows one weight matrix through LoRA, with the input and output of every step, and ends with a PyTorch implementation that post-trains the toy Transformer of Chapter 3.

Your resume says "SFT & RL post-training": expect to be asked what exactly is trained, why it fits in memory, and what it cannot do.

The example. The toy Transformer of Chapter 3 (d=8d = 8d=8, h=2h = 2h=2, dff=32d_{ff} = 32dff​=32) is first trained on two sentence pairs, which stands in for pretraining, and then post-trained on a third pair, we watch video → nous regardons video, that it gets wrong. Every attention module holds four matrices WQ,WK,WV,WO∈R8×8W^{Q}, W^{K}, W^{V}, W^{O} \in \mathbb{R}^{8 \times 8}WQ,WK,WV,WO∈R8×8, and LoRA with r=2r = 2r=2 is put on all of them. The real-size reference is LLaMA-7B, where the same matrices are 4096×40964096 \times 40964096×4096 and r=16r = 16r=16 is typical.

Where LoRA enters Chapter 3. Nothing in the walkthrough is rewritten; a few of its matrices get a correction next to them:

Chapter 3 stepmatricesin the toywith LoRA
step 1, embeddings EEE and positions PPPfrozenunchanged

Done once after training, step 2 is again the plain Q=XWQ′Q = X W^{Q\prime}Q=XWQ′ of Chapter 3 with a matrix of the original shape: no extra parameters, no extra latency. Subtracting the same term restores WQW^{Q}WQ, and one frozen model can serve several tasks by swapping the small pairs.

Step 9 · Rank, scale, and where. (r, α, which matrices)  ⟶  capacity and cost(r,\ \alpha,\ \text{which matrices}) \;\longrightarrow\; \text{capacity and cost}(r, α, which matrices)⟶capacity and cost

The rank bounds how much can be learned: r=8r = 8r=8 to 161616 is enough to change format or style, r=64r = 64r=64 to 128128128 is used when a genuinely new capability is taught. α\alphaα is usually set to 2r2r2r, which keeps the size of ΔQ\Delta QΔQ comparable when rrr changes. Adapting the FFN matrices W1,W2W_1, W_2W1​,W2​ of step 4 as well as the projections of step 2 is closer to full fine-tuning than adapting attention only. The usual recipe for a vision-language model, step 10 of Chapter 4, is to freeze the vision encoder, put LoRA on the LLM, and train the projector in full.

Step 10 · What LoRA does not do. θfrozen  ⟶  θfrozen\theta_{\text{frozen}} \;\longrightarrow\; \theta_{\text{frozen}}θfrozen​⟶θfrozen​

LoRA matches full fine-tuning on narrow adaptation and, because the base weights are untouched, forgets less; it underperforms when a task needs substantial new knowledge, and a task where LoRA fails badly is a task that needs full fine-tuning. Less forgetting is not none: in the toy below, training the adapters on the new pair alone makes the model answer the old pairs with the new sentence, and mixing the old pairs into the post-training data is what keeps them. QLoRA stores the frozen weights in 4 bits and trains the adapters in bf16; DoRA splits the correction into a magnitude and a direction.

PyTorch implementation: LoRA on the toy Transformer#

lora_linear.py wraps any nn.Linear in the layer of steps 2–4 and applies it to the projections WQ,WK,WV,WOW^{Q}, W^{K}, W^{V}, W^{O}WQ,WK,WV,WO of every attention module of the model of Chapter 3. The tests check that the layer starts exactly at the pretrained one, that only WdownW_{\text{down}}Wdown​ and WupW_{\text{up}}Wup​ receive gradients and that those gradients match the formulas of step 6, that ΔWQ\Delta W^{Q}ΔWQ has rank at most rrr, that merging is exact, and that post-training the toy model leaves every frozen weight bitwise unchanged.

bash
.venv-transformer/bin/python lora_linear.py                   # runs the example below
.venv-transformer/bin/python -m unittest -v test_lora_linear  # 8 tests
python
import math

import torch
from torch import Tensor, nn
from torch.nn import functional as F

from transformer_encoder_decoder import Transformer, greedy_decode   # the toy model of Chapter 2

Steps 2 to 4 and 8 — the layer. down is WdownW_{\text{down}}Wdown​ (random) and up is WupW_{\text{up}}Wup​ (zero); forward multiplies by down before up, and merge folds ΔWQ\Delta W^{Q}ΔWQ into the stored weight, which PyTorch keeps transposed as [d_out, d_in].

python
class LoRALinear(nn.Module):
    """Q = X W_Q + (alpha / r) (X W_down) W_up, with W_Q frozen and only W_down, W_up trainable."""

    def __init__(self, base: nn.Linear, r: int, alpha: float):
        super().__init__()
        self.base = base
        for parameter in base.parameters():
            parameter.requires_grad = False                            # step 2: W_Q (and a bias) frozen
        d_in, d_out = base.in_features, base.out_features
        self.scale = alpha / r                                         # alpha / r
        self.down = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(d_in, r) / math.sqrt(d_in))   # W_down: random, so that W_up gets a gradient
        self.up = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(r, d_out))                       # W_up: zero, so that Delta W = 0 at the start
        self.merged = False

    def delta_w(self) -> Tensor:
        return self.scale * self.down @ self.up                        # Delta W: [d, d], rank <= r

    def forward(self, x: Tensor) -> Tensor:
        q = self.base(x)                                               # step 2: X W_Q
        if self.merged:
            return q
        return q + self.scale * (x @ self.down) @ self.up              # steps 3-4: X W_down first, then W_up

    @torch.no_grad()
    def merge(self) -> None:
        """Step 8: W_Q <- W_Q + Delta W, once. The layer then costs exactly what a plain Linear costs."""
        if not self.merged:
            self.base.weight += self.delta_w().T                       # weight is stored as [d_out, d_in]
            self.merged = True

    @torch.no_grad()
    def unmerge(self) -> None:
        if self.merged:
            self.base.weight -= self.delta_w().T
            self.merged = False

Step 1 — which weights. add_lora freezes the whole model and replaces every Linear called w_q, w_k, w_v or w_o by the wrapped layer; the two helpers merge all adapters and count parameters.

python
def add_lora(model: nn.Module, r: int, alpha: float, names=("w_q", "w_k", "w_v", "w_o")) -> list:
    """Step 1: freeze the whole model, then wrap every Linear called `names` (W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O) in a LoRALinear."""
    for parameter in model.parameters():
        parameter.requires_grad = False
    adapters = []
    for module in list(model.modules()):
        for name, child in list(module.named_children()):
            if isinstance(child, nn.Linear) and name in names:
                adapter = LoRALinear(child, r, alpha)
                setattr(module, name, adapter)
                adapters.append(adapter)
    return adapters


def merge_all(model: nn.Module) -> None:
    for module in model.modules():
        if isinstance(module, LoRALinear):
            module.merge()


def count_parameters(model: nn.Module) -> tuple:
    trainable = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad)
    return trainable, sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())

The example. main() trains the toy model in full on two pairs, which stands in for pretraining, adds LoRA with r=2r = 2r=2, and post-trains only WdownW_{\text{down}}Wdown​ and WupW_{\text{up}}Wup​ on the new pair mixed with the two old ones. It then checks that the frozen weights did not change and that merging does not change the logits.

python
SRC = ["<pad>", "<bos>", "<eos>", "we", "watch", "a", "short", "video", "you"]
TGT = ["<pad>", "<bos>", "<eos>", "nous", "regardons", "video", "une", "courte", "tu", "regardes"]


def example(source: str, target: str) -> tuple:
    """Source ids, teacher-forcing decoder input (BOS + target) and next-token labels (target + EOS)."""
    s = torch.tensor([[SRC.index(word) for word in source.split()]])
    full = torch.tensor([[1] + [TGT.index(word) for word in target.split()] + [2]])
    return s, full[:, :-1], full[:, 1:]


def train(model: nn.Module, examples: list, steps: int, lr: float = 1e-2) -> float:
    """Minimize the next-token loss of Chapter 2 over whatever parameters are trainable."""
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([p for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad], lr=lr)
    for _ in range(steps):
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = sum(F.cross_entropy(model(s, t).reshape(-1, len(TGT)), y.reshape(-1), ignore_index=0)
                   for s, t, y in examples) / len(examples)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
    return loss.item()


def translate(model: nn.Module, s: Tensor) -> str:
    return " ".join(TGT[i] for i in greedy_decode(model.eval(), s)[0].tolist()[1:])


def main() -> None:
    torch.manual_seed(2)
    model = Transformer(len(SRC), len(TGT))                             # d = 8, h = 2, d_ff = 32
    old = [example("we watch a short video", "nous regardons une courte video"),
           example("you watch video", "tu regardes video")]
    new = example("we watch video", "nous regardons video")

    loss = train(model.train(), old, 400)                               # stands in for pretraining
    print(f"pretrained on two pairs (all parameters), loss {loss:.3f}")
    for s, _, _ in old + [new]:
        print(f"  {' '.join(SRC[i] for i in s[0].tolist()):24s} -> {translate(model, s)}")

    adapters = add_lora(model, r=2, alpha=4.0)                          # step 1: W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O of every attention
    frozen = {name: p.clone() for name, p in model.named_parameters() if not p.requires_grad}
    trainable, total = count_parameters(model)
    print(f"LoRA r=2 on {len(adapters)} matrices: {trainable} of {total} parameters trainable "
          f"({100 * trainable / total:.0f}%); each 8x8 matrix gets W_down [8,2] and W_up [2,8]")
    print(f"  before training Delta W = 0, so the new pair still gives: {translate(model, new[0])}")

    loss = train(model.train(), [new] + old, 300)                       # steps 5-7: only W_down and W_up move
    unchanged = all(torch.equal(p, frozen[name]) for name, p in model.named_parameters() if name in frozen)
    print(f"LoRA trained on the new pair plus the two old ones: loss {loss:.3f}, frozen weights unchanged: {unchanged}")
    for s, _, _ in [new] + old:
        print(f"  {' '.join(SRC[i] for i in s[0].tolist()):24s} -> {translate(model, s)}")

    before = model.eval()(new[0], new[1])
    merge_all(model)                                                    # step 8
    print(f"merged: same logits {torch.allclose(before, model(new[0], new[1]), atol=1e-6)}; "
          f"one attention matrix is again a plain {tuple(adapters[0].base.weight.shape)} weight")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Chapter guide: Every generative model written the same way: what one call takes and returns, the loss it is trained with, one worked example. First the autoencoder and the VAE, then the discrete tokenizers from VQ-VAE to FSQ, then GANs and diffusion, then learned compression, where the latent becomes bits, and finally the Cosmos tokenizer step by step. Chapter 3 supplies attention and the Transformer block; 01_video_domain.md supplies the classical codecs.

xxx is the input, zzz the latent, x^\hat xx^ the reconstruction; fϕf_\phifϕ​ is the encoder and gθg_\thetagθ​ the decoder; KKK is a codebook size and ddd a latent width; DDD is distortion (in 6.2.2 and 6.3.1 only, DDD is also the GAN discriminator), RRR bits, and λ\lambdaλ the price of a bit. sg⁡[⋅]\operatorname{sg}[\cdot]sg[⋅] is stop-gradient: the value passes forward, no gradient passes back.

6.1 Autoencoders & VAEs#

6.1.1 Autoencoder#

One call. x∈RH×W×3  ⟶  z=fϕ(x)∈Rh×w×d  ⟶  x^=gθ(z)∈RH×W×3x \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} \;\longrightarrow\; z = f_\phi(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times w \times d} \;\longrightarrow\; \hat x = g_\theta(z) \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}x∈RH×W×3⟶z=fϕ​(x)∈Rh×w×d⟶x^=gθ​(z)∈RH×W×3

LAE(ϕ,θ)=Ex∥x−gθ(fϕ(x))∥22\mathcal{L}_{\text{AE}}(\phi, \theta) = \mathbb{E}_x \big\lVert x - g_\theta(f_\phi(x)) \big\rVert_2^2LAE​(ϕ,θ)=Ex​​x−gθ​(fϕ​(x))​22​

The only thing that makes this more than the identity is the bottleneck: hwd≪3HWh w d \ll 3 H Whwd≪3HW, so the encoder has to choose what to keep. With a linear encoder and decoder and the squared loss, the optimum is the principal subspace of the data, PCA; the nonlinear version keeps the same idea with a curved subspace. Example: a 256×256256 \times 256256×256 RGB image is 196,608196{,}608196,608 numbers; a 16×16×25616 \times 16 \times 25616×16×256 latent is 65,53665{,}53665,536, three times fewer, but they are still floats, so nothing has been turned into bits yet.

Two things an autoencoder does not give you. There is no distribution on zzz, so a random zzz decodes to garbage: it is not a generative model. And there is no rate: the latent is as expensive as its float count. 6.4 adds quantization and an entropy model to turn zzz into bits, and the objective becomes D+λRD + \lambda RD+λR; 6.2 makes zzz discrete so that it can be transmitted or fed to a transformer.

6.1.2 VAE#

The model. A prior p(z)=N(0,I)p(z) = \mathcal{N}(0, I)p(z)=N(0,I) and a decoder pθ(x∣z)p_\theta(x \mid z)pθ​(x∣z), usually N(gθ(z),σx2I)\mathcal{N}(g_\theta(z), \sigma_x^2 I)N(gθ​(z),σx2​I) for images. The likelihood of a data point is an integral over every latent that could have produced it, and it is intractable:

pθ(x)=∫pθ(x∣z) p(z) dzp_\theta(x) = \int p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)\, dzpθ​(x)=∫pθ​(x∣z)p(z)dz

The encoder as an approximate posterior. x  ⟶  qϕ(z∣x)=N(μϕ(x), diag⁡ σϕ2(x))x \;\longrightarrow\; q_\phi(z \mid x) = \mathcal{N}\big(\mu_\phi(x),\ \operatorname{diag}\,\sigma_\phi^2(x)\big)x⟶qϕ​(z∣x)=N(μϕ​(x), diagσϕ2​(x)): the encoder returns two vectors of width ddd, a mean and a log-variance, not a point.

The ELBO. For any qqq, the log-likelihood splits exactly into three terms:

log⁡pθ(x)=Eqϕ(z∣x)[log⁡pθ(x∣z)]−DKL(qϕ(z∣x) ∥ p(z))⏟ELBO(ϕ,θ; x)+DKL(qϕ(z∣x) ∥ pθ(z∣x))⏟≥0, the gap\log p_\theta(x) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\big[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)\big] - D_{\text{KL}}\big(q_\phi(z \mid x)\,\|\,p(z)\big)}_{\text{ELBO}(\phi, \theta;\, x)} + \underbrace{D_{\text{KL}}\big(q_\phi(z \mid x)\,\|\,p_\theta(z \mid x)\big)}_{\ge 0,\ \text{the gap}}logpθ​(x)=ELBO(ϕ,θ;x)Eqϕ​(z∣x)​[logpθ​(x∣z)]−DKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∥p(z))​​+≥0, the gapDKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∥pθ​(z∣x))​​

The gap is how far the encoder's posterior is from the true one. Maximizing the ELBO therefore both raises the likelihood and tightens the bound; it cannot exceed log⁡pθ(x)\log p_\theta(x)logpθ​(x). The training loss is the negative ELBO per sample:

LVAE=Eqϕ(z∣x)[−log⁡pθ(x∣z)]⏟reconstruction+DKL(qϕ(z∣x) ∥ p(z))⏟regularization\mathcal{L}_{\text{VAE}} = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\big[-\log p_\theta(x \mid z)\big]}_{\text{reconstruction}} + \underbrace{D_{\text{KL}}\big(q_\phi(z \mid x)\,\|\,p(z)\big)}_{\text{regularization}}LVAE​=reconstructionEqϕ​(z∣x)​[−logpθ​(x∣z)]​​+regularizationDKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∥p(z))​​

With the Gaussian decoder, −log⁡pθ(x∣z)=∥x−gθ(z)∥2/(2σx2)+const-\log p_\theta(x \mid z) = \lVert x - g_\theta(z) \rVert^2 / (2\sigma_x^2) + \text{const}−logpθ​(x∣z)=∥x−gθ​(z)∥2/(2σx2​)+const, so the reconstruction term is an MSE whose weight relative to the KL is set by σx2\sigma_x^2σx2​. With a Bernoulli decoder it is binary cross-entropy.

The KL in closed form. With both distributions diagonal Gaussians:

DKL(N(μ,diag⁡σ2) ∥ N(0,I))=12∑j=1d(μj2+σj2−1−log⁡σj2)D_{\text{KL}}\big(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \operatorname{diag}\sigma^2)\,\|\,\mathcal{N}(0, I)\big) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{j=1}^{d} \big(\mu_j^2 + \sigma_j^2 - 1 - \log \sigma_j^2\big)DKL​(N(μ,diagσ2)∥N(0,I))=21​j=1∑d​(μj2​+σj2​−1−logσj2​)
TermPenalizesZero when
μj2\mu_j^2μj2​a mean away from 000μj=0\mu_j = 0μj​=0
σj2−1−log⁡σj2\sigma_j^2 - 1 - \log \sigma_j^2σj2​−1−logσj2​a variance away from 111; it is ≥0\ge 0≥0 because t−1−log⁡t≥0t - 1 - \log t \ge 0t−1−logt≥0σj=1\sigma_j = 1σj​=1

Derivation: DKL=Eq[log⁡q(z)−log⁡p(z)]D_{\text{KL}} = \mathbb{E}_q[\log q(z) - \log p(z)]DKL​=Eq​[logq(z)−logp(z)], and under qqq the expectation of (zj−μj)2/σj2(z_j - \mu_j)^2 / \sigma_j^2(zj​−μj​)2/σj2​ is 111 while that of zj2z_j^2zj2​ is μj2+σj2\mu_j^2 + \sigma_j^2μj2​+σj2​, which gives −12log⁡σj2−12+12(μj2+σj2)-\tfrac12 \log \sigma_j^2 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac12(\mu_j^2 + \sigma_j^2)−21​logσj2​−21​+21​(μj2​+σj2​) per dimension. Example with d=2d = 2d=2, μ=(0.5,0)\mu = (0.5, 0)μ=(0.5,0) and σ=(1,0.5)\sigma = (1, 0.5)σ=(1,0.5): the first dimension contributes 12⋅0.25=0.125\tfrac12 \cdot 0.25 = 0.12521​⋅0.25=0.125 nats, the second 12(0.25−1+1.386)=0.318\tfrac12 (0.25 - 1 + 1.386) = 0.31821​(0.25−1+1.386)=0.318 nats, together 0.4430.4430.443 nats, or 0.640.640.64 bits.

The reparameterization trick. The reconstruction term needs a sample z∼qϕ(z∣x)z \sim q_\phi(z \mid x)z∼qϕ​(z∣x), and a sample has no gradient with respect to μ\muμ and σ\sigmaσ. Write it as

z=μϕ(x)+σϕ(x)⊙ε,ε∼N(0,I)z = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)z=μϕ​(x)+σϕ​(x)⊙ε,ε∼N(0,I)

Now μ\muμ and σ\sigmaσ enter through ordinary arithmetic and the randomness sits in ε\varepsilonε, which has no parameters. One sample per data point is enough in practice; the KL term needs none, because it has the closed form above.

The tension, and the two failure modes. The reconstruction term wants zzz to carry everything about xxx; the KL wants every q(z∣x)q(z \mid x)q(z∣x) to equal N(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0, I)N(0,I), which carries nothing. The balance is a latent that is compact but informative, and the KL is what makes the space smooth, so that a zzz between two encodings decodes to something in between. If the KL wins completely, posterior collapse: q(z∣x)=p(z)q(z \mid x) = p(z)q(z∣x)=p(z) for every xxx, the decoder ignores zzz, which a powerful autoregressive decoder can afford. Fixes: KL warm-up, free bits (a floor on the per-dimension KL), β<1\beta < 1β<1, or a weaker decoder. If the reconstruction wins completely, the latent has no structure and sampling gives garbage.

β\betaβ-VAE is a rate–distortion objective. Weighting the KL,

Lβ=Eq[−log⁡pθ(x∣z)]+β DKL(qϕ(z∣x) ∥ p(z))\mathcal{L}_\beta = \mathbb{E}_q\big[-\log p_\theta(x \mid z)\big] + \beta\, D_{\text{KL}}\big(q_\phi(z \mid x)\,\|\,p(z)\big)Lβ​=Eq​[−logpθ​(x∣z)]+βDKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∥p(z))

is D+λRD + \lambda RD+λR with the KL as the rate: the KL in bits is the cost of transmitting zzz to a receiver who knows the prior, and β\betaβ is the exchange rate between a bit and a unit of distortion. β>1\beta > 1β>1 gives a more disentangled, blurrier model; β<1\beta < 1β<1 a sharper, less structured one. 6.4 makes this literal: a learned codec is a VAE whose prior is the entropy model and whose KL is counted by an arithmetic coder.

Coding: VAE reparameterization and diagonal-Gaussian KL [READY]View exercise
  • Prompt: implement the pathwise sample and the closed-form KL; say why the KL needs no sample and the reconstruction term needs one.
  • Shape / cost: mu, logvar: [B, d]; both functions are O(B d).
  • Pitfalls: the encoder usually returns logvar, so std = exp(0.5 * logvar); sum the KL over dimensions and average over the batch, and state which; reduce the reconstruction term the same way or β\betaβ silently changes; the closed form holds only for the diagonal-Gaussian prior and posterior.
python
def reparameterize(mu, logvar):
    std = torch.exp(0.5 * logvar)                    # sigma, from the log-variance the encoder returns
    return mu + std * torch.randn_like(std)          # z = mu + sigma * eps

def diagonal_gaussian_kl(mu, logvar):
    return 0.5 * (mu.square() + logvar.exp() - 1.0 - logvar).sum(dim=-1)   # nats, per sample

These two functions are the whole VAE-specific machinery; the rest of a VAE is an encoder, a decoder and a reconstruction loss. No local training script exists; the learned-compression scaffold is an autoencoder with noisy scalar quantization, not a VAE.

6.2 Discrete Tokenizers: VQ-VAE, VQGAN, FSQ and Friends#

A continuous latent is a grid of floats. A tokenizer turns each position into an integer, an index into a finite set of codes that encoder and decoder share, so the latent can be sent as bits or read by a transformer as a vocabulary. The models in this chapter differ in where the codes come from and in how they are trained; they share one example.

The example. A 256×256256 \times 256256×256 RGB image through an encoder with downsampling factor f=16f = 16f=16 gives a 16×1616 \times 1616×16 grid, N=256N = 256N=256 positions. With a codebook of K=1024K = 1024K=1024 codes each position costs log⁡21024=10\log_2 1024 = 10log2​1024=10 bits, so the image costs 2,5602{,}5602,560 bits before any entropy coding, about 0.040.040.04 bits per pixel. The latent width is d=256d = 256d=256 unless stated.

6.2.1 VQ-VAE#

One call. x  ⟶  ze=fϕ(x)∈RN×d  ⟶  k∈{1,…,K}N  ⟶  zq∈RN×d  ⟶  x^=gθ(zq)x \;\longrightarrow\; z_e = f_\phi(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d} \;\longrightarrow\; k \in \{1, \dots, K\}^{N} \;\longrightarrow\; z_q \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d} \;\longrightarrow\; \hat x = g_\theta(z_q)x⟶ze​=fϕ​(x)∈RN×d⟶k∈{1,…,K}N⟶zq​∈RN×d⟶x^=gθ​(zq​)

The codebook is a learned table E={e1,…,eK}⊂RdE = \{e_1, \dots, e_K\} \subset \mathbb{R}^dE={e1​,…,eK​}⊂Rd. Each encoder vector is replaced by its nearest code:

ki=arg⁡min⁡j ∥ze,i−ej∥2,zq,i=ekik_i = \underset{j}{\arg\min}\ \lVert z_{e,i} - e_j \rVert_2, \qquad z_{q,i} = e_{k_i}ki​=jargmin​ ∥ze,i​−ej​∥2​,zq,i​=eki​​

Only the indices kkk are transmitted or modeled; the decoder looks them up in the same table.

The loss has three terms, because the nearest-code step has zero gradient almost everywhere and the table would otherwise never learn:

LVQ-VAE=∥x−gθ(zq)∥22⏟reconstruction+∥sg⁡[ze]−ek∥22⏟codebook+β ∥ze−sg⁡[ek]∥22⏟commitment,β≈0.25\mathcal{L}_{\text{VQ-VAE}} = \underbrace{\big\lVert x - g_\theta(z_q) \big\rVert_2^2}_{\text{reconstruction}} + \underbrace{\big\lVert \operatorname{sg}[z_e] - e_k \big\rVert_2^2}_{\text{codebook}} + \beta\, \underbrace{\big\lVert z_e - \operatorname{sg}[e_k] \big\rVert_2^2}_{\text{commitment}}, \qquad \beta \approx 0.25LVQ-VAE​=reconstruction​x−gθ​(zq​)​22​​​+codebook​sg[ze​]−ek​​22​​​+βcommitment​ze​−sg[ek​]​22​​​,β≈0.25
TermGradient reachesWhat it does
reconstruction, through the straight-through estimator zq←ze+sg⁡[zq−ze]z_q \leftarrow z_e + \operatorname{sg}[z_q - z_e]zq​←ze​+sg[zq​−ze​]decoder, and the encoder as if zqz_qzq​ were zez_eze​the usual autoencoder signal; the table gets nothing from it
codebookthe chosen code eke_kek​ onlypulls eke_kek​ toward the encoder outputs assigned to it
commitmentthe encoder onlykeeps zez_eze​ near the code it chose, so the straight-through copy stays a good approximation

The straight-through estimator is the identity in the backward pass: the decoder's gradient at zqz_qzq​ is handed to zez_eze​ unchanged. It is a biased estimate, and the commitment term is what keeps the bias small by keeping ∥ze−ek∥\lVert z_e - e_k \rVert∥ze​−ek​∥ small.

Why two extra terms, and why each has its own stop-gradient. Start from what breaks without them. The nearest-code step has zero gradient: moving zez_eze​ inside its cell does not change zqz_qzq​, so the encoder receives nothing. The straight-through copy repairs that, but the way it is written, zq=ze+sg⁡[ek−ze]z_q = z_e + \operatorname{sg}[e_k - z_e]zq​=ze​+sg[ek​−ze​], routes the decoder's gradient to zez_eze​ and gives the table nothing, so the codes would stay at their random initialization forever. The codebook term fixes exactly that: its gradient 2(ek−ze)2(e_k - z_e)2(ek​−ze​) moves the chosen code toward the encoder outputs assigned to it, a k-means step, and the sg⁡\operatorname{sg}sg on zez_eze​ keeps it from moving the encoder. The commitment term fixes a second problem: the straight-through copy is only a good approximation while zq≈zez_q \approx z_ezq​≈ze​, because it applies a gradient computed at eke_kek​ to a point that may be far from eke_kek​. Without it the encoder outputs drift and grow, jump between cells, and the codes chase a moving target. The commitment gradient 2β(ze−ek)2\beta(z_e - e_k)2β(ze​−ek​) pulls zez_eze​ back toward the code it chose, and the sg⁡\operatorname{sg}sg on eke_kek​ keeps it from moving the table.

A single term ∥ze−ek∥2\lVert z_e - e_k \rVert^2∥ze​−ek​∥2 without stop-gradients would push both sides with the same force, and the two sides should not move alike: the table should follow the encoder fully (weight 111), while the encoder, which is already steered by the reconstruction loss, should only be held lightly (weight β=0.25\beta = 0.25β=0.25), or it would snap onto the current codes and stop exploring. The two stop-gradients are what make the two weights independent: the codebook chases the encoder, the encoder commits to the codebook. In the example above, with ze=(0.7,−0.2)z_e = (0.7, -0.2)ze​=(0.7,−0.2) and e1=(0.9,0.1)e_1 = (0.9, 0.1)e1​=(0.9,0.1), the codebook term moves e1e_1e1​ by a gradient of (0.4,0.6)(0.4, 0.6)(0.4,0.6) toward zez_eze​, the commitment term moves zez_eze​ by (−0.1,−0.15)(-0.1, -0.15)(−0.1,−0.15) toward e1e_1e1​, a quarter of the force, and the reconstruction gradient at e1e_1e1​ is copied to zez_eze​ unchanged. The EMA variant below makes the division explicit: the table is updated by running averages instead of a loss, and only the commitment term remains.

EMA codebook. The codebook term can be replaced by a running k-means: with the assignment counts nkn_knk​ and sums of the batch,

Nk←γNk+(1−γ) nk,mk←γ mk+(1−γ)∑i: ki=kze,i,ek←mkNk,γ≈0.99N_k \leftarrow \gamma N_k + (1 - \gamma)\, n_k, \qquad m_k \leftarrow \gamma\, m_k + (1 - \gamma) \sum_{i:\, k_i = k} z_{e,i}, \qquad e_k \leftarrow \frac{m_k}{N_k}, \qquad \gamma \approx 0.99Nk​←γNk​+(1−γ)nk​,mk​←γmk​+(1−γ)i:ki​=k∑​ze,i​,ek​←Nk​mk​​,γ≈0.99

Each code moves to the running mean of the vectors assigned to it; only the commitment term remains in the loss. It is more stable than the gradient version and is what most implementations use.

A two-dimensional example. d=2d = 2d=2, four codes, one encoder vector ze=(0.7,−0.2)z_e = (0.7, -0.2)ze​=(0.7,−0.2):

e1:4=(0.9,0.1), (−0.5,0.8), (−0.6,−0.7), (2,2)∥ze−ej∥2=0.13, 2.44, 1.94, 6.53  ⇒  k=1,zq=(0.9,0.1)\begin{aligned} e_{1:4} &= (0.9, 0.1),\ (-0.5, 0.8),\ (-0.6, -0.7),\ (2, 2) \\ \lVert z_e - e_j \rVert^2 &= 0.13,\ 2.44,\ 1.94,\ 6.53 \;\Rightarrow\; k = 1,\quad z_q = (0.9, 0.1) \end{aligned}e1:4​∥ze​−ej​∥2​=(0.9,0.1), (−0.5,0.8), (−0.6,−0.7), (2,2)=0.13, 2.44, 1.94, 6.53⇒k=1,zq​=(0.9,0.1)​

The codebook term pulls e1e_1e1​ toward (0.7,−0.2)(0.7, -0.2)(0.7,−0.2); the commitment term pushes zez_eze​ toward (0.9,0.1)(0.9, 0.1)(0.9,0.1); e4e_4e4​ receives nothing, and if no vector ever lands nearest to it, it never will.

Codebook collapse. That last sentence is the standard failure: a code that is never the nearest gets no gradient, stays where it was initialized, and is dead; large codebooks end up with a few hundred live codes. Measure it with the usage histogram pkp_kpk​ over a dataset and its perplexity exp⁡(−∑kpklog⁡pk)\exp(-\sum_k p_k \log p_k)exp(−∑k​pk​logpk​), which equals KKK only when every code is used equally. Fixes: EMA updates, re-initializing dead codes to random encoder outputs, k-means initialization, a lower code dimension with a projection and ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​-normalized codes (ViT-VQGAN runs K=8192K = 8192K=8192 this way), or replacing the learned table by a fixed grid, which is FSQ (6.2.3). On underwater images AquaScope found 519519519 of VQGAN's 1,0241{,}0241,024 codes never used and merged the table to 646464 codes with usage-weighted k-means, 10→610 \to 610→6 bits per index.

6.2.2 VQGAN#

The same quantizer with two more losses on the decoder, so that reconstructions are sharp instead of blurry:

LVQGAN=∥x−x^∥1+LLPIPS(x,x^)⏟Lrec+Lcodebook+β Lcommit+λadv LG\mathcal{L}_{\text{VQGAN}} = \underbrace{\lVert x - \hat x \rVert_1 + \mathcal{L}_{\text{LPIPS}}(x, \hat x)}_{\mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{codebook}} + \beta\, \mathcal{L}_{\text{commit}} + \lambda_{\text{adv}}\, \mathcal{L}_GLVQGAN​=Lrec​∥x−x^∥1​+LLPIPS​(x,x^)​​+Lcodebook​+βLcommit​+λadv​LG​

The perceptual term compares features of a frozen VGG rather than pixels, layer by layer, with learned channel weights wlw_lwl​:

LLPIPS(x,x^)=∑l1HlWl∑h,w∥wl⊙(φl(x)hw−φl(x^)hw)∥22\mathcal{L}_{\text{LPIPS}}(x, \hat x) = \sum_l \frac{1}{H_l W_l} \sum_{h, w} \big\lVert w_l \odot \big(\varphi_l(x)_{hw} - \varphi_l(\hat x)_{hw}\big) \big\rVert_2^2LLPIPS​(x,x^)=l∑​Hl​Wl​1​h,w∑​​wl​⊙(φl​(x)hw​−φl​(x^)hw​)​22​

φl(x)hw∈RCl\varphi_l(x)_{hw} \in \mathbb{R}^{C_l}φl​(x)hw​∈RCl​ is the layer-lll activation at position (h,w)(h, w)(h,w), unit-normalized along the channel axis, so with wl=1w_l = 1wl​=1 each term is a cosine distance. A squared pixel loss is minimized by the conditional mean of all images consistent with the codes, which is blurry; a feature loss is minimized by images with the right texture statistics.

The adversarial term uses a patch discriminator DDD that classifies P×PP \times PP×P patches, P≪H,WP \ll H, WP≪H,W, rather than the whole image, with the hinge loss:

LD=Ex[max⁡(0, 1−D(x))]+Ex[max⁡(0, 1+D(x^))],LG=− Ex[D(x^)]\mathcal{L}_D = \mathbb{E}_x\big[\max(0,\ 1 - D(x))\big] + \mathbb{E}_x\big[\max(0,\ 1 + D(\hat x))\big], \qquad \mathcal{L}_G = -\,\mathbb{E}_x\big[D(\hat x)\big]LD​=Ex​[max(0, 1−D(x))]+Ex​[max(0, 1+D(x^))],LG​=−Ex​[D(x^)]

DDD is trained to push real patches above +1+1+1 and reconstructions below −1-1−1; the decoder is trained to raise D(x^)D(\hat x)D(x^). The adversarial loss is switched on only after a warm-up, and its weight is set adaptively from the gradients at the decoder's last layer GLG_LGL​:

λadv=∥∇GLLrec∥∥∇GLLG∥+δ,δ=10−6\lambda_{\text{adv}} = \frac{\lVert \nabla_{G_L} \mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}} \rVert}{\lVert \nabla_{G_L} \mathcal{L}_G \rVert + \delta}, \qquad \delta = 10^{-6}λadv​=∥∇GL​​LG​∥+δ∥∇GL​​Lrec​∥​,δ=10−6

so that the two losses pull on the decoder with comparable force whatever their scales; if the reconstruction gradient has norm 0.80.80.8 and the adversarial one 0.050.050.05, the weight is 161616. The published models use f=16f = 16f=16, K=1024K = 1024K=1024 or 16,38416{,}38416,384, d=256d = 256d=256; a second stage trains a transformer on the token grid, p(ki∣k<i)p(k_i \mid k_{<i})p(ki​∣k<i​), for generation, which is also exactly the entropy model of 6.2.8. The GAN loss buys sharpness at the cost of pixel fidelity: a reconstruction can contain detail that was never in the input, the perception–distortion trade-off of 6.4.5. Every generative codec in this book, GenStream's and AquaScope's included, is a VQGAN-trained decoder at heart.

One call. z∈RN×d  ⟶  u=zW∈RN×d′  ⟶  z^∈∏iGi, k∈{0,…,∏iLi−1}z \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d} \;\longrightarrow\; u = z W \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d'} \;\longrightarrow\; \hat z \in \prod_i \mathcal{G}_i,\ k \in \{0, \dots, \prod_i L_i - 1\}z∈RN×d⟶u=zW∈RN×d′⟶z^∈∏i​Gi​, k∈{0,…,∏i​Li​−1}, with W∈Rd×d′W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d'}W∈Rd×d′ a learned projection, d′d'd′ small (333 to 666 in the paper's recommended configurations, fewer than 101010 in general) and Gi\mathcal{G}_iGi​ the LiL_iLi​ grid values of coordinate iii

The FSQ paper's recommended levels for a 2162^{16}216 vocabulary are L=(8,8,8,5,5,5)L = (8, 8, 8, 5, 5, 5)L=(8,8,8,5,5,5), 64,00064{,}00064,000 codes and 15.9715.9715.97 bits per token, and the kkk formula packs the six digits in mixed radix. The price is a uniform, axis-aligned grid in few dimensions; the encoder and decoder adapt to it, and the paper reports quality on par with VQ. FSQ is the quantizer of the Cosmos discrete tokenizer, whose step 7 in 6.5 traces it on real shapes, with a full side-by-side against VQ in the note under that step.

6.2.4 LFQ: lookup-free quantization#

One call. z∈RN×d  ⟶  q=sign⁡(z)∈{−1,+1}N×d,ki=∑j=1d1[zij>0] 2j−1z \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d} \;\longrightarrow\; q = \operatorname{sign}(z) \in \{-1, +1\}^{N \times d},\quad k_i = \sum_{j=1}^{d} \mathbf{1}[z_{ij} > 0]\, 2^{j-1}z∈RN×d⟶q=sign(z)∈{−1,+1}N×d,ki​=∑j=1d​1[zij​>0]2j−1

Each coordinate becomes one bit, so the vocabulary is K=2dK = 2^dK=2d with no table at all: MAGVIT-v2 uses d=18d = 18d=18, 262,144262{,}144262,144 codes, far beyond what a learned table could keep alive. Example: z=(0.7,−0.2,1.3)→q=(+1,−1,+1)z = (0.7, -0.2, 1.3) \to q = (+1, -1, +1)z=(0.7,−0.2,1.3)→q=(+1,−1,+1), bits (1,0,1)(1, 0, 1)(1,0,1), k=5k = 5k=5. The loss adds two terms to the reconstruction (and the adversarial terms of a VQGAN-style decoder):

LLFQ=Lrec+β∥z−sg⁡[q]∥22+γ(Ex[H(p(k∣x))]−H(Ex[p(k∣x)]))\mathcal{L}_{\text{LFQ}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}} + \beta \lVert z - \operatorname{sg}[q] \rVert_2^2 + \gamma \Big( \mathbb{E}_x\big[H(p(k \mid x))\big] - H\big(\mathbb{E}_x[p(k \mid x)]\big) \Big)LLFQ​=Lrec​+β∥z−sg[q]∥22​+γ(Ex​[H(p(k∣x))]−H(Ex​[p(k∣x)]))

p(k∣x)p(k \mid x)p(k∣x) is a softmax over −∥z−ck∥2-\lVert z - c_k \rVert^2−∥z−ck​∥2 for the codes ckc_kck​, which factorizes per dimension because the codes are the corners of a hypercube. The first entropy term asks each input to be confident about its code; the second, subtracted, asks the codes to be used uniformly across the data. Together they are the entropy penalty that keeps a huge vocabulary from collapsing onto a few corners. Gradients again pass by the straight-through estimator.

6.2.5 RVQ: residual vector quantization#

One call. z  ⟶  (k(1),…,k(S))z \;\longrightarrow\; (k^{(1)}, \dots, k^{(S)})z⟶(k(1),…,k(S)), SSS indices per position

r0=z,qs=arg⁡min⁡e∈Es ∥rs−1−e∥2,rs=rs−1−qs,z^=∑s=1Sqsr_0 = z, \qquad q_s = \underset{e \in E_s}{\arg\min}\ \lVert r_{s-1} - e \rVert_2, \qquad r_s = r_{s-1} - q_s, \qquad \hat z = \sum_{s=1}^{S} q_sr0​=z,qs​=e∈Es​argmin​ ∥rs−1​−e∥2​,rs​=rs−1​−qs​,z^=s=1∑S​qs​

Stage sss quantizes what the earlier stages left over, with its own codebook EsE_sEs​, so SSS stages of KKK codes reach a precision that one codebook would need KSK^SKS codes for, at Slog⁡2KS \log_2 KSlog2​K bits per position. Toy with scalars and codebooks {0,2,4}\{0, 2, 4\}{0,2,4}, {−1,0,1}\{-1, 0, 1\}{−1,0,1}, {−0.5,0,0.5}\{-0.5, 0, 0.5\}{−0.5,0,0.5}: z=3.7→q=(4,0,−0.5)z = 3.7 \to q = (4, 0, -0.5)z=3.7→q=(4,0,−0.5), z^=3.5\hat z = 3.5z^=3.5, residual 0.20.20.2. The stages are ordered by importance, so dropping the last ones gives a coarser reconstruction without re-encoding: SoundStream streams audio this way with 444 to 242424 stages of K=1024K = 1024K=1024, 333 to 181818 kbps at 757575 frames per second, and EnCodec with 222 to 323232; the same idea gives a token stream that can shed refinement under bandwidth pressure. Training is VQ-VAE training per stage, with the straight-through sum and commitment terms on each residual.

6.2.6 TiTok: a one-dimensional token sequence#

Every tokenizer above keeps a grid: one index per spatial position, N=(H/f)(W/f)N = (H/f)(W/f)N=(H/f)(W/f). TiTok drops the grid. A ViT encoder reads the patch embeddings together with NNN learned latent tokens appended to the sequence, and only the outputs at the latent positions are kept and quantized, with K=4096K = 4096K=4096 in the released models; the decoder reads the quantized latent tokens plus one mask token per patch and produces the image, in the paper through a frozen VQGAN decoder during a two-stage training. NNN is a free choice, 323232 to 256256256 per image, far fewer than any grid, and the tokens spend capacity where the image needs it rather than one per patch. AquaScope's setting is N=64N = 64N=64 tokens of 121212 bits, 768768768 bits for a 256×256256 \times 256256×256 image, which is what fits an underwater acoustic link; with a grid tokenizer the same image was 256256256 indices of 666 bits after clustering, 1,5361{,}5361,536 bits. The cost is that a wrong token no longer maps to one patch: the error spreads over the image, which is why AquaScope fine-tunes the decoder under injected token errors (the 2%2\%2% BER figure of 6.4.5).

6.2.8 Bits per token: the fixed baseline and a learned prior#

Transmitting the indices as they are costs Nlog⁡2KN \log_2 KNlog2​K bits, 2,5602{,}5602,560 for the example, and that figure is blind to the content. A prior over the token sequence turns it into a real rate: with a causal transformer giving p(ki∣k<i)p(k_i \mid k_{<i})p(ki​∣k<i​) and an arithmetic coder,

R=∑i=1N−log⁡2pθ(ki∣k<i),E[R]=N(H(k)+DKL(pdata ∥ pθ)),H(k)≤log⁡2KR = \sum_{i=1}^{N} -\log_2 p_\theta(k_i \mid k_{<i}), \qquad \mathbb{E}[R] = N \big( H(k) + D_{\text{KL}}(p_{\text{data}} \,\|\, p_\theta) \big), \qquad H(k) \le \log_2 KR=i=1∑N​−log2​pθ​(ki​∣k<i​),E[R]=N(H(k)+DKL​(pdata​∥pθ​)),H(k)≤log2​K

The entropy H(k)H(k)H(k) of the true token distribution is at most log⁡2K\log_2 Klog2​K per token; the prior pays that plus a KL term for how wrong it is, so a prior beats the fixed length only when it is better than uniform on the data it is run on, and under domain shift it can cost more than Nlog⁡2KN \log_2 KNlog2​K, one reason the fixed-length stream is the safe fallback. The saving comes from the structure of real images: neighbouring tokens are correlated, a sky token predicts more sky, so the conditional distribution is far from uniform. For K=1024K = 1024K=1024 this typically takes 101010 bits per token down to 444 to 666. Encoder and decoder run the same prior on the same context, so decoding is serial, one token after another, which is the latency cost of 6.4; and because the arithmetic coder needs bit-identical probabilities on both ends, the prior has to run deterministically. Without a prior, the fixed length is also what makes a token stream loss-tolerant: any index can be read on its own, which is the property GenStream and AquaScope rely on (6.4.4, 6.4.7).

Coding: VQ with a straight-through estimator [READY]View exercise

Likely prompt: "Implement vector quantization without killing the encoder gradient. How would you turn the indices into fewer than log⁡2K\log_2 Klog2​K bits per token?"

  • Shapes: flattened encoder tokens z_e: [B, N, D]; codebook [K, D]; indices [B, N]; quantized vectors [B, N, D].
  • Cost: the distance matrix is O(B N K D) time and O(B N K) memory; a prior for the rate is a causal transformer over N tokens, O(N^2 D) per image and serial at decode time.
  • Pitfalls: detach the right side of each loss; monitor usage and perplexity for collapse; N log2 K is only the fixed-length baseline, the real rate comes from the prior; the EMA variant drops the codebook loss and updates the table outside the optimizer. The original VQ-VAE and VQGAN papers define the terms.
python
def vector_quantize(z_e, codebook, beta=0.25):
    # z_e: [B, N, D], codebook: [K, D]
    distance = (z_e.square().sum(-1, keepdim=True)
                + codebook.square().sum(-1)[None, None]
                - 2 * z_e @ codebook.t())                   # ||z_e - e_k||^2 for every pair, [B, N, K]
    indices = distance.argmin(dim=-1)                     # k_i:  [B, N]
    z_q = F.embedding(indices, codebook)                  # e_k:  [B, N, D]
    z_st = z_e + (z_q - z_e).detach()                     # straight-through: forward z_q, backward z_e
    codebook_loss = (z_q - z_e.detach()).square().mean()  # moves e_k toward z_e
    commitment = (z_e - z_q.detach()).square().mean()     # keeps z_e near e_k
    return z_st, indices, codebook_loss + beta * commitment

[READY] for the quantizer itself; the causal token prior with a shared integer CDF is [TODO], and [READY] arithmetic_coding.py supplies the static arithmetic-coder round trip it would plug into.

6.3 GANs & Diffusion#

Two ways to train a decoder to produce images that look real rather than images that minimize a pixel error. The GAN is what makes the VQGAN decoders of 6.2 sharp; diffusion is the generative family behind today's image and video models, and the Cosmos world models of 6.5 run it in a tokenizer's latent.

6.3.1 GAN#

One call. z∼p(z)  ⟶  G(z)∈RH×W×3z \sim p(z) \;\longrightarrow\; G(z) \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}z∼p(z)⟶G(z)∈RH×W×3, judged by D:RH×W×3→RD: \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} \to \mathbb{R}D:RH×W×3→R

min⁡Gmax⁡D Ex∼pdata[log⁡D(x)]+Ez∼p(z)[log⁡(1−D(G(z)))]\min_G \max_D\ \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}}\big[\log D(x)\big] + \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p(z)}\big[\log\big(1 - D(G(z))\big)\big]Gmin​Dmax​ Ex∼pdata​​[logD(x)]+Ez∼p(z)​[log(1−D(G(z)))]

For a fixed GGG the best discriminator is D∗(x)=pdata(x)/(pdata(x)+pG(x))D^*(x) = p_{\text{data}}(x) / (p_{\text{data}}(x) + p_G(x))D∗(x)=pdata​(x)/(pdata​(x)+pG​(x)), and plugging it back in makes the generator's objective 2 JS(pdata ∥ pG)−log⁡42\,\text{JS}(p_{\text{data}} \,\|\, p_G) - \log 42JS(pdata​∥pG​)−log4: a GAN minimizes the Jensen–Shannon divergence between the data and what it generates, without ever writing down a density. Two things go wrong in practice:

  • Vanishing gradient. When DDD wins, log⁡(1−D(G(z)))\log(1 - D(G(z)))log(1−D(G(z))) saturates and GGG stops learning. The fix is the non-saturating loss −log⁡D(G(z))-\log D(G(z))−logD(G(z)), or a loss that is linear in DDD: the hinge loss, used by VQGAN, and the Wasserstein loss with a gradient penalty,
LDhinge=E[max⁡(0,1−D(x))]+E[max⁡(0,1+D(G(z)))]LDWGAN-GP=E[D(G(z))]−E[D(x)]+γ Ex~[(∥∇x~D(x~)∥2−1)2]\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}_D^{\text{hinge}} &= \mathbb{E}\big[\max(0, 1 - D(x))\big] + \mathbb{E}\big[\max(0, 1 + D(G(z)))\big] \\[4pt] \mathcal{L}_D^{\text{WGAN-GP}} &= \mathbb{E}\big[D(G(z))\big] - \mathbb{E}\big[D(x)\big] + \gamma\, \mathbb{E}_{\tilde x}\big[(\lVert \nabla_{\tilde x} D(\tilde x) \rVert_2 - 1)^2\big] \end{aligned}LDhinge​LDWGAN-GP​​=E[max(0,1−D(x))]+E[max(0,1+D(G(z)))]=E[D(G(z))]−E[D(x)]+γEx~​[(∥∇x~​D(x~)∥2​−1)2]​

with x~\tilde xx~ on random segments between real and generated samples, and in both cases LG=−E[D(G(z))]\mathcal{L}_G = -\mathbb{E}[D(G(z))]LG​=−E[D(G(z))]. Spectral normalization of DDD and the R1 penalty γ2Ex∥∇xD(x)∥2\tfrac{\gamma}{2}\mathbb{E}_x \lVert \nabla_x D(x) \rVert^22γ​Ex​∥∇x​D(x)∥2 on real samples serve the same purpose: keep DDD smooth so that its gradient is informative.

  • Mode collapse. GGG finds a few outputs that fool DDD and stops covering the data; nothing in the objective rewards diversity directly.

For codecs and restoration the GAN is an auxiliary loss, not the model: a decoder trained with reconstruction plus λadvLG\lambda_{\text{adv}} \mathcal{L}_Gλadv​LG​ produces texture instead of blur, with the adaptive weight and patch discriminator of 6.2.2. A patch discriminator scores every P×PP \times PP×P patch and averages, so it judges texture statistics rather than global layout, has few parameters and works at any resolution; it is the standard choice in pix2pix, VQGAN and neural codecs. What it buys is realism; what it costs is fidelity, which is the trade-off of 6.4.5.
