The denoiser was a U-Net; the DiT in §3 replaces it with a transformer over 2×22 \times 22×2 latent patches, conditioned by adaLN-Zero.

6.3.3 Flow matching#

Most models since SD3 and Flux use a simpler parameterization of the same idea. Draw a data point x0x_0x0​ and a noise sample x1∼N(0,I)x_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)x1​∼N(0,I), connect them by a straight line and train a network to predict the line's velocity:

xt=(1−t) x0+t x1,t∼U(0,1),LFM=Et, x0, x1∥vθ(xt,t)−(x1−x0)∥22x_t = (1 - t)\, x_0 + t\, x_1, \qquad t \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1), \qquad \mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}} = \mathbb{E}_{t,\, x_0,\, x_1} \big\lVert v_\theta(x_t, t) - (x_1 - x_0) \big\rVert_2^2xt​=(1−t)x0​+tx1​,t∼U(0,1),LFM​=Et,x0​,x1​​​vθ​(xt​,t)−(x1​−x0​)​22​

Sampling integrates the ODE dx/dt=vθ(x,t)dx/dt = v_\theta(x, t)dx/dt=vθ​(x,t) from t=1t = 1t=1 (noise) to t=0t = 0t=0 (data), with Euler steps xt−Δ=xt−Δ vθ(xt,t)x_{t - \Delta} = x_t - \Delta\, v_\theta(x_t, t)xt−Δ​=xt​−Δvθ​(xt​,t). The straight-line path replaces the variance schedule, there is no αˉt\bar\alpha_tαˉt​ table, and the velocity target is the same for every point on the line, so the learned field is close to straight and few steps suffice. DDPM is the same family with a curved path and the noise ε\varepsilonε as the target instead of the velocity; the two are related by a change of variables, not by a different principle.

6.3.4 Video diffusion and world models#

A video model adds the time axis to the denoiser: 3D attention over all space-time tokens, or the factorized spatial-then-temporal attention of TimeSformer in §3, and the same chain runs on a clip. Two costs decide the design. Memory, because a 161616-frame clip has 16×16\times16× the tokens of an image, which is why video models run in a video tokenizer's latent, 8×8\times8× down in time and 888 to 16×16\times16× in space (6.5). And temporal consistency, which the per-frame losses of this chapter do not enforce; the fix is attention across frames inside the denoiser and losses on flow-warped neighbours in the tokenizer. The Cosmos world models are this design at scale: a diffusion model on the continuous 8×8×88 \times 8 \times 88×8×8 latent and an autoregressive model on the discrete 8×16×168 \times 16 \times 168×16×16 tokens, both of 6.5.

Coding: diffusion forward noising [TOY]View exercise
  • Prompt: sample xtx_txt​ directly from x0x_0x0​, then form the noise-prediction target; explain why no loop over earlier timesteps is required.
  • Shape / cost: x0, noise and the output share [B, C, H, W]; alpha_bar_t is gathered per sample as [B, 1, 1, 1]; elementwise, O(BCHW).
  • Pitfalls: use the cumulative αˉt\bar\alpha_tαˉt​, not the per-step αt\alpha_tαt​; broadcast one schedule value per sample; the loss compares the model's prediction to the same noise that produced x_t; do not detach the prediction.
python
def q_sample(x0, alpha_bar_t, noise):
    return alpha_bar_t.sqrt() * x0 + (1.0 - alpha_bar_t).sqrt() * noise   # x_t in one line

def noise_prediction_loss(model, x0, t, alpha_bar):
    noise = torch.randn_like(x0)
    x_t = q_sample(x0, alpha_bar[t].view(-1, 1, 1, 1), noise)
    return (model(x_t, t) - noise).square().mean()                          # L_simple

The two functions are the training step; the schedule, the sampler (DDPM or DDIM), timestep sampling and classifier-free guidance are [TODO].

6.4 Learned & Generative Compression#

The models of 6.1 to 6.3 become a codec once the latent is turned into bits. This section is that step: the objective, the quantizer, the entropy model that decides the rate, the two shapes a learned codec can take, and what a decoder that hallucinates is allowed to do.

6.4.1 The core idea#

Replace the hand-crafted transform, quantizer and entropy model with networks trained end-to-end on the rate–distortion objective.

One call (this section keeps Ballé's letters: yyy is the latent and zzz the hyper-latent of 6.4.3). x  ⟶  y=ga(x)  ⟶  y^=Q(y)  ⟶  bits  ⟶  x^=gs(y^)x \;\longrightarrow\; y = g_a(x) \;\longrightarrow\; \hat y = Q(y) \;\longrightarrow\; \text{bits} \;\longrightarrow\; \hat x = g_s(\hat y)x⟶y=ga​(x)⟶y^​=Q(y)⟶bits⟶x^=gs​(y^​)

y=ga(x)analysis transform, the encodery^=Q(y)=round⁡(y)scalar quantization, one integer per latent elementbits←AC⁡(y^, pψ(y^))arithmetic coding under a learned priorx^=gs(y^)synthesis transform, the decoder\begin{aligned} y &= g_a(x) && \text{analysis transform, the encoder} \\[2pt] \hat y &= Q(y) = \operatorname{round}(y) && \text{scalar quantization, one integer per latent element} \\[2pt] \text{bits} &\leftarrow \operatorname{AC}\big(\hat y,\ p_\psi(\hat y)\big) && \text{arithmetic coding under a learned prior} \\[2pt] \hat x &= g_s(\hat y) && \text{synthesis transform, the decoder} \end{aligned}yy^​bitsx^​=ga​(x)=Q(y)=round(y)←AC(y^​, pψ​(y^​))=gs​(y^​)​​analysis transform, the encoderscalar quantization, one integer per latent elementarithmetic coding under a learned priorsynthesis transform, the decoder​

Training objective, in one common convention:

L=D(x,x^)⏟distortion+λ E[∑i−log⁡2pψ(y^i)]⏟R, expected bits\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{D(x, \hat x)}_{\text{distortion}} + \lambda\, \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_i -\log_2 p_\psi(\hat y_i)\Big]}_{R,\ \text{expected bits}}L=distortionD(x,x^)​​+λR, expected bitsE[i∑​−log2​pψ​(y^​i​)]​​

Some papers instead write L = R + λD; then larger λ means more quality / rate, whereas in D + λR it means more rate pressure. State the convention before interpreting a sweep. For bpp, divide the summed code length (including side latents) by the number of input pixels.

Why −log p(ŷ) is the bitrate: Shannon's source coding theorem says the optimal code length for a symbol is −log₂ p. An arithmetic coder achieves that up to a negligible constant. So minimizing the negative log-likelihood of the latent under the model is minimizing the compressed size. Say this crisply — it's the one-line justification for the whole field.

Note the structural identity with the VAE (6.1.2): D+λRD + \lambda RD+λR is the negative ELBO with a Lagrangian weight. Learned compression is a VAE whose prior is used as an entropy model and whose KL is a real bit count.

Coding: learned codec forward + RD lossView exercise

Likely prompt: "Write the train/eval forward pass of a learned codec. Where does the gradient cross quantization, and what exactly does λ control?"

  • Local code: [TOY] learned_compression.py — LearnedCompressionModel.forward, rd_loss, and train_step show the complete control flow. [READY] ml_coding_torch.py — rate_distortion_loss is the clean algebra-only drill.
  • Shapes: x:[B,3,H,W] → y:[B,M,H/8,W/8] → x_hat:[B,3,H,W] for the current three stride-2 layers. A real model must define padding/cropping for dimensions not divisible by 8.
  • Cost: convolutional work and activation memory are linear in B·H·W; the decoder usually owns the largest activation maps.
  • Pitfalls: training uses uniform noise while evaluation rounds; D+λR and R+λD reverse the meaning of increasing λ; the returned likelihood is not automatically a real bpp.
python
def forward(self, x):
    y = self.g_a(x)
    if self.training:
        y_hat = y + torch.empty_like(y).uniform_(-0.5, 0.5)
    else:
        y_hat = torch.round(y)
    x_hat = self.g_s(y_hat)
    likelihood = self.entropy_model(y_hat)
    return x_hat, y_hat, likelihood

def rd_objective(x, x_hat, rate_bpp, lam):
    distortion = (x - x_hat).square().mean()
    return distortion + lam * rate_bpp

6.4.2 The quantization problem#

round() has zero gradient almost everywhere, so you can't backprop through it. Three standard surrogates:

MethodHowNotes
Additive uniform noise (Ballé)ỹ = y + u, u ~ U(−½, ½) during trainingMakes the density a continuous relaxation; the resulting model is a proper VAE with a uniform posterior. Train/test mismatch is the drawback.
Straight-through estimatorforward: round; backward: identityExact forward pass, biased gradient
Mixed / "universal" quantizationnoise for the rate term, STE for the distortion termWhat most modern codecs actually do; the rate term is still fitted to the noisy latent, so the estimated bits keep a train/test mismatch against the rounded symbols that are coded

The train/test mismatch is a real, askable weakness: noise-based training optimizes for a noisy latent, but inference uses a rounded one. Later work (soft-to-hard annealing, quantization-aware fine-tuning of the last epochs) closes the gap.

6.4.3 Entropy models — where the gains actually come from#

The transform matters less than most people assume; the entropy model is where learned codecs win.

Factorized prior (baseline): each latent channel gets its own learned 1-D CDF, independent across space. Cheap, weak.

Hyperprior (Ballé 2018), the key idea. A second, smaller latent z=ha(y)z = h_a(y)z=ha​(y) is quantized and sent as side information, a few percent of the bits, and the decoder expands it into a scale for every element of y^\hat yy^​; the mean-and-scale form written here is Minnen 2018's extension:

L=D(x,x^)+λ(E[−log⁡2p(y^∣z^)]+E[−log⁡2p(z^)])(μ,σ)=hs(z^),p(y^i∣z^)=∫y^i−1/2y^i+1/2N(u; μi,σi2) du=Φ(y^i+1/2−μiσi)−Φ(y^i−1/2−μiσi)\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L} &= D(x, \hat x) + \lambda \Big( \mathbb{E}\big[-\log_2 p(\hat y \mid \hat z)\big] + \mathbb{E}\big[-\log_2 p(\hat z)\big] \Big) \\[4pt] (\mu, \sigma) &= h_s(\hat z), \qquad p(\hat y_i \mid \hat z) = \int_{\hat y_i - 1/2}^{\hat y_i + 1/2} \mathcal{N}(u;\ \mu_i, \sigma_i^2)\, du = \Phi\Big(\tfrac{\hat y_i + 1/2 - \mu_i}{\sigma_i}\Big) - \Phi\Big(\tfrac{\hat y_i - 1/2 - \mu_i}{\sigma_i}\Big) \end{aligned}L(μ,σ)​=D(x,x^)+λ(E[−log2​p(y^​∣z^)]+E[−log2​p(z^)])=hs​(z^),p(y^​i​∣z^)=∫y^​i​−1/2y^​i​+1/2​N(u; μi​,σi2​)du=Φ(σi​y^​i​+1/2−μi​​)−Φ(σi​y^​i​−1/2−μi​​)​

The probability of an integer symbol is the Gaussian mass of its unit bin, not the density at its centre; z^\hat zz^ itself is coded under a learned factorized prior. Why it works: the latent is not stationary — a latent element over a textured region has high variance, one over the sky has low variance. A single global distribution must be wide enough to cover both, so it wastes bits everywhere. The hyperprior transmits a tiny description of the local scale so each element gets a tight, well-matched distribution. Spending 3% of your bits to halve the entropy of the other 97% is a huge win. This "spend side information to sharpen the prior" argument is the single most important concept in the area — and it's structurally identical to HEVC signalling per-CTU quantization/SAO parameters.

Autoregressive context model (Minnen 2018): additionally condition on already-decoded neighbors, p(ŷ_i | ŷ_{<i}, ẑ). Another ~10% rate. But it serializes decoding — each element waits for its neighbors, so decode time explodes. This is the classic rate/latency tradeoff of the field.

Checkerboard / channel-wise context (checkerboard: He 2021; channel groups: Minnen & Singh 2020 and ELIC, He 2022): split the latent into two interleaved halves or into channel groups; decode group 1 in parallel, use it as context for group 2. Recovers most of the autoregressive gain with 2–10 passes instead of N. This is exactly the kind of "make it parallel" answer interviewers want.

Coding: quantized likelihood, estimated bpp, and real bitsView exercise

Likely prompt: "Your network returned a Gaussian likelihood tensor. Turn it into bpp, then tell me why that number can still differ from the file size."

  • Local code: [TOY] learned_compression.py currently evaluates a Gaussian PDF and averages −log₂ over latent elements. That is a useful warning example, not a correct actual-bpp implementation. [READY] arithmetic_coding.py round-trips symbols under a static frequency model; learned integer-CDF integration is [TODO].
  • Shapes: y_hat, mu, scale:[B,M,H',W']; optional hyper-latent z_hat:[B,M_z,H_z,W_z]; bits_y and bits_z are scalars; normalize by B·H·W, not by the number of latent elements.
  • Cost: likelihood evaluation is O(B·M·H'·W'); autoregressive arithmetic coding is linear in symbol count but serial, while checkerboard/channel groups trade a few sequential passes for parallelism.
  • Pitfalls: a density value is not the probability of an integer symbol; count hyperlatents, headers/CDF tables, padding, and coder termination; encoder and decoder need the same quantized CDF bit-for-bit. See the scale-hyperprior paper.
python
def gaussian_bin_prob(y_hat, mu, scale, eps=1e-9):
    scale = scale.clamp_min(1e-6)
    normal = torch.distributions.Normal(mu, scale)
    # Probability mass assigned to the integer-centered quantization bin.
    prob = normal.cdf(y_hat + 0.5) - normal.cdf(y_hat - 0.5)
    return prob.clamp_min(eps)

def estimated_bpp(prob_y, input_shape, prob_z=None):
    batch, _, height, width = input_shape
    bits = -torch.log2(prob_y).sum()
    if prob_z is not None:
        bits = bits - torch.log2(prob_z).sum()
    return bits / (batch * height * width)

6.4.4 Two paradigms#

Paradigm 1 — Hybrid neural codec (H.264-shaped)#

Keep predict → residual → entropy-code, replace each module with a network. DVC, FVC, DCVC / DCVC-DC / DCVC-FM.

text
Input frame
   ↓ optical flow network                 (motion estimation)
   ↓ compress the flow field itself       (an autoencoder + entropy model)
   ↓ warp reference → predicted frame     (motion compensation)
   ↓ residual = input − predicted   ... OR ...
   ↓ [DCVC] condition the encoder on the predicted *feature*, don't subtract
   ↓ autoencoder → latent y → quantize → arithmetic code with hyperprior

The DCVC insight worth knowing: "Deep Contextual Video Compression" replaces subtraction with conditioning. Residual coding hard-codes the reference's role as r = x − pred; conditional coding exposes the context and lets the network learn how to use it. The precise information-theory statement is H(X|C) ≤ H(X). If pred is determined by C, then X ↔ R=X−pred(C) is bijective for fixed C, so H(X|C) = H(R|C); the practical advantage comes from a richer conditional model, not from an unconditional "conditioning is always strictly better" inequality. DCVC-FM and successors report gains over VVC (VTM) on standard test sets in BD-rate terms.

  • Latent is continuous, scalar-quantized, arithmetic-coded.
  • Optimized for D + λ·R in this book's convention (the DVC and DCVC papers write λ·D + R, so their λ runs the other way), with D = MSE or MS-SSIM.
  • Reconstruction is deterministic and high-fidelity.
Paradigm 2 — VQ / generative codec#
text
Input image/video
   ↓ CNN/ViT encoder → continuous latent z_e
   ↓ vector quantization → nearest codebook entry
   ↓ token grid (e.g. 16×16 indices from a codebook of K=1024)
   ↓ entropy-code the token sequence
   ↓ [transmitted]
   ↓ decoder (often GAN- or diffusion-trained) → reconstruction

Naive cost: 16×16 × log₂(1024) = 2560 bits, fixed and statistics-blind.

Why put a prior on the tokens: token indices are far from uniform, and neighbors are highly correlated (a sky token predicts more sky). Modeling p(k_i | k_<i) with an autoregressive transformer and arithmetic-coding against it typically takes K=1024 tokens from 10 bits down to 4–6 bits/token.

text
Encode token i:  feed k_<i to the transformer → p(·|k_<i) over K codes
                 arithmetic-encode the true k_i under that distribution
Decode token i:  same transformer, same context → same distribution
                 arithmetic-decode k_i, append, continue

Both sides share the pre-trained transformer weights out-of-band, like a dictionary. Only the arithmetic-coded output goes on the wire.

VQGAN (6.2.2) adds LPIPS and patch-discriminator losses to VQ-VAE, making reconstructions sharp instead of blurry; it is the basis for most generative codecs. The token prior that takes K=1024K = 1024K=1024 from 101010 bits to 444 to 666 per token is worked through in 6.2.8.

Core differences:

Hybrid (H.264-shaped)VQ / generative
Latentcontinuous → scalar quantizeddiscrete codebook indices
Pipelinepredict + residual/context + entropy codetokenize → entropy code indices
Entropy modelhyperprior / spatial context on p(ŷ)autoregressive transformer on p(k_i|k_<i)
Objectiverate-distortion (MSE/MS-SSIM)perceptual + adversarial
Reconstructiondeterministic, faithfulcan hallucinate plausible detail
Sweet spotmid-to-high bitrate, objective metricsvery low bitrate, visual quality
Error behaviorgraceful-isha corrupted token can change semantics
Coding: closed-loop references, random access, and error propagationView exercise

Likely prompt: "Extend a single-image learned codec to video. Which reference does the encoder use, when do you reset state, and what happens after one corrupted P-frame?"

  • Local code: [TOY] video_encoding_pipeline.py — encode_video inserts periodic I-frames and feeds the reconstructed prior frame back as the reference. It is encoder-only and classical, but it demonstrates the invariant a learned codec must keep.
  • Shapes: frame x_t:[B,3,H,W]; reconstructed reference or feature state s_{t-1}; an intra frame uses None/reset state. Multiple reference features multiply memory by DPB depth.
  • Cost: coding remains O(T·H·W) at fixed architecture, but latency and memory depend on reference count and whether future frames are allowed.
  • Pitfalls: conditioning on the original previous frame during training causes train/decode drift; long GOPs improve rate but amplify loss propagation and seek latency; scene cuts need intra refresh; packet loss, model-version metadata, motion bits, and hyperlatents all belong in the rate/system story. Compare the DVC and DCVC predictive structures.
python
def encode_sequence(frames, gop, encode_one, is_scene_cut):
    state, packets = None, []
    for t, frame in enumerate(frames):
        intra = (t % gop == 0) or is_scene_cut(frame)
        if intra:
            state = None
        packet, reconstruction, next_state = encode_one(
            frame, reference_state=state, intra=intra
        )
        packets.append(packet)
        # Never feed the unavailable original frame into the next prediction loop.
        state = next_state if next_state is not None else reconstruction
    return packets

6.4.5 The rate-distortion-perception tradeoff#

The theorem (Blau & Michaeli): at a fixed rate, you cannot simultaneously minimize distortion and maximize perceptual quality. Forcing the output distribution to match the source distribution (perfect "realism") costs you at most a 2× increase in MSE — but it does cost you.

Practical reading: below ~0.1 bpp, hybrid codecs go blurry and blocky, while generative codecs still produce convincing images — that are not the same image. Which you want depends entirely on the application:

ApplicationWant
Medical, forensic, scientific, machine vision inputfidelity — hallucination is a correctness bug
Consumer streaming, video calls, photo storageperception — nobody diffs pixels
Your AquaScope case (situational awareness underwater)the interesting middle — you need the semantics to survive, not the pixels

Say this in an interview: "The right question isn't distortion vs perception, it's what the downstream consumer is. For underwater situational awareness, a reconstruction that preserves object identity and position at 2% BER beats a pixel-faithful one that doesn't arrive." That's the kind of framing that turns a metric argument into a systems argument.

Diffusion as decoder (ultra-low bitrate): transmit a very coarse latent (a few hundred bits), then sample a plausible image with a conditional diffusion model. The diffusion model doesn't compress — it synthesizes the missing high frequencies. Representative: CDC, PerCo (which goes down to 0.003 bpp). Costs: many denoising steps, and stochastic sampling may produce a different reconstruction unless the seed and sampling path are fixed.

6.4.6 Learned vs traditional — the honest tradeoff#

Better:

  • Low-bitrate visual quality — no fixed block grid, so no blocking artifacts.
  • Can optimize a perceptual loss (LPIPS) or an adversarial loss directly.
  • Joint optimization with downstream tasks (compression + super-resolution, or compression optimized for a detector's accuracy).
  • Adapts to a content domain by fine-tuning — a codec specialized for video calls, or for underwater imagery.

Worse:

  • Decode speed: neural inference, 10–100× slower, wants a GPU. Traditional decode is a fixed-function block that costs milliwatts.
  • No hardware acceleration: every phone has an H.264/HEVC/AV1 decoder in silicon. None has a neural-codec decoder.
  • High bitrate: the advantage disappears; traditional codecs are already near the fidelity ceiling.
  • No standard / interop: the decoder is the model weights. Version skew between encoder and decoder is catastrophic, and shipping a 100 MB decoder is its own problem.
  • Determinism: floating-point non-determinism across platforms breaks the entropy decoder — arithmetic coding needs bit-exact probabilities on both sides. This is a real, underappreciated blocker; the fix is integer/deterministic entropy-model arithmetic.
  • Rate control: hitting an exact bitrate target is easy with QP, hard with a λ-parameterized model (you need multiple models or a conditional/variable-rate one).

The realistic 2026 position to state: neural codecs win decisively at very low bitrate and in domain-specific settings; traditional codecs own general-purpose deployment because of hardware, standards, and determinism. The interesting near-term deployments are hybrids — neural pre/post-processing around a standard codec, or neural tools inside a standard (which is what JVET's NNVC exploration is).

MAGVIT-v2 (6.2.4)LFQ (lookup-free quantization), huge vocabulary, joint image+videoshowed a good tokenizer beats diffusion on video generation benchmarks
Cosmos Tokenizer (6.5)continuous and discrete, causal spatiotemporal, high compression ratiosyour GenStream backbone — and Nvidia will ask about it
FSQ (6.2.3)scalar quantization to a small level set; no codebook lossthe simple, collapse-free alternative
EnCodec / SoundStream (6.2.5)RVQ, streaming, scalablethe audio analogue; RVQ's scalability is the transferable idea

Causal vs non-causal tokenizers — the point that matters for streaming: a causal temporal tokenizer only looks at past frames, so you can encode and emit as frames arrive. A non-causal one needs the whole clip. Cosmos is causal by design for exactly this reason (every released Cosmos video tokenizer is). If you're doing real-time streaming with a tokenizer, causality is non-negotiable, and you should say so.

Token adaptation for network dynamics (your GenStream contribution): the natural knob in a token-based codec is how many tokens you send, not a QP. That maps cleanly onto bandwidth adaptation — but unlike QP, token count changes the semantic content that survives, so the quality/rate curve is content-dependent in a different way. Exploiting "video context diversity" — that different regions/scenes tolerate token reduction very differently — is the interesting part. Expect: "how is this different from just lowering the bitrate?" Answer: QP degrades everything uniformly and predictably; token dropping degrades selectively, so you can preserve what matters if you know what matters.

6.5 The Cosmos Tokenizer, Step by Step#

NVIDIA's Cosmos tokenizer turns a video into a short grid of latent vectors or integer tokens and back. It is the autoencoder of 6.1.1 with three choices that fit it to video: a fixed wavelet transform does the first factor of 4 along every axis, every layer is causal in time so frames are never read before they exist, and the discrete version quantizes with FSQ (6.2.3) instead of a learned codebook. Only the decoder's output is supervised, with pixel, perceptual, motion and adversarial losses (6.3.1). The tokenizer is the latent space of the Cosmos world models: their diffusion models generate CV8×8×8 latents and their autoregressive models predict DV8×16×16 tokens. Each step states its input and output; the shapes of the example were traced through the released network.

Note · How FSQ differs from VQ. Both turn a vector into one of finitely many codes and send only the code's index. They differ in where the codes come from. VQ (6.2.1) keeps a learned table of KKK vectors and picks the nearest one. FSQ fixes the codes to a grid and rounds each coordinate on its own:

VQ:k=arg⁡min⁡j∈{1,…,K}∥u−ej∥2,z^=ek,e1,…,eK∈Rd learnedFSQ:z^i=round⁡(uˉi)⌊Li/2⌋ for each i,k=the digits of z^ in mixed radix,no parameters\begin{aligned} \text{VQ:}\quad & k = \arg\min_{j \in \{1, \dots, K\}} \lVert u - e_j \rVert^2, \qquad \hat z = e_k, \qquad e_1, \dots, e_K \in \mathbb{R}^d \text{ learned} \\[6pt] \text{FSQ:}\quad & \hat z_i = \frac{\operatorname{round}(\bar u_i)}{\lfloor L_i / 2 \rfloor} \text{ for each } i, \qquad k = \text{the digits of } \hat z \text{ in mixed radix}, \qquad \text{no parameters} \end{aligned}VQ:FSQ:​k=argj∈{1,…,K}min​∥u−ej​∥2,z^=ek​,e1​,…,eK​∈Rd learnedz^i​=⌊Li​/2⌋round(uˉi​)​ for each i,k=the digits of z^ in mixed radix,no parameters​

A two-dimensional example. Take u=(0.7,−0.2)u = (0.7, -0.2)u=(0.7,−0.2). VQ has K=4K = 4K=4 learned entries. FSQ has L=(3,3)L = (3, 3)L=(3,3), whose 999 codes are the fixed points {−1,0,1}2\{-1, 0, 1\}^2{−1,0,1}2:

VQ:e1:4=(0.9,0.1), (−0.5,0.8), (−0.6,−0.7), (2,2)∥u−ej∥2=0.13, 2.44, 1.94, 6.53  ⇒  k=1,z^=(0.9,0.1)FSQ:uˉ=1.001tanh⁡u=(0.60,−0.20)  ⇒  z^=(1,0)digits (2,1)  ⇒  k=2+3⋅1=5\begin{aligned} \text{VQ:}\quad & e_{1:4} = (0.9, 0.1),\ (-0.5, 0.8),\ (-0.6, -0.7),\ (2, 2) \\ & \lVert u - e_j \rVert^2 = 0.13,\ 2.44,\ 1.94,\ 6.53 \;\Rightarrow\; k = 1,\quad \hat z = (0.9, 0.1) \\[6pt] \text{FSQ:}\quad & \bar u = 1.001 \tanh u = (0.60, -0.20) \;\Rightarrow\; \hat z = (1, 0) \\ & \text{digits } (2, 1) \;\Rightarrow\; k = 2 + 3 \cdot 1 = 5 \end{aligned}VQ:FSQ:​e1:4​=(0.9,0.1), (−0.5,0.8), (−0.6,−0.7), (2,2)∥u−ej​∥2=0.13, 2.44, 1.94, 6.53⇒k=1,z^=(0.9,0.1)uˉ=1.001tanhu=(0.60,−0.20)⇒z^=(1,0)digits (2,1)⇒k=2+3⋅1=5​

VQ cuts the plane into the Voronoi cells of the eje_jej​, and the cells move as the entries learn. FSQ cuts it into fixed squares.

Why VQ needs two extra losses. The straight-through estimator writes z^=u+sg⁡[ek−u]\hat z = u + \operatorname{sg}[e_k - u]z^=u+sg[ek​−u], so the reconstruction gradient reaches uuu but never the table. The table needs a loss of its own, and the encoder needs to be held near the table:

LVQ=Lrec+∥sg⁡[u]−ek∥2⏟codebook: ek moves toward u+β ∥u−sg⁡[ek]∥2⏟commitment: u stays near ek,β≈0.25\mathcal{L}_{\text{VQ}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}} + \underbrace{\lVert \operatorname{sg}[u] - e_k \rVert^2}_{\text{codebook: } e_k \text{ moves toward } u} + \beta\, \underbrace{\lVert u - \operatorname{sg}[e_k] \rVert^2}_{\text{commitment: } u \text{ stays near } e_k}, \qquad \beta \approx 0.25LVQ​=Lrec​+codebook: ek​ moves toward u∥sg[u]−ek​∥2​​+βcommitment: u stays near ek​∥u−sg[ek​]∥2​​,β≈0.25

Without the commitment term, uuu can drift far from every entry. The straight-through copy then ignores a large gap ek−ue_k - uek​−u and the gradient becomes a poor guide. The EMA variant replaces the codebook term by setting each eke_kek​ to the running mean of the uuu assigned to it, a k-means step per batch.

Why VQ collapses. Both extra terms touch only the chosen entry eke_kek​. An entry that is never the nearest to any uuu, like e4=(2,2)e_4 = (2, 2)e4​=(2,2) above, gets no gradient and stays where it was initialized, unused. If only 300300300 of K=1024K = 1024K=1024 entries are ever used, a token carries at most log⁡2300=8.2\log_2 300 = 8.2log2​300=8.2 bits instead of 101010. The FSQ paper measures this in its MaskGIT experiments: VQ uses fewer than half its codes once K>211K > 2^{11}K>211 and no more than about 2102^{10}210 codes even in larger codebooks, while FSQ uses almost all of 2142^{14}214. The fixes in 6.2.1, such as dead-code resets, EMA and k-means initialization, all patch this failure.

Why FSQ needs none of it. There is no table, so nothing has to be pulled and nothing can be left behind. z^\hat zz^ is a fixed function of uuu, and the only trained parts are the encoder, which learns where to put uuu, and the decoder, which learns what each grid point means. Every one of the ∏iLi\prod_i L_i∏i​Li​ codes is reached by moving each scalar into the right interval. However large uuu grows, tanh⁡\tanhtanh keeps uˉ\bar uuˉ inside the grid, which does the job of the commitment loss in VQ. The whole objective is the reconstruction loss of step 9.

What FSQ gives up. VQ can place its codes anywhere in Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd, densely where the data are dense. FSQ's codes form a uniform, axis-aligned grid in a few dimensions: the paper notes d<10d < 10d<10 for FSQ against d≥512d \ge 512d≥512 for typical VQ. The learned layers around the grid make up for it. The projection of step 6 and the encoder bend the data to fit the grid, and the decoder reads it back. With this design the FSQ paper reports performance competitive with VQ on image generation, depth estimation, colorization and panoptic segmentation.

The indices become codes, a 1×1×11 \times 1 \times 11×1×1 convolution maps 666 channels back to 161616, and the encoder runs in mirror image: three residual blocks per level instead of two, the same bottleneck attention, and upsampling instead of downsampling:

The temporal step repeats every latent frame except the first, so m+1m + 1m+1 frames become 2m+12m + 12m+1, the inverse of step 4. Example: 3×45×803 \times 45 \times 803×45×80, then 3×90×1603 \times 90 \times 1603×90×160 (spatial), then 5×180×3205 \times 180 \times 3205×180×320 (spatial and temporal); an output convolution to 192192192 channels; the inverse Haar transform gives 202020 frames of 720×1280720 \times 1280720×1280, and the 333 extra copies of frame 000 are dropped: 171717 frames.

Step 9 · Training losses. (x0:T, x^0:T)  ⟶  L(x_{0:T},\ \hat x_{0:T}) \;\longrightarrow\; \mathcal{L}(x0:T​, x^0:T​)⟶L

Two stages, and only the decoder output is supervised. Stage 111:

L1=∥x^0:T−x0:T∥1,LPerc=1L∑l=1L∑tαl∥VGGl(x^t)−VGGl(xt)∥1\mathcal{L}_1 = \big\lVert \hat x_{0:T} - x_{0:T} \big\rVert_1, \qquad \mathcal{L}_{\text{Perc}} = \frac{1}{L} \sum_{l=1}^{L} \sum_{t} \alpha_l \big\lVert \text{VGG}_l(\hat x_t) - \text{VGG}_l(x_t) \big\rVert_1L1​=​x^0:T​−x0:T​​1​,LPerc​=L1​l=1∑L​t∑​αl​​VGGl​(x^t​)−VGGl​(xt​)​1​

Stage 222 fine-tunes with an optical-flow loss, a Gram-matrix loss and an adversarial loss (6.3.1):

LFlow=1T∑t=1T∥OF(x^t,x^t−1)−OF(xt,xt−1)∥1+1T∑t=0T−1∥OF(x^t,x^t+1)−OF(xt,xt+1)∥1LGram=1L∑l=1L∑tαl∥GMl(x^t)−GMl(xt)∥1\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}_{\text{Flow}} &= \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \big\lVert \text{OF}(\hat x_t, \hat x_{t-1}) - \text{OF}(x_t, x_{t-1}) \big\rVert_1 + \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \big\lVert \text{OF}(\hat x_t, \hat x_{t+1}) - \text{OF}(x_t, x_{t+1}) \big\rVert_1 \\[6pt] \mathcal{L}_{\text{Gram}} &= \frac{1}{L} \sum_{l=1}^{L} \sum_{t} \alpha_l \big\lVert \text{GM}_l(\hat x_t) - \text{GM}_l(x_t) \big\rVert_1 \end{aligned}LFlow​LGram​​=T1​t=1∑T​​OF(x^t​,x^t−1​)−OF(xt​,xt−1​)​1​+T1​t=0∑T−1​​OF(x^t​,x^t+1​)−OF(xt​,xt+1​)​1​=L1​l=1∑L​t∑​αl​​GMl​(x^t​)−GMl​(xt​)​1​​

VGGl\text{VGG}_lVGGl​ is layer lll of a pretrained VGG-19, OF\text{OF}OF an optical-flow estimator (the paper cites RAFT), and GMl\text{GM}_lGMl​ the Gram matrix of a layer's features, which measures texture statistics. Each term fixes a different failure: L1\mathcal{L}_1L1​ alone gives blur, the perceptual loss makes features match, the flow loss makes the motion between reconstructed frames match the real motion so the video does not flicker, the Gram loss restores sharp texture, and the adversarial loss adds detail where compression is heaviest. There is no commitment loss, because FSQ needs none, and no KL term, because the latent is a plain autoencoder's. Images and videos alternate in the mini-batches, which works because an image is a one-frame video under the causal design. The paper does not give the loss weights.

The PSNR values are the paper's Cosmos-0.1 models on DAVIS; the later Cosmos-Tokenize1 checkpoints share the architecture and were trained on longer clips. Two readings matter. First, the discrete tokens cost 2.52.52.5 to 444 dB against the continuous latent at the same ratio, the price of 15.9715.9715.97 bits per position against 161616 floating-point numbers. Second, causal does not mean frame by frame. Latent frame j≥1j \ge 1j≥1 needs frames up to sTjs_T jsT​j, so the encoder emits one latent frame per sTs_TsT​ input frames. What causality buys is that it never waits for more than that and never needs the rest of the clip, whereas a non-causal tokenizer must hold the whole window before emitting anything. The image tokenizers, CI and DI, have one-frame delay and no temporal compression. For streaming, sTs_TsT​ is the trade between rate and delay.

Chapter link ↗

One request, followed through everything a serving system does with the decoder-only model of Chapter 3: the prompt is pushed through the model once, every later token is produced one step at a time against a cache, and tokens are drawn from the logits. Each step states its input, the operation and its output, with the cost next to it; the recurring question is not what is computed, which Chapter 3 settled, but how many bytes and FLOPs it takes and which of the two is the limit.

The example. LLaMA-3-8B in BF16 on one H100: L=32L = 32L=32 layers, d=4096d = 4096d=4096, h=32h = 32h=32 query heads, hkv=8h_{kv} = 8hkv​=8 key/value heads (GQA), dk=128d_k = 128dk​=128, dff=14,336d_{\text{ff}} = 14{,}336dff​=14,336, vocabulary V=128,256V = 128{,}256V=128,256, N=8.03×109N = 8.03 \times 10^{9}N=8.03×109 parameters, 161616 GB in BF16. Of these, Nmat=7.50×109N_{\text{mat}} = 7.50 \times 10^{9}Nmat​=7.50×109 sit in the matrices that multiply activations (the rest is the input embedding table, which is only looked up), so the bytes a step must stream are Wbytes=2Nmat≈15 GBW_{\text{bytes}} = 2 N_{\text{mat}} \approx 15\,\text{GB}Wbytes​=2Nmat​≈15GB. A request with a prompt of n=1,000n = 1{,}000n=1,000 tokens asks for m=200m = 200m=200 new tokens. The GPU moves β=3.35 TB/s\beta = 3.35\,\text{TB/s}β=3.35TB/s from its memory and performs π=989 TFLOP/s\pi = 989\,\text{TFLOP/s}π=989TFLOP/s in BF16, so its ridge point is π/β≈295\pi / \beta \approx 295π/β≈295 FLOP per byte: a kernel that does fewer FLOPs per byte it reads is waiting on memory, one that does more is waiting on arithmetic. One token costs 128128128 KiB; 8,1928{,}1928,192 tokens cost 1.071.071.07 GB per sequence, 161616 sequences at that length cost as much as the weights. hkvh_{kv}hkv​ is in the formula and hhh is not: GQA shares each key/value head among h/hkv=4h / h_{kv} = 4h/hkv​=4 query heads, which is why LLaMA-3-8B's cache is 4×4\times4× smaller than LLaMA-2-7B's (hkv=32h_{kv} = 32hkv​=32, 512512512 KiB per token) at the same ddd. Everything else about serving follows from this formula: long context is expensive in memory before it is expensive in compute, the cache is stored in fixed-size blocks so that sequences of unknown final length do not fragment memory (paged attention), prompts shared by many requests are cached once (prefix caching), and the cache is quantized to 8 or 4 bits when memory is the constraint.

Step 3 · One decode step. xt∈{0,…,V−1}, {Kℓ,Vℓ}1:t−1  ⟶  zt∈RV, {Kℓ,Vℓ}1:tx_t \in \{0, \dots, V-1\},\ \{K_\ell, V_\ell\}_{1:t-1} \;\longrightarrow\; \mathbf z_t \in \mathbb{R}^{V},\ \{K_\ell, V_\ell\}_{1:t}xt​∈{0,…,V−1}, {Kℓ​,Vℓ​}1:t−1​⟶zt​∈RV, {Kℓ​,Vℓ​}1:t​

The new token is embedded at position ttt, and in every layer its single query reads the whole cache:

qt=xtWQ,kt=xtWK,vt=xtWV(kt,vt appended to the cache)at=softmax⁡ ⁣(qtK1:t⊤dk)V1:tper head\begin{aligned} q_t &= x_t W^{Q}, \qquad k_t = x_t W^{K}, \qquad v_t = x_t W^{V} \qquad (k_t, v_t \text{ appended to the cache}) \\[6pt] a_t &= \operatorname{softmax}\!\Big( \frac{q_t K_{1:t}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}} \Big) V_{1:t} \qquad \text{per head} \end{aligned}qt​at​​=xt​WQ,kt​=xt​WK,vt​=xt​WV(kt​,vt​ appended to the cache)=softmax(dk​​qt​K1:t⊤​​)V1:t​per head​

The arithmetic is tiny and the traffic is not: every weight matrix is read once to produce one token, and so is the cache; only the embedding table is spared, because a lookup gathers one 888 KB row and multiplies nothing.

FLOPsstep≈2Nmat+4tdL≈15.5 GFLOP,bytesstep≈Wbytes+c t≈15.1 GB,Istep≈1\text{FLOPs}_{\text{step}} \approx 2 N_{\text{mat}} + 4 t d L \approx 15.5\,\text{GFLOP}, \qquad \text{bytes}_{\text{step}} \approx W_{\text{bytes}} + c\,t \approx 15.1\,\text{GB}, \qquad I_{\text{step}} \approx 1FLOPsstep​≈2Nmat​+4tdL≈15.5GFLOP,bytesstep​≈Wbytes​+ct≈15.1GB,Istep​≈1

One sequence cannot be decoded faster than about 220220220 tokens per second on this GPU no matter how fast its arithmetic is; the step is memory-bound by a factor of nearly 300300300. This asymmetry is the whole subject of inference optimization. Anything that shrinks the bytes helps decode nearly in proportion: weights in INT4 (Wbytes≈3.9W_{\text{bytes}} \approx 3.9Wbytes​≈3.9 GB with scales) bring the step to 1.21.21.2 ms, and a smaller cache (GQA, quantized cache) matters once c tc\,tct is comparable with WbytesW_{\text{bytes}}Wbytes​. Anything that only adds FLOPs is free until III reaches the ridge. The time per output token, TPOT, is this number.

Step 4 · Batching. BBB sequences, each at its own length tbt_btb​   ⟶  \;\longrightarrow\;⟶ one step for all of them

The weights are read once per step whatever BBB is; the caches are not shared. So

timestep(B)≈max⁡ ⁣(2NmatBπ, Wbytes+c∑btbβ),throughput=Btimestep(B)\text{time}_{\text{step}}(B) \approx \max\!\Big( \frac{2 N_{\text{mat}} B}{\pi},\ \frac{W_{\text{bytes}} + c \sum_b t_b}{\beta} \Big), \qquad \text{throughput} = \frac{B}{\text{time}_{\text{step}}(B)}timestep​(B)≈max(π2Nmat​B​, βWbytes​+c∑b​tb​​),throughput=timestep​(B)B​

At t=1,000t = 1{,}000t=1,000: B=8B = 8B=8 takes 4.84.84.8 ms for 1,7001{,}7001,700 tokens/s, B=64B = 64B=64 takes 7.07.07.0 ms for 9,2009{,}2009,200 tokens/s, B=256B = 256B=256 takes 14.514.514.5 ms for 17,70017{,}70017,700 tokens/s. Batching amortizes the weight read, which is why it raises decode throughput by an order of magnitude at a modest cost in latency, and why it barely helps prefill, which was compute-bound already. It does not amortize the cache read: per generated token the cache costs c tc\,tct bytes against 2Nmat2 N_{\text{mat}}2Nmat​ FLOPs, so decode stays memory-bound at any batch size once t>2Nmat/(c⋅π/β)≈400t > 2 N_{\text{mat}} / (c \cdot \pi / \beta) \approx 400t>2Nmat​/(c⋅π/β)≈400 tokens. Two more limits bound BBB. Memory: Bmax⁡(t)=(HBM−2N)/(c t)B_{\max}(t) = (\text{HBM} - 2N) / (c\,t)Bmax​(t)=(HBM−2N)/(ct) with all 161616 GB of weights resident, about 120120120 sequences of 4,0964{,}0964,096 tokens or 606060 of 8,1928{,}1928,192 on 808080 GB. Arrivals: requests do not start and finish together, so the batch is rebuilt every step (continuous batching), a finishing sequence is replaced by a waiting one, and long prompts are prefilled in chunks interleaved with decode steps so that one n=30,000n = 30{,}000n=30,000 arrival does not freeze everyone else's tokens for a second.

Temperature changes the shape, truncation removes the tail where a single draw of a 10−410^{-4}10−4 token derails the text; top-ppp adapts the cut to the shape (one token when the model is sure, many when it is not), which fixed kkk does not. The order matters: temperature first, then truncation, then renormalization. For anything that is scored or compared, including a quality model's outputs, use T=0T = 0T=0: the result is then a deterministic function of the prompt.

PyTorch implementation: KV cache and sampling#

inference_kv_cache.py implements the steps on a toy decoder-only model: two layers with d=32d = 32d=32, trained on four sentences over a nine-word vocabulary. test_inference_kv_cache.py checks the claims: decoding against the cache reproduces the full forward pass to 10−910^{-9}10−9, the cache-size formula gives 128128128 KiB per token for LLaMA-3-8B, the sampling rules give the numbers of step 5 and their limits (T→0T \to 0T→0, k=1k = 1k=1, p=1p = 1p=1), and seeded sampling is reproducible and never leaves the truncated set.

bash
.venv-transformer/bin/python inference_kv_cache.py
.venv-transformer/bin/python -m unittest -v test_inference_kv_cache

The model. Step 2 of Chapter 3 with a causal mask, written so that past keys and values are reused: cache holds K1:t−1K_{1:t-1}K1:t−1​ and V1:t−1V_{1:t-1}V1:t−1​ of the layer, the new keys and values are concatenated, and the mask is shifted by t_past so that the new rows see everything before them. Block and CausalLM use the pre-norm order of Chapter 4, x←x+MHA⁡(LN⁡(x))x \leftarrow x + \operatorname{MHA}(\operatorname{LN}(x))x←x+MHA(LN(x)) then x←x+FFN⁡(LN⁡(x))x \leftarrow x + \operatorname{FFN}(\operatorname{LN}(x))x←x+FFN(LN(x)), with GELU and a final LayerNorm before the head, rather than the post-norm block of Chapter 3, steps 3 and 4; the cache argument does not depend on that choice.

python
from __future__ import annotations

import math

import torch
from torch import Tensor, nn
python
class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    """Step 2 of Chapter 2 with a causal mask, written so that past keys and values are reused."""

    def __init__(self, d_model: int, num_heads: int):
        super().__init__()
        self.num_heads, self.d_k = num_heads, d_model // num_heads
        self.w_q = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
        self.w_k = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
        self.w_v = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
        self.w_o = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x: Tensor, cache: dict | None = None) -> tuple[Tensor, dict]:
        batch, t_new, d_model = x.shape
        heads = lambda z: z.view(batch, t_new, self.num_heads, self.d_k).transpose(1, 2)  # [B, h, t_new, d_k]
        q, k, v = heads(self.w_q(x)), heads(self.w_k(x)), heads(self.w_v(x))
        if cache is not None:                        # step 3: the past is read, never recomputed
            k = torch.cat([cache["k"], k], dim=2)
            v = torch.cat([cache["v"], v], dim=2)
        t_past = k.shape[2] - t_new
        scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(self.d_k)      # [B, h, t_new, t_past + t_new]
        causal = torch.ones(t_new, t_past + t_new, dtype=torch.bool, device=x.device).tril(diagonal=t_past)
        scores = scores.masked_fill(~causal, float("-inf"))
        out = (scores.softmax(dim=-1) @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(batch, t_new, d_model)
        return self.w_o(out), {"k": k, "v": v}


class Block(nn.Module):
    """Pre-norm block:  x' = x + Attention(LN(x));  x'' = x' + FFN(LN(x'))."""

    def __init__(self, d_model: int, num_heads: int, d_ff: int):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.attention = CausalSelfAttention(d_model, num_heads)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.ffn = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model))

    def forward(self, x: Tensor, cache: dict | None = None) -> tuple[Tensor, dict]:
        a, cache = self.attention(self.norm1(x), cache)
        x = x + a
        return x + self.ffn(self.norm2(x)), cache


def sinusoidal_positions(max_len: int, d_model: int) -> Tensor:
    """The fixed table P of Chapter 2, step 1."""
    position = torch.arange(max_len, dtype=torch.float64)[:, None]
    frequency = 10000.0 ** (-torch.arange(0, d_model, 2, dtype=torch.float64) / d_model)
    table = torch.zeros(max_len, d_model, dtype=torch.float64)
    table[:, 0::2], table[:, 1::2] = torch.sin(position * frequency), torch.cos(position * frequency)
    return table


class CausalLM(nn.Module):
    """A decoder-only Transformer: embeddings + positions, L pre-norm blocks, final norm, LM head."""

    def __init__(self, vocab_size: int, d_model: int = 32, num_heads: int = 4, d_ff: int = 64,
                 num_layers: int = 2, max_len: int = 256):
        super().__init__()
        self.d_model = d_model
        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)
        self.register_buffer("positions", sinusoidal_positions(max_len, d_model).float())
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList(Block(d_model, num_heads, d_ff) for _ in range(num_layers))
        self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(d_model, vocab_size, bias=False)

    def forward(self, ids: Tensor, caches: list | None = None, start: int = 0) -> tuple[Tensor, list]:
        """ids: [B, t_new] token ids that sit at positions start .. start + t_new - 1.
        Returns the logits of every new position, [B, t_new, V], and the updated cache of every layer."""
        x = self.embedding(ids) * math.sqrt(self.d_model) + self.positions[start:start + ids.shape[1]].to(ids.device)
        updated = []
        for i, block in enumerate(self.blocks):
            x, cache = block(x, None if caches is None else caches[i])
            updated.append(cache)
        return self.lm_head(self.norm(x)), updated

Steps 1 to 3. prefill runs the prompt once and keeps every layer's cache; decode_step feeds one token at position t_past; cache_bytes is the formula of step 2; generate is the generation loop, prefill once and then one decode step per token, with use_cache=False as the quadratic alternative that recomputes the whole prefix.

python
def prefill(model: CausalLM, ids: Tensor) -> tuple[Tensor, list]:
    """Step 1: the whole prompt in one pass. Returns the logits of the last position and every layer's cache."""
    logits, caches = model(ids)
    return logits[:, -1], caches


def decode_step(model: CausalLM, token: Tensor, caches: list) -> tuple[Tensor, list]:
    """Step 3: one new token reads the cache and appends its own key and value. token: [B]."""
    start = caches[0]["k"].shape[2]
    logits, caches = model(token[:, None], caches, start=start)
    return logits[:, -1], caches


def cache_bytes(num_layers: int, kv_heads: int, d_head: int, tokens: int, batch: int = 1, bytes_per_value: int = 2) -> int:
    """Step 2: 2 (K and V) x layers x KV heads x d_head x tokens x batch x bytes per value."""
    return 2 * num_layers * kv_heads * d_head * tokens * batch * bytes_per_value


@torch.no_grad()
def generate(model: CausalLM, prompt: Tensor, max_new_tokens: int, sample, use_cache: bool = True) -> Tensor:
    """Steps 1 and 3 in a loop: prefill once, then one decode step per token. `sample` maps logits [B, V] to tokens [B]."""
    ids = prompt
    logits, caches = prefill(model, ids)
    for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
        token = sample(logits)
        ids = torch.cat([ids, token[:, None]], dim=1)
        if use_cache:
            logits, caches = decode_step(model, token, caches)
        else:                                        # the quadratic alternative: rerun the whole prefix
            logits = model(ids)[0][:, -1]
    return ids

Step 5. filtered_probabilities applies the temperature, then the truncations, then renormalizes; temperature=0 returns the one-hot of the arg max. The top-ppp mask keeps a token while the mass before it is below ppp, so the token that crosses ppp survives and at least one token always does.

python
def filtered_probabilities(logits: Tensor, temperature: float = 1.0, top_k: int | None = None,
                           top_p: float | None = None, min_p: float | None = None) -> Tensor:
    """Step 5: temperature, then truncation, then renormalisation. logits [B, V] -> probabilities [B, V]."""
    if temperature <= 0:                             # the T -> 0 limit: all mass on the arg max (greedy)
        return nn.functional.one_hot(logits.argmax(dim=-1), logits.shape[-1]).to(logits.dtype)
    probs = (logits / temperature).softmax(dim=-1)
    keep = torch.ones_like(probs, dtype=torch.bool)
    if top_k is not None:                            # the k largest probabilities
        keep &= probs >= probs.topk(top_k, dim=-1).values[..., -1:]
    if top_p is not None:                            # the smallest prefix of the sorted list whose mass reaches p
        sorted_probs, order = probs.sort(dim=-1, descending=True)
        mass_before = sorted_probs.cumsum(dim=-1) - sorted_probs
        keep &= torch.zeros_like(keep).scatter(-1, order, mass_before < top_p)
    if min_p is not None:                            # at least a fraction min_p of the largest probability
        keep &= probs >= min_p * probs.amax(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
    probs = probs * keep
    return probs / probs.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)


def repetition_penalty(logits: Tensor, context: Tensor, penalty: float) -> Tensor:
    """Logits of tokens already in the context are divided by `penalty` when positive and multiplied when negative."""
    logits = logits.clone()
    for b in range(logits.shape[0]):
        seen = context[b].unique()
        z = logits[b, seen]
        logits[b, seen] = torch.where(z > 0, z / penalty, z * penalty)
    return logits


def sample_next(logits: Tensor, temperature: float = 1.0, top_k: int | None = None, top_p: float | None = None,
                min_p: float | None = None, generator: torch.Generator | None = None) -> Tensor:
    probs = filtered_probabilities(logits, temperature, top_k, top_p, min_p)
    return torch.multinomial(probs, 1, generator=generator).squeeze(-1)

The demo trains the model, verifies the cache against a full pass, prints the table of step 5, compares greedy decoding with and without the cache, and draws one sampled continuation:

python
CORPUS = ("the cat sat on the mat . the dog sat on the log . "
          "the cat saw the dog on the log . the dog saw the cat on the mat .")
WORDS = sorted(set(CORPUS.split()))
IDS = torch.tensor([[WORDS.index(w) for w in CORPUS.split()]])


def train(model: CausalLM, steps: int, lr: float = 5e-3) -> float:
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    for _ in range(steps):
        logits, _ = model(IDS[:, :-1])
        loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, logits.shape[-1]), IDS[:, 1:].reshape(-1))
        optimizer.zero_grad(), loss.backward(), optimizer.step()
    return loss.item()


def words(ids: Tensor) -> str:
    return " ".join(WORDS[i] for i in ids[0].tolist())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = CausalLM(len(WORDS), d_model=32, num_heads=4, d_ff=64, num_layers=2)
    print(f"model: 2 layers, d=32, trained to loss {train(model, 400):.3f}; vocabulary of {len(WORDS)} words")

    with torch.no_grad():
        full, _ = model(IDS)                                       # every position in one pass
        logits, caches = prefill(model, IDS[:, :4])
        cached = [logits]
        for t in range(4, IDS.shape[1]):
            logits, caches = decode_step(model, IDS[:, t], caches)
            cached.append(logits)
        gap = (torch.stack(cached, dim=1) - full[:, 3:]).abs().max().item()
    print(f"cache matches full recompute: {gap < 1e-4} (max |diff| {gap:.1e} over {IDS.shape[1] - 4} decode steps)")
    print(f"KV cache of LLaMA-3-8B: {cache_bytes(32, 8, 128, 1) // 1024} KiB per token, "
          f"{cache_bytes(32, 8, 128, 8192) / 1e9:.2f} GB at 8192 tokens")

    z = torch.tensor([[2.0, 1.0, 0.5, 0.0, -1.0]])
    show = lambda p: "[" + " ".join(f"{v:.3f}" for v in p[0].tolist()) + "]"
    print(f"sampling on logits {z[0].tolist()}:")
    print(f"  T=1.0     -> {show(filtered_probabilities(z))}")
    print(f"  T=0.5     -> {show(filtered_probabilities(z, temperature=0.5))}")
    print(f"  top-k=2   -> {show(filtered_probabilities(z, top_k=2))}")
    print(f"  top-p=0.9 -> {show(filtered_probabilities(z, top_p=0.9))}")

    prompt = IDS[:, :2]
    greedy = lambda logits: logits.argmax(dim=-1)
    with_cache = generate(model, prompt, 12, greedy)
    without = generate(model, prompt, 12, greedy, use_cache=False)
    print(f'greedy from "{words(prompt)}": {words(with_cache[:, 2:])}')
    print(f"greedy with cache == greedy without cache: {torch.equal(with_cache, without)}")
    generator = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
    sampled = generate(model, prompt, 12, lambda logits: sample_next(logits, temperature=1.0, top_p=0.9, generator=generator))
    print(f'sampled at T=1, top-p=0.9: {words(sampled[:, 2:])}')

Chapter guide: Start system-design answers with order-of-magnitude estimates: whether parameters fit, how many FLOPs training requires, and how the KV cache grows with context and concurrency. Discuss frameworks only after that.

8.1 Count parameters, FLOPs, and memory#

A matrix multiplication [M,K] @ [K,N] performs approximately 2MKN FLOPs, counting one multiply and one add. Let a dense model have P parameters in its major matmuls and process T training tokens:

text
forward FLOPs  ≈ 2 · P · T
training FLOPs ≈ 6 · P · T       # forward + two backward matmuls
wall time      ≈ total_FLOPs / (num_devices · peak_FLOPs/s · MFU)

This first-order rule ignores attention O(L·T_context²·d), embeddings, MoE routing, and recomputation. Attention can no longer be ignored at long context lengths. For MoE, estimate FLOPs using active parameters per token, while memory must still hold all experts.

First divide accelerator memory into four buckets:

  1. Weights: BF16/FP16 usually use 2 bytes per parameter; INT8 uses about 1 and INT4 about 0.5, plus scale metadata.
  2. Gradients: commonly 2 or 4 bytes per parameter.
  3. Optimizer states: Adam's FP32 m,v together use 8 bytes per parameter; some implementations also keep an FP32 master weight.
  4. Activations: grow with microbatch size, sequence length, hidden size, and layer count; checkpointing trades recomputation for storage.

A 7B model therefore needs about 14 GB for BF16 weights alone. A common Adam configuration may already require roughly 12–16 bytes per parameter before activations. Always state assumptions about dtypes, master weights, gradients, and sharding. Inference has no optimizer or gradient states, but it adds the KV cache of Chapter 7, which can dominate with long contexts and high concurrency.

8.2 Scaling laws: what they do and do not promise#

Empirical scaling laws commonly model reducible loss as a power-law decline with parameter count, data, or compute. Their purpose is not to claim that larger models must exhibit emergence; they help allocate a fixed budget among more parameters, more independent data, and more training steps.

  • Early fits from Kaplan et al. emphasized the sample efficiency of larger models.
  • Within its experimental regime, Chinchilla found that compute-optimal training scales model size and training tokens at roughly the same rate as budget grows. Many earlier large models were therefore undertrained relative to their parameter count.
  • The familiar "about 20 tokens per parameter" is an empirical point for a particular model family, dataset, and budget range, not a physical constant.
  • Training-optimal is not product-optimal: a smaller model trained longer can have lower inference latency and serving cost. Data quality, deduplication, repeated epochs, target domain, and downstream post-training all shift the optimum.

8.3 A 60-second budgeting checklist#

  1. Write down P, tokens, dtype, context, batch/concurrency; do not report only "model size."
  2. Estimate training compute with 6PT, then use MFU to turn peak FLOPs into achievable time.
  3. Estimate weights, optimizer states, gradients, activations, and KV separately; identify whether capacity or bandwidth is the constraint.
  4. Add checkpointing, evaluation, failed runs, and data-pipeline overhead. A theoretical lower bound is not a project schedule.

Primary sources: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models · Chinchilla / compute-optimal training · Transformer math and the 6PT approximation

09GPUs & the Roofline Model3 sections
Chapter link ↗

Chapter guide: FLOPs tell you how much arithmetic is required; the roofline model tells you whether the hardware is computing or waiting for data. This is why fewer FLOPs do not guarantee lower latency.

9.1 The three hard limits#

A kernel is constrained by at least three resources: compute throughput, memory or communication bandwidth, and memory capacity.

text
arithmetic_intensity = FLOPs / bytes_moved
achievable_FLOPs/s <= min(peak_compute,
                          memory_bandwidth * arithmetic_intensity)
T_lower_bound >= max(FLOPs / peak_compute,
                     bytes_moved / memory_bandwidth)

Low arithmetic intensity lies in the bandwidth-bound region; high intensity is required to saturate Tensor Cores. Large matmuls raise intensity by reusing tiles on chip. Elementwise operations, normalization, and small-batch decode repeatedly read and write large tensors while doing little arithmetic, making them more likely to be limited by bandwidth or launch overhead.

9.2 Memory hierarchy and practical optimization#

A useful memory-hierarchy model is: registers/shared memory (small and fast) → L2 → HBM (large but distant) → host/network. Optimization is not blindly reducing arithmetic; it is keeping data close and reusing it:

  • Tiling: repeatedly use blocks that fit in on-chip storage for matmul or attention. Reducing HBM IO is the central idea behind FlashAttention.
  • Kernel fusion: combine adjacent operations such as bias, activation, and normalization so intermediate tensors are written back less often.
  • Batching: let multiple tokens reuse loaded weights, usually improving throughput while increasing queueing and tail latency.
  • Layout / shape: Tensor-Core-friendly dimensions and contiguous access determine whether an operation actually uses the fast path.
  • Zero-copy pipeline: avoid CPU↔GPU round trips. Video deployment should keep decode→preprocess→model on the device in particular.

9.3 What to measure#

Use a profiler first to separate kernel time, memory copies, CPU launch gaps, and collectives; then inspect achieved bandwidth, Tensor Core utilization, occupancy, and MFU. The roofline is an upper-bound model that omits dependencies, synchronization, scheduling, and small-kernel launch costs, so the final answer must return to wall-clock measurements.

Primary sources: Google DeepMind scaling book: rooflines · NVIDIA CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide · FlashAttention

10Precision, Efficiency & Deployment5 sections
Chapter link ↗

Chapter guide: Low precision, pruning, and distillation count as optimizations only when the target hardware uses the corresponding kernels and end-to-end quality still meets the bar. Report parameters, FLOPs, bandwidth, and latency separately.

Your resume claims "on-device inference optimization" and a 4-bit iOS deployment — this section must be airtight.

10.1 Quantization#

The basic mapping:

text
Symmetric:   q = round(x / s),            s = max|x| / (2^{b−1} − 1)
Asymmetric:  q = round(x / s) + z,        s = (max−min)/(2^b − 1),  z = zero-point

Granularity (biggest quality lever): per-tensor → per-channel → per-group (e.g. 128 weights share a scale). Finer = better quality, more metadata.

What goes wrong with INT8, and the fixes:

  • Outliers: one large value forces a big scale, crushing the resolution of everything else. In LLMs, specific activation channels have persistent huge outliers (the "emergent outlier features" phenomenon above ~6B params). → SmoothQuant migrates the difficulty from activations into weights via a per-channel scaling that's mathematically absorbed into the previous layer; LLM.int8() keeps outlier channels in fp16.
  • Asymmetric activations: ReLU/GELU outputs are mostly positive, so symmetric INT8 wastes half the range → use asymmetric.
  • Layer sensitivity: embeddings, the LM head, the first and last layers, and attention logits are far more sensitive → keep them at higher precision (mixed precision).
  • Error accumulation across layers, especially in a recurrent or residual-heavy structure.

Methods:

MethodTypeNotes
PTQpost-trainingfast, needs a small calibration set
QATduring trainingsimulate quantization in the forward pass (fake-quant + straight-through estimator), best quality, expensive
GPTQweight-only PTQlayer-wise, uses second-order (Hessian) information to compensate quantization error across remaining weights
AWQweight-only PTQprotects the ~1% of weight channels that matter most (identified by activation magnitude) via per-channel scaling
GGUF K-quantsweight-onlyllama.cpp's format: mixed block sizes, Q4_K_M is the popular quality/size point
NF4weight-onlyQLoRA's 4-bit "normal float," information-theoretically optimal for normally-distributed weights

For image/video models specifically: after quantizing, don't only check PSNR — check for visual artifacts and temporal flicker, because quantization error is spatially structured and can vary frame to frame, producing shimmer that a per-frame metric completely misses. That's a strong, domain-specific point to make.

On-device (your iOS/LLMFarm case): 4-bit weight-only quantization on a 3B model → ~1.7 GB, which fits in the per-app memory budget. The real constraints on a phone are (1) memory ceiling and OOM-kill, (2) memory bandwidth — decode is bandwidth-bound, (3) sustained thermal throttling — the first 30 s of benchmarking lies, and (4) energy per token. Expect "how did you measure it?" — the answer should mention sustained load, not a single cold run.

10.2 Pruning and distillation#

Pruning: remove weights (unstructured) or whole channels/heads/layers (structured).

  • Unstructured pruning cuts parameter count but gives no speedup without sparse-tensor hardware support. Say this — it's a common misconception the interviewer may be testing.
  • Structured pruning (channels, heads, layers) gives real speedup. Layer dropping is surprisingly effective for LLMs (the middle layers are the most redundant).

Knowledge distillation: train a small student to match a large teacher.

text
L = α·L_task + (1−α)·L_KD
L_KD = T² · KL( softmax(z_teacher/T) ‖ softmax(z_student/T) )

Higher temperature T softens the teacher's distribution, exposing the "dark knowledge" of relative class similarities. The T² factor keeps gradient magnitudes comparable across temperatures.

  • Feature/intermediate distillation (match hidden states, attention maps) usually beats logit-only distillation.
  • For generative models: sequence-level distillation — train the student on the teacher's generated outputs. This is how most small instruct models are made.

Prefer distillation or structured pruning over unstructured pruning if you actually need the model to run faster.

Coding: Quantize/dequantize + distillation KL [TODO · P1]View exercise
  • Prompt: derive symmetric/asymmetric affine qparams, quantize/dequantize per tensor and per channel, then implement softened teacher→student distillation.
  • Shape / cost: quantization is elementwise O(P) plus reductions over the chosen scale axis; logit KD is O(NC).
  • Pitfalls: handle zero dynamic range, integer clipping, zero-point rounding, and scale broadcasting. In PyTorch, kl_div(log_student, teacher_probs) represents KL(teacher || student)—argument order is easy to reverse.
python
def quantize_dequantize(x, bits=8, axis=None, asymmetric=False):
    """TODO: choose scale/zero-point, clamp integer q, then dequantize."""
    raise NotImplementedError

def distillation_loss(student_logits, teacher_logits, temperature):
    log_p_student = F.log_softmax(student_logits / temperature, dim=-1)
    p_teacher = F.softmax(teacher_logits / temperature, dim=-1)
    return F.kl_div(log_p_student, p_teacher, reduction="batchmean") * temperature**2

No local quantization or KD helper exists. The KD snippet is the checked loss direction; adding both implementations and edge-case tests remains [TODO].

10.3 Parameters vs FLOPs vs latency#

  • Parameters → memory footprint.
  • FLOPs → theoretical compute.
  • Latency → what the user experiences.

Lower FLOPs ≠ lower latency. The gap comes from memory bandwidth, arithmetic intensity, kernel launch overhead, operator fusion, and how well the shape maps onto the hardware's tiling. Depthwise convolutions and attention are the canonical examples of low-FLOP, bandwidth-bound operations.

Roofline framing (worth having): arithmetic intensity = FLOPs / bytes moved. Below the machine balance point you're bandwidth-bound and only reducing memory traffic helps; above it you're compute-bound and only reducing FLOPs helps. LLM decode sits far to the left; prefill and convolutions sit further right. Always profile on the target device.

Go deeper: How to Scale Your Model (DeepMind). Part 1 is the cleanest treatment of rooflines and arithmetic intensity; the transformer and inference chapters derive the FLOP/byte accounting for attention, FFN, and KV cache from first principles. The worked exercises ("at what batch size does a matmul become compute-bound on this chip?") are exactly the shape of efficiency-round questions.

10.4 Latency-reduction checklist#

  1. Profile first — find the actual bottleneck, don't guess from parameter count.
  2. Quantize (FP16 → INT8 → INT4 weight-only), checking quality at each step.
  3. Operator fusion (conv+BN+ReLU → one kernel; fused attention).
  4. Structured pruning or distillation to a smaller architecture.
  5. Reduce input resolution, or tile and process regions.
  6. Replace global attention with windowed/local attention; use FlashAttention.
  7. Cache and reuse temporal features across frames (video-specific, big win).
  8. Depthwise separable convolutions — but verify actual latency, not FLOPs.
  9. Avoid dynamic shapes and unsupported ops; they force fallback to CPU.
  10. Batching (throughput) vs single-stream (latency) — know which you're optimizing.
  11. For LLMs: KV cache, continuous batching, speculative decoding, paged attention.

10.5 Deployment stacks#

TargetStackGotchas
Nvidia GPUTensorRT, Triton, TensorRT-LLMop coverage, plugin authoring, engine build time; INT8 calibration
AppleCoreML, ANE, MPS, MLXANE supports a restricted op set — unsupported ops silently fall back to GPU/CPU; fixed shapes preferred; fp16 native
AndroidNNAPI, TFLite, QNN, ExecuTorchhuge device fragmentation
Server LLMvLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLMcontinuous batching, paged attention, prefix caching
On-device LLMllama.cpp / GGUF, MLC, MLX, LLMFarmmemory ceiling, thermal throttling
Cross-platformONNX Runtimeoperator-set version mismatches

"Works offline but fails on device" — the checklist:

  • Unsupported operators → silent CPU fallback → 10× slowdown.
  • Precision mismatch (FP32 offline vs FP16/INT8 on device).
  • Memory pressure / OOM at the target resolution or context length.
  • Thermal throttling — sustained performance is often 50–70% of peak.
  • Preprocessing mismatch: RGB vs YUV, normalization constants, bit depth, resize interpolation, color space.
  • Different batch size, sequence length, or temporal-window assumptions.
  • Camera-pipeline differences: color space, HDR tone mapping, compression artifacts on the input.
  • Dynamic shapes triggering recompilation every call.
11Parallelism3 sections
Chapter link ↗

Chapter guide: Parallelism is not a switch; it partitions tensors across memory, compute, and communication. A complete answer first states what each device retains, then identifies the required collective.

11.1 Collective operations#

CollectiveWhat each rank receivesCommon use
AllReduceThe reduction of all inputs, identical on every deviceDDP gradient sum/average
ReduceScatterIts assigned shard of the reduced resultFSDP/ZeRO sharded gradients
AllGatherThe concatenation of every rank's shardsTemporarily reconstruct sharded parameters/activations
AllToAllA distinct shard from every other rankMoE token dispatch
Send/RecvA point-to-point tensor from an adjacent stagePipeline parallelism

ReduceScatter + AllGather is semantically equivalent to AllReduce, but separating them allows the intermediate result to remain sharded. Every participating rank must call a collective with matching count and dtype; a missing rank can cause the operation to hang.

11.2 Data parallelism and FSDP / ZeRO#

  • DDP: every device holds the complete model and receives a different data shard; gradients are AllReduced during backward. Scaling the batch is simple, but weights, gradients, and optimizer states are replicated, so one device must hold the full state.
  • ZeRO/FSDP: shard optimizer states, gradients, and parameters by stage. Parameters are AllGathered before computation and gradients are ReduceScattered afterward. This saves memory but shifts the problem toward communication, prefetching, and scheduling.
  • Gradient accumulation increases global batch size and reduces optimizer-step frequency, but does not magically shrink the model or activations for one microbatch. Activation checkpointing is a separate axis that exchanges recomputation for memory.

11.3 Tensor, pipeline, sequence, and expert parallelism#

  • Tensor parallelism (TP): split matrices or heads within a layer. Every layer requires collectives, so TP belongs inside a node with fast NVLink; frequent communication performs poorly across a slow network.
  • Pipeline parallelism (PP): split by layers into stages, then use microbatches to fill the pipeline. Communication is less frequent, at the cost of pipeline bubbles, stage imbalance, and a more complex schedule.
  • Sequence/context parallelism: split activations along the token dimension to reduce activation memory for long contexts; attention must still exchange K/V or partial results.
  • Expert parallelism: distribute MoE experts and route tokens with AllToAll; load imbalance and cross-node bandwidth are the main hazards.

Real systems commonly combine three or four parallel dimensions. First satisfy capacity, then keep high-frequency collectives inside the fastest interconnect domain, and finally tune microbatches so compute can overlap communication. Near the strong-scaling limit, adding devices can make training slower.

Primary sources: NCCL collective semantics · Megatron-LM tensor parallelism · GPipe · ZeRO

12Metrics, Evaluation & Debugging5 sections
Chapter link ↗

Chapter guide: Metrics must correspond to the product decision and the independent-sample unit. Rule out data leakage and pipeline bugs before discussing model capacity.

12.1 Classification metrics#

text
Precision = TP/(TP+FP)     of predicted positives, how many are right
Recall    = TP/(TP+FN)     of actual positives, how many did we catch
F1        = 2PR/(P+R)      harmonic mean — punishes a low value in either
  • AUC-ROC: TPR vs FPR across thresholds. 0.5 random, 1.0 perfect. Fine when classes are roughly balanced.
  • AUC-PR: better for imbalanced data — ROC-AUC looks deceptively high when negatives dominate, because FPR barely moves.
  • Calibration: is a predicted 0.8 actually right 80% of the time? Measure with ECE / reliability diagrams. Matters whenever a downstream system thresholds your score — e.g. a brand-conflict check.
Coding: Confusion matrix / precision / recall / F1 / ROC-AUC [READY · P1]View exercise
  • Prompt: compute metrics without sklearn and explain how the answer changes with threshold, class imbalance, and ties.
  • Shape / cost: labels/scores [N]; confusion/P-R-F1 are O(N). The teaching ROC implementation checks all unique thresholds and is up to O(N²) after sorting, rather than the optimal cumulative O(N log N) approach.
  • Pitfalls: choose the positive label explicitly; define zero-denominator behavior; include both ROC endpoints; group equal scores rather than making tie order affect AUC; prefer PR-AUC for extreme imbalance.
python
tp = np.sum((y_pred == pos_label) & (y_true == pos_label))
fp = np.sum((y_pred == pos_label) & (y_true != pos_label))
fn = np.sum((y_pred != pos_label) & (y_true == pos_label))
precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp > 0 else 0.0
recall = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn > 0 else 0.0
f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) \
    if precision + recall > 0 else 0.0

Full implementation (NumPy, including ROC-AUC) · Torch confusion/P-R-F1. PR-AUC and calibration/ECE are [TODO].

12.2 Regression / ranking metrics (for quality models)#

For anything predicting a continuous human score:

  • PLCC (Pearson) after a monotonic logistic fit → accuracy of predicted value.
  • SRCC (Spearman) → do you rank correctly?
  • KRCC (Kendall) → rank, robust to ties.
  • RMSE / MAE in the score's own units.

SRCC vs PLCC is a real decision: SRCC is what you want for "which encode is better"; PLCC for "does this clear our absolute quality bar." Report both. See the UGC-VQA drill in 04 §6.

Coding: PSNR / SSIM / temporal consistency [READY + TOY · P1]View exercise
  • Prompt: implement PSNR from MSE, outline windowed SSIM, and warp adjacent frames with flow before measuring temporal error.
  • Shape / cost: PSNR is linear in pixels; local global-SSIM approximation is also O(HWC); bilinear warping is O(THWC) excluding flow estimation.
  • Pitfalls: state max_val, color space, bit depth, crop, and aggregation convention. Global SSIM is not standard windowed SSIM. The Torch SSIM mixes unbiased variance with population covariance, and its temporal helper creates grid tensors on CPU and has a flow-normalization/sign contract that needs repair.
python
def psnr(img1, img2, max_val=255.0):
    mse = np.mean((img1.astype(float) - img2.astype(float)) ** 2)
    if mse == 0:
        return float("inf")
    return 10 * np.log10(max_val ** 2 / mse)

Full PSNR plus teaching versions of global SSIM/warp (NumPy) · Torch version. PSNR is [READY]; SSIM and temporal warp are [TOY] until the boundaries above are fixed. PLCC/SRCC/KRCC implementations are [TODO].

12.3 Bias-variance#

text
Expected error = Bias² + Variance + Irreducible noise
  • High bias, low variance → too simple, consistently wrong → more capacity, better features.
  • Low bias, high variance → too complex, unstable → regularize, more data, less capacity.

Regularization trades a little bias for a lot of variance reduction — usually a net win.

12.4 Debugging playbook#

Training loss falls, validation is bad:

  1. Overfitting (model too large / data too small).
  2. Data leakage — random frame split instead of scene/clip split for video; duplicate items across splits; a feature that encodes the label.
  3. Train/val domain mismatch (different camera, compression level, scene type, device).
  4. Augmentation applied at train but not val, or differently.
  5. Metric computed inconsistently (PSNR on YUV vs displayed RGB; different crop/border handling).
  6. Label or preprocessing inconsistency between the two paths.
  7. Temporal leakage — future frames visible during training.

Loss doesn't decrease at all:

  • LR too high (diverging) or too low (stuck); check by overfitting a single batch to ~zero loss — if you can't, the bug is in the model or data pipeline, not the optimizer.
  • Labels misaligned/shuffled relative to inputs.
  • Missing/incorrect normalization.
  • Dead ReLUs / bad init.
  • Wrong loss reduction (mean vs sum) interacting with LR.
  • Gradients not flowing (a detach, a no_grad, a frozen module you meant to train).

Good PSNR, bad visual quality: L2 predicts the conditional mean → blur. PSNR is blind to sharpness, texture realism, and temporal stability. Fix with perceptual/adversarial/diffusion losses; always look at the images.

Loss spikes / NaN mid-training: LR too high, bad batch, fp16 overflow (switch to bf16), division by near-zero in a normalization, or exploding attention logits (add QK-norm or logit soft-capping). Standard mitigation: gradient clipping, skip batches with non-finite loss, checkpoint and resume from before the spike.

12.5 Evaluating generative and LLM outputs#

  • Automatic: perplexity (only meaningful within a fixed tokenizer), task benchmarks, exact match, pass@k for code.
  • LLM-as-judge: cheap and scalable, but biased toward length, position (first option), and its own style. Mitigate with pairwise comparison, position swapping, and a rubric. Always validate against human labels on a subset.
  • Human eval: the ground truth. Same rigor as subjective video testing — multiple raters, inter-rater agreement (Krippendorff's α / Cohen's κ), confidence intervals.
  • Benchmark contamination: assume any public benchmark is partly in the pretraining data. Prefer held-out, freshly collected, or private evaluation sets — which is exactly the argument for building your own benchmark, as you did.
Coding: Classic ML + preprocessing [TOY · P2]View exercise
  • Prompt: vectorize KNN, implement K-means with an empty-cluster rule, normalize from training statistics only, and shuffle/split reproducibly.
  • Shape / cost: brute-force KNN is O(MND) for M queries and N training points; K-means is O(iterations·N·K·D).
  • Pitfalls: avoid leakage by fitting normalization on train only; video splits must be by scene/clip rather than adjacent frames; recompute final K-means labels if the iteration budget ends immediately after a centroid update.
python
dists = np.linalg.norm(X[:, None] - centroids[None], axis=2)  # [N, K]
labels = np.argmin(dists, axis=1)
new_centroids = np.array([
    X[labels == i].mean(axis=0) if (labels == i).any() else centroids[i]
    for i in range(k)
])

Existing implementations and data utilities (NumPy) · Torch subset. KNN and the basic utilities are useful interview baselines, but K-means can return labels from the previous centroids when max_iter expires immediately after an update, so the grouped entry remains [TOY] until fixed.
